Christians who recognize spiritual realities beneath visible events.
Followers of Jesus who refuse to allow temporary chaos to distract them from eternal truth.
The question is not whether we live in difficult times.
The question is whether we understand them.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy of our generation is not moral decline.
Never before have so many people been connected while feeling so alone.
Never before have so many voices spoken while so little truth is heard.
Never before have people consumed so much content while understanding so little purpose.
And somewhere in the noise, many believers have stopped listening for God.
The sons of Issachar remind us that discernment requires more than awareness.
Because understanding the times begins with understanding the Author of time.
No amount of news analysis can replace prayer.
No cultural expertise can substitute for Scripture.
No intellectual brilliance can produce what only the Holy Spirit reveals.
The men of Issachar knew what Israel should do because they first understood what God was doing.
The believers who will impact this generation most powerfully will not necessarily be the loudest.
They will be the most discerning.
Not those who chase every trend.
Those who remain anchored in Christ.
Not those who predict the future.
Those who trust the One who holds it.
Yet there is another layer to this story that makes it even more personal.
The tribe of Issachar was not famous for military dominance.
Because usefulness in God's Kingdom has never depended on status.
Many believers disqualify themselves because they feel ordinary.
But Scripture tells a different story.
The Gospel itself is the story of God taking ordinary people and rewriting extraordinary futures.
It is the story of scandal becoming grace.
The Apostle Paul understood this personally.
A man marked by scandal became a monument of grace.
The same Christ who transformed Paul still transforms lives today.
Perhaps that is why the story of Issachar remains so powerful.
It reminds us that God is not searching for celebrities.
The Church does not need more trend followers.
More believers who know God's Word.
More Christians who recognize spiritual seasons.
More disciples who can lovingly guide others through confusion.
More followers of Jesus who stand firm when culture shifts beneath their feet.
Because every generation reaches moments when understanding the times becomes essential.
And this generation is no exception.
The question is not whether God is moving.
The question is whether we are paying attention.
Perhaps you feel overwhelmed by everything happening around you.
Perhaps you look at the world and wonder what comes next.
Perhaps you feel exhausted by constant uncertainty.
God has never lost control of history.
The same Lord who guided Israel through transition still governs every moment today.
The same Christ who fulfilled prophecy still rules over nations.
The same Savior who conquered death still builds His Church.
And the same Holy Spirit who gave discernment to Issachar still grants wisdom to believers who seek Him.
If this message stirred something inside you, do not simply move on.
Ask God to make you a person who understands the times and knows what obedience requires.
What do you believe God is teaching His people in this generation?
Your testimony may encourage someone fighting a battle you cannot see.
If your desire is truly to glorify God, strengthen Gospel outreach, equip believers, and help others encounter the life-changing message of Christ, your support becomes part of that Kingdom work.
Because one generation's discernment can shape another generation's destiny.
And sometimes the difference between confusion and clarity is simply recognizing that God is still speaking.
The people who change history are often the people who first learn to recognize heaven's timing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF PRISCILLA
paragraphs: The Woman Who Quietly Helped Shape the Early Church
And sometimes the people who change the world are not the ones standing behind pulpits, sitting on thrones, or having books named after them.
Sometimes they are the ones opening their homes.
And disappearing from the spotlight before anyone notices what they just accomplished.
Priscilla was one of those people.
Even fewer understand why the Holy Spirit preserved her name in Scripture.
Yet hidden within the pages of the New Testament is the remarkable account of a woman whose influence quietly reached some of the most important leaders of the early Church.
A woman who risked her life for the Gospel.
A woman who helped disciple one of Christianity's greatest preachers.
A woman whose ministry challenges modern believers to rethink what true spiritual influence really looks like.
This is the untold story of Priscilla.
And before it ends, you may find yourself asking a question that changes everything:
What if the greatest ministry is not the one everyone sees?
What if the greatest ministry is the one Heaven remembers?
The First Time We Meet Priscilla
The first appearance of Priscilla occurs in Acts 18.
Luke introduces her alongside her husband Aquila.
"They found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla..." (Acts 18:2)
In ancient culture, husbands were normally mentioned first.
Yet throughout the New Testament, Priscilla's name frequently appears before Aquila's.
This has caused biblical scholars for centuries to ask why.
Some suggest she may have come from a prominent Roman family.
Others believe she possessed exceptional spiritual maturity.
Still others think her ministry role was especially influential.
While certainty is impossible, one thing is undeniable:
The Holy Spirit repeatedly preserved her name in a position rarely granted to women in ancient historical records.
That should make us pay attention.
Priscilla and Aquila were not living comfortable lives when Paul met them.
The Roman historian Suetonius records that Emperor Claudius expelled many Jews from Rome around AD 49.
Many believers today know that feeling.
Priscilla understood what it felt like to have life interrupted.
Yet what looked like disaster became divine positioning.
Had Rome never expelled them, they might never have met Paul.
And if they never met Paul, countless lives might have remained untouched.
Sometimes God is working through the very disruption we are praying Him to remove.
Acts 18 tells us Paul lived and worked with Priscilla and Aquila because they shared the same trade.
Literally, one who makes tents or leather shelters.
Conversations about Christ while earning a living.
Just faithful believers doing ordinary work for an extraordinary Kingdom.
Many modern Christians underestimate the holiness of ordinary faithfulness.
Yet Priscilla reminds us that some of God's greatest work happens in workshops, offices, kitchens, classrooms, construction sites, and living rooms.
Before she ever taught anyone publicly, she served God faithfully in everyday life.
The Church in Her Living Room
One detail about Priscilla's life appears repeatedly.
"Greet also the church in their house."
The word "ἐκκλησία" (ekklēsia) became the New Testament term for church.
But originally it referred to a gathered assembly.
The Church was not a building.
And Priscilla opened her home so those people could gather.
Hosting Christians could attract unwanted attention.
Yet she opened her doors anyway.
Priscilla created space where ministry could happen.
The Day She Corrected a Famous Preacher
Then comes one of the most fascinating moments in the entire New Testament.
Acts 18 introduces a brilliant preacher named Apollos.
"He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say they humiliated him.
It does not say they embarrassed him publicly.
It does not say they attacked him.
It says they took him aside.
The Greek phrase "ἀκριβέστερον" (akribe steron) means "more accurately" or "more precisely."
Priscilla helped strengthen a gifted preacher's understanding of truth.
And because she did, Apollos went on to become one of the most influential Christian leaders in the first century.
A woman many Christians barely remember helped disciple a preacher many Christians still study.
What if some of the most important people you will ever influence are not famous yet?
What if God places future leaders in your path?
Will you care enough to help them grow?
Risking Her Life for the Gospel
Paul later writes these astonishing words:
The Greek literally suggests exposing one's neck to danger.
We are never told exactly what happened.
Priscilla was willing to suffer for Christ.
She was willing to suffer for God's servants.
She was willing to place herself in danger for the Kingdom.
What are we willing to risk?
What are we willing to sacrifice?
How valuable is the Gospel to us?
Because for Priscilla, Jesus was worth everything.
The Forgotten Heroes of the Kingdom
There is no recorded sermon from Priscilla.
No biblical book bears her name.
No miracle is directly attributed to her.
No chapter centers exclusively on her story.
But her influence echoes for centuries.
Perhaps that is why her story matters so much today.
We live in a culture obsessed with visibility.
"And your Father who sees in secret will reward you."
Much of her work happened behind closed doors.
What Her Story Means for Us
They wonder whether their service matters.
Priscilla's story answers with a resounding yes.
The Kingdom is built not only by those standing on stages.
It is built by faithful servants whose names may never trend on earth but are known in Heaven.
And perhaps that is the greatest lesson hidden inside the story of Priscilla.
You do not have to be famous to be fruitful.
You do not have to be visible to be valuable.
You do not have to stand in front of crowds to change eternity.
Sometimes the people who change the world are simply the people who make room for God to work.
Maybe you are tempted to quit.
The same God who saw Priscilla sees you.
The same God who used Priscilla can use you.
And the same Jesus who transformed the Roman world through hidden servants is still doing it today.
One day, many of Heaven's greatest heroes will be people earth barely noticed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS ASK BLIND BARTIMAEUS WHAT HE WANTED?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS ASK BLIND BARTIMAEUS WHAT HE WANTED?
And hidden inside one of the shortest conversations in the Gospel of Mark is a question so shocking that many readers pass over it without ever realizing its depth.
A blind man is sitting beside the road.
Yet when Jesus finally stands before him, He asks:
“What do you want me to do for you?”
At first glance, the question feels almost absurd.
Why would Jesus ask a blind man what he wanted?
Couldn't the Son of God already see his need?
Didn't Jesus already know exactly what he was going to ask?
The answer reveals something breathtaking about the heart of Christ.
And if you have ever felt unseen, unheard, overlooked, forgotten, ashamed, broken, or trapped inside a life you never wanted, this story may change the way you understand Jesus forever.
Jesus is leaving Jericho on His final journey toward Jerusalem.
The weight of redemption is drawing near.
Yet Jesus stops for one blind beggar sitting in the dust.
The name Bartimaeus comes from the Aramaic prefix “Bar,” meaning “son of.”
This detail is remarkable because Mark rarely names those Jesus heals.
The Holy Spirit preserved his name.
Because Jesus does not define people by their wounds.
Many people spend their lives believing their failures are their identity.
The Gospel has always been about restoring names that sin tried to erase.
As Bartimaeus hears that Jesus is passing by, something ignites inside him.
“And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, ‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!’”
This is not merely a request.
It is a confession of faith.
“Son of David” is a Messianic title.
In Hebrew thought, this points directly to God's promised King.
While many people around Jesus still struggled to understand who He was, a blind beggar could see what others could not.
Sometimes suffering produces a clarity that comfort never can.
“Son of David, have mercy on me.”
The word ἐλέησόν (eleēson) carries profound meaning.
Mercy that enters the mess instead of standing at a distance.
Bartimaeus was not demanding a miracle.
He was appealing to the character of God.
And then something painfully familiar happens.
The crowd tries to silence him.
“Many rebuked him and told him to be quiet.”
The world often tells desperate people to stay silent.
Don't let anyone know you're hurting.
His desperation became louder than their criticism.
His faith became stronger than their rejection.
His hope became greater than their shame.
The One holding the universe together by His power stops for a blind beggar no one else wanted to hear.
The King of Kings pauses for a man sitting in the dust.
The Creator listens to a cry everyone else wanted silenced.
The same people who tried to silence him now tell him:
“Take heart. Get up. He is calling you.”
Human approval is one of the most unstable things in the world.
The next moment they celebrate you.
His love was never based on the crowd's opinion.
“Throwing aside his cloak, he jumped up and came to Jesus.”
This detail is easy to miss.
But it is loaded with significance.
For a blind beggar, the cloak was more than clothing.
Perhaps the very garment spread before him each day to collect alms.
Yet when Jesus calls, he leaves it behind.
Faith often requires releasing what has become comfortable.
Even when comfort is all you have left.
“What do you want me to do for you?”
“What do you desire that I should do for you?”
Because Jesus is not interested in treating people like projects.
The question is not for Jesus' information.
But Bartimaeus needed to articulate it.
Needed to bring it into the light.
Needed to voice the hope he had carried inside his heart for years.
There is something transformative about speaking your deepest need before God.
Prayer is opening ourselves to God.
Jesus asks the same question today.
Not because He does not know.
Because He wants relationship rather than robotic religion.
Many people spend years around church language while never honestly bringing their wounds before Christ.
What do you want Me to do for you?
What do you need from Me?
Before Bartimaeus receives physical sight, he demonstrates spiritual sight.
He already knows who Jesus is.
“Go. Your faith has made you well.”
The verb σέσωκέν (sesōken) comes from σῴζω (sōzō).
A word meaning not merely healed.
The miracle was never just about eyes.
And immediately Bartimaeus receives his sight.
Yet the story does not end there.
“Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road.”
That is the evidence of true transformation.
Many people want Jesus to change their circumstances.
The miracle became the doorway to discipleship.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because every believer has been Bartimaeus.
The Gospel is the story of Christ stopping for people the world overlooks.
People everyone else had already written off.
Maybe you've been carrying wounds nobody knows.
Maybe you've learned to survive but not truly live.
Maybe you've become so accustomed to spiritual blindness that you've forgotten what hope feels like.
What do you want Me to do for you?
And when you bring your need before Him, you will discover what Bartimaeus discovered beside that road long ago.
Jesus is still stopping for people.
If this spoke to something deep inside your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What would your answer be if Jesus asked you today, “What do you want Me to do for you?”
Your story may encourage someone else more than you realize.
If you desire to glorify God through helping spread the Gospel, supporting this ministry and sharing its content are meaningful ways to participate in that mission.
The same Jesus who stopped for Bartimaeus is still stopping for people today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Man Who Lent Jesus a Tomb
paragraphs:
The Man Who Lent Jesus a Tomb
The Borrowed Grave That Changed Every Grave Forever
Not because death had touched it.
But because it had never been meant for Him.

Before dawn broke over Jerusalem, before angels shook the earth, before history split itself into “before” and “after,” there was a silent tomb carved into rock. A wealthy man's tomb. New. Untouched. Reserved for a future that suddenly would never arrive as planned.
Fewer remember the man who provided the tomb.
Yet without him, one of the most profound demonstrations of God's sovereignty, prophecy, courage, grace, and redemption would have unfolded differently.
Not Joseph the earthly father of Jesus.
A man hidden in the shadows until the darkest moment in history demanded that he step into the light.

And in a Gospel filled with fishermen, zealots, tax collectors, prostitutes, religious leaders, Roman governors, and crowds, Joseph appears almost unexpectedly—as though Heaven had been quietly preparing him for one sacred assignment.
But that simple act reveals something astonishing.
Because Joseph's story is not ultimately about a tomb.
It is about what happens when grace rewrites a life.
It is about how God uses ordinary people to participate in extraordinary redemption.
And it is about how one borrowed grave became proof that Jesus never intended to stay dead.

The Gospel writers tell us that Joseph was a wealthy man (Matthew 27:57), a respected member of the council (Mark 15:43), a good and righteous man who had not consented to the condemnation of Jesus (Luke 23:50–51), and a disciple of Jesus who had previously followed Him secretly for fear of the Jewish authorities (John 19:38).
How many believers know exactly what that feels like?
Yet remaining silent because the cost feels too high.
The Sanhedrin held influence, reputation, social standing, and religious authority.
To publicly identify with Jesus after the crucifixion could destroy everything Joseph had built.
Yet something happened between the trial and the burial.
When nearly everyone else disappeared, Joseph stepped forward.
The Greek text of Mark 15:43 says Joseph "τολμήσας" (tolmēsas) went to Pilate.
The word carries the sense of daring, courage, boldness.
The disciple who once hid now stood publicly before the Roman governor requesting the body of an executed criminal.
At the exact moment when following Jesus appeared most hopeless, Joseph's faith became most visible.
Isn't that often how God works?
Sometimes courage is not proven when crowds are cheering.
Sometimes courage is proven when the crowd has left.
When there is nothing to gain.
When there is everything to lose.
Joseph walked into Pilate's presence knowing that every eye could now connect him to Jesus.
"He was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with the rich in His death" (Isaiah 53:9).
The Hebrew text contains the remarkable phrase:
"With a rich man in His death."
Hundreds of years before Joseph was born.
Hundreds of years before Rome existed.
God had already written Joseph into the story.
Joseph believed he owned a tomb.
In reality, God had reserved it.
What Joseph viewed as his possession was actually part of Heaven's plan.
How much of what we call ours has actually been entrusted to us for God's purposes?
Joseph teaches us that stewardship is often revealed through surrender.
Rock-hewn burial chambers were signs of significant wealth.
This was not a spare cave.
Not because he expected a return.
Not because he knew Easter Sunday was coming.
And grace often asks us to place valuable things into God's hands without demanding explanations.
Then comes one of the most beautiful ironies in Scripture.
Because Jesus only needed it for a weekend.
The grave was borrowed because death itself was about to become temporary.
Every funeral humanity had ever known carried the same painful message:
But when Jesus entered Joseph's tomb, He transformed the meaning of every grave that would follow.
The resurrection was not merely an event.
Death would no longer have the final word.
The Apostle Paul later celebrated this victory:
"Death has been swallowed up in victory."
The Greek text of 1 Corinthians 15:54 uses the phrase:

"κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος"
(katepothē ho thanatos eis nikos)
Joseph could not have fully understood it while the stone was being rolled into place.
The body of Jesus wrapped in linen.
How many people today stand beside situations that appear hopeless?
Joseph's tomb reminds us that God often performs His greatest work inside places that appear completely sealed.
The stone was never a problem for God.
The darkness was never a problem for God.
The grave was never a problem for God.
And whatever tomb-like circumstance you are facing today is not beyond His power either.
Because the story of Jesus has always been the story of God bringing life where death appears to have won.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
The cross itself was a scandal.
Paul would later describe Christ crucified as a stumbling block and foolishness to many.
Yet God transformed the greatest injustice in human history into the greatest display of love the world has ever seen.
Only God writes stories like that.
Only God takes execution and turns it into salvation.
Only God takes betrayal and turns it into redemption.
Only God takes graves and turns them into testimonies.
Only God takes sinners and turns them into saints.
Only God takes your story and rewrites it through Jesus Christ.
Perhaps that is why Joseph's story continues to resonate so deeply.
Many believers see themselves in him.
Just ordinary people trying to follow Jesus while wrestling with fear.
And yet Joseph reminds us that your defining moment may still be ahead of you.
Your greatest act of faithfulness may not be behind you.
Your most courageous obedience may still be waiting.
Your story is not determined by how long you remained silent.
Your story is determined by what you do when Jesus calls you forward.
The man who once followed secretly became forever remembered publicly.
Not because he preached a sermon.
Not because he performed a miracle.
Not because he led an army.
But because he surrendered what he had to the Savior.
And that is still how God works today.
The Kingdom advances through surrendered people.
People who offer what they have.
People who stop asking, "What will this cost me?"
And start asking, "How can this glorify Christ?"

If this article has strengthened your faith, challenged your heart, deepened your understanding of Scripture, or helped you see Jesus more clearly, consider becoming part of the mission that helps bring biblical truth, discipleship resources, Christ-centered teaching, and Gospel-centered storytelling to more people around the world.
If we truly desire to glorify God, supporting Gospel-centered ministry is not merely a transaction—it is participation in Kingdom work.
Someone scrolling today may be standing beside a tomb they believe is the end of their story. Let them discover what Joseph discovered.
The stone is never the end when Jesus is involved.
What tomb has God asked you to trust Him with?
The tomb Joseph surrendered became the stage for the greatest victory in history.
Perhaps the thing you're afraid to place in God's hands is where your miracle is waiting.
Because graves are temporary when the Author of Life walks in.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DAY GOD TRIED TO KILL MOSES
paragraphs: THE DAY GOD TRIED TO KILL MOSES
Some passages in Scripture feel safe.
And then there are passages that stop you cold.
Passages that seem to shatter everything you thought you understood about God.
“On the way, at a lodging place, the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.”
That is not a verse most people frame on their wall.
God had just called Moses from the burning bush.
Promised to use him to confront Pharaoh and liberate Israel.
Yet suddenly, in the darkness of a desert journey, God Himself appears ready to kill the very man He had chosen.
What happened between the burning bush and Egypt?
Why would the God who called Moses now stand against him?
And what does this terrifying encounter reveal about our own lives today?
To understand the moment, we must first understand the man.
Moses was not standing before God as a perfect servant.
He was a complicated mixture of faith and failure.
For forty years he had lived in Midian after killing an Egyptian.
From the flames of the bush, God declared His covenant faithfulness and His intention to rescue Israel.
Yet despite all his objections, God remained patient.
Moses would lead God's people out of bondage.
But there was one hidden problem.
Something Moses had apparently tolerated for years.
Something no one in Egypt knew.
Something that would never appear on a résumé.
His son had not been circumcised.
At first glance, that may seem insignificant to modern readers.
But in Scripture, circumcision was never merely a medical procedure.
It was the sign God gave Abraham.
“This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised.”
The Hebrew word for covenant is בְּרִית (berith).
A covenant was not a casual agreement.
It was a binding relationship established by God Himself.
To reject the covenant sign was to reject covenant loyalty.
“Any uncircumcised male... shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant.”
Moses was about to represent God's covenant before an entire nation.
Yet apparently he was neglecting the covenant within his own household.
The issue was not merely external ritual.
The issue was whether the messenger himself would bow before the message he carried.
“The LORD met him and sought to kill him.”
The Hebrew language intentionally communicates danger and urgency.
The God of grace is also the God of holiness.
The God who delivers slaves is also the God who refuses compromise.
But covenant obedience is often where enthusiasm disappears.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a sobering truth.
God cares more about our character than our platform.
More about our obedience than our influence.
But being chosen did not exempt him from accountability.
“Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, ‘Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!’”
Scholars debate several elements of the passage.
But the central point remains unmistakable.
The covenant sign was finally administered.
The entire encounter exposes a reality many modern Christians desperately need to hear.
Private disobedience eventually collides with public calling.
God is not impressed by ministry while covenant faithfulness is neglected.
The Lord who sees the crowds also sees the secrets.
The Lord who opens doors also examines hearts.
The Lord who appoints leaders also disciplines His children.
The frightening scene at the lodging place is not evidence of divine cruelty.
It is evidence of divine consistency.
God was preparing Moses for one of the greatest assignments in redemptive history.
And before confronting Pharaoh, Moses himself had to be confronted.
Before leading a nation, he had to submit.
Before delivering others, he had to obey.
Jacob wrestled before he walked differently.
Isaiah was cleansed before he preached.
Peter was broken before he strengthened his brothers.
Paul was blinded before he truly saw.
God often does His deepest work in private places long before He works through us publicly.
And perhaps that is why this strange story remains so relevant.
Many people today want God to change their circumstances.
But God first wants to transform them.
We ask Him to bless our plans.
He asks us to surrender our hearts.
We ask Him to rewrite our story.
He asks us to trust the Author.
The deeper message hidden within Exodus 4 is not merely about circumcision.
It is about the danger of compartmentalized faith.
It is about the impossibility of truly following God while reserving areas of life for ourselves.
The New Testament takes this truth even further.
Physical circumcision pointed toward a deeper spiritual reality.
The Greek phrase is περιτομὴ καρδίας (peritomē kardias).
God has always been after more than external compliance.
This is where the story suddenly becomes personal.
Most of us are not carrying an uncircumcised son through the wilderness.
But many of us carry hidden compromises.
Areas we assume God will overlook because we are otherwise serving Him.
The terrifying beauty of Exodus 4 is that God loves His people too much to leave them there.
The same God who stopped Moses is the God who sent Moses.
The same God who confronted him is the God who used him.
The same God who threatened judgment is the God who delivered a nation through him.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ fulfilled perfectly what Moses never could.
Where Moses compromised, Christ remained faithful.
Where Moses deserved judgment, Christ bore judgment.
At the cross, holiness and mercy embraced.
The One who had every right to condemn became the sacrifice that saves.
This is why the story ultimately points beyond Moses.
And perhaps someone reading this today feels the weight of God's conviction.
You know there are places in your life where God has been calling you deeper.
You know there are areas where surrender has been delayed.
You know there are conversations you've avoided.
The God who confronts is also the God who restores.
The God who exposes is also the God who heals.
The God who disciplines is also the God who redeems.
The lodging place was not the end of Moses' story.
What looked like destruction became preparation.
What looked like judgment became mercy.
What looked like scandal became grace.
Because that is what God does.
He takes broken people, confronts what must change, and rewrites their story for His glory.
Maybe that is your story too.
Maybe the place you fear most is actually where grace is waiting.
Maybe the confrontation you've resisted is the doorway to freedom.
Maybe the conviction you've been feeling is evidence that God has not given up on you.
And maybe, just maybe, the chapter that feels like the end is actually where redemption begins.
What area of your life has God been calling you to surrender?
Supporting this ministry is one practical way believers can participate in spreading biblical truth and glorifying God through Gospel-centered media.
The God who confronted Moses in the darkness was already preparing him for deliverance in the daylight.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Gideon’s Real Battle Wasn’t Midian
paragraphs:
Gideon’s Real Battle Wasn’t Midian
The enemy standing in front of him looked terrifying. The enemy living inside him looked impossible.
There are battles that make headlines.
And there are battles that make history.
The battle against Midian was the one everyone saw.
The battle inside Gideon was the one God cared about most.
Most Christians know Gideon as the reluctant warrior who defeated an army with only three hundred men. We remember the torches. The jars. The trumpets. The impossible victory.
But if that is all we see, we miss the very heart of the story.
Because Gideon's real battle was never Midian.
It was the scandal of believing what God said about him.
And if we're honest, that's where many of us live today.
We pray for God to remove the Midians around us while He is trying to heal the Midian within us.
The story begins during one of Israel's darkest periods. The people had abandoned the Lord and embraced idolatry. As a result, Midian oppressed Israel for seven devastating years.
Scripture tells us the Israelites hid in caves and mountain strongholds. They planted crops only to watch Midianites swarm in and destroy everything.
Imagine working all year for a harvest that never reaches your table.
Imagine wondering if God has forgotten you.
The Hebrew text says he was threshing wheat in a winepress (Judges 6:11).
A winepress was not designed for threshing wheat.
A place where a frightened man could work without being noticed.
Yet that is exactly where God shows up.
The Angel of the LORD appears and says:
"The LORD is with you, mighty warrior." (Judges 6:12)
Because Gideon is none of those things.
Yet God speaks to him according to who He is creating him to become.
This is one of the great themes of Scripture.
God often introduces people to themselves before they know who they are.
Abram becomes Abraham before nations exist.
Simon becomes Peter before stability appears.
Saul becomes Paul before ministry begins.
And Gideon becomes a mighty warrior while hiding in a winepress.
The world identifies you by your current condition.
God identifies you by His redemptive intention.
That truth alone has rescued countless believers from despair.
Because many followers of Christ are still living in winepresses.
They have accepted labels given by failure.
The God who calls things into existence that do not yet exist has not lost His ability to rewrite stories.
And honestly, that's what makes him relatable.
He asks questions many believers secretly ask today.
"If the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us?" (Judges 6:13)
That question has echoed through generations.
God is not threatened by honest questions.
What He opposes is unbelief that refuses to listen to His answer.
God does not begin by explaining every circumstance.
Because sometimes God's answer is not an explanation.
Before Gideon can confront Midian, however, another enemy must fall.
This is where the story becomes deeply personal.
God's first assignment is not military.
Before national revival comes household repentance.
Before public victory comes private obedience.
Before God changes a nation, He often changes a heart.
Gideon tears down the altar under cover of darkness because he is still afraid.
The Bible does not glorify perfection.
And that gives hope to every believer who thinks courage means feeling fearless.
Biblical courage has never been the absence of fear.
The New Testament echoes this reality.
The Greek word for weakness is:
God's power is not hindered by weakness.
It is often revealed through it.
That truth reaches its ultimate fulfillment at the Cross.
Jesus did not save humanity through worldly displays of power.
He saved humanity through sacrificial surrender.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like scandal became grace.
What looked like an ending became redemption.
This is why Gideon's story ultimately points beyond Gideon.
Every judge in Israel was imperfect.
Only Jesus stands as the perfect Deliverer.
The One who faced not merely human enemies but sin, death, and hell itself.
The One who never doubted the Father's will.
The One who never hid in fear.
The One who conquered through complete obedience.
When Gideon eventually assembles an army, something unexpected happens.
From a military perspective, it is madness.
From a Kingdom perspective, it is revelation.
"Lest Israel boast against me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.'" (Judges 7:2)
Human pride is one of the greatest obstacles to spiritual transformation.
God often reduces our dependence on ourselves so we can discover dependence on Him.
Many believers spend years praying for greater strength.
Sometimes God answers by revealing greater weakness.
Because self-sufficiency cannot sustain spiritual victory.
The Gospel was never designed to make us impressive.
It was designed to make Christ visible.
And so Gideon marches with three hundred men carrying jars, torches, and trumpets.
And when the moment comes, God brings confusion into the enemy camp.
The victory belongs entirely to the Lord.
Grace leaves no room for boasting.
Perhaps that is why Gideon's story continues to resonate centuries later.
Because most of us know what it feels like to stand in a winepress.
We know the exhausting pressure of trying to become someone we don't feel capable of being.
Yet God still approaches frightened people and calls them by redeemed names.
The greatest miracle in Gideon's story was never the defeat of Midian.
The greatest miracle was the transformation of Gideon himself.
And maybe that is the miracle God wants to perform in us.
Because the enemy in front of you may not be your greatest battle.
The fear within you might be.
The shame you've carried for years might be.
The lie you've believed about yourself might be.
But Jesus Christ is still rewriting stories.
And no amount of failure has the authority to overrule His grace.
Maybe that's why you're still reading.
Maybe this article found you in your own winepress.
Maybe you've been hiding behind a smile.
And maybe today the voice of God is breaking through all the noise.
Not calling you what you've been.
Calling you what His grace can make you.
If this stirred something deep inside your spirit, don't ignore it.
Not because content matters more than the Gospel.
But because Gospel-centered ministry is sustained by believers who choose to participate in the mission.
If you want to help spread biblical truth, discipleship, encouragement, evangelism, and Christ-centered transformation to more people around the world, your support helps make that possible.
Because one encounter with grace can change a life forever.
And one shared testimony can become someone else's rescue story.
The same God who found Gideon in a winepress is still finding people in broken places today.
The battle that feels impossible may be the very place where God introduces you to the person His grace has been creating all along.
The God who called Gideon by his future is still calling people beyond their past.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT DO ANGELS ACTUALLY LOOK LIKE?
paragraphs: WHAT DO ANGELS ACTUALLY LOOK LIKE?
The Images That Shatter Everything We Thought We Knew
Most people think they know what angels look like.
The kind of figure that belongs on a Christmas card, a church mural, or the cover of a children's Bible.
That image is almost nowhere in Scripture.
And once you actually read the Bible for yourself, the real question is not why angels look beautiful.
The real question is why almost every person who encounters one is immediately overwhelmed with fear.
Something about biblical angels is so powerful, so otherworldly, so overwhelming that one phrase echoes throughout Scripture like a thunderclap:
Why would angels repeatedly say that?
Because whatever stood before human eyes was far more terrifying—and far more glorious—than popular imagination has ever captured.
The Bible does not present angels as cute decorations around heaven.
It presents them as servants of the King of Kings, warriors of divine authority, living manifestations of God's power, holiness, judgment, and glory.
To understand what angels actually look like, we have to set aside centuries of artwork and return to the text itself.
Back to the eyewitnesses who fell on their faces before what they saw.
The First Surprise: "Angel" Is Not a Description
The Hebrew word most commonly translated as angel is:
Neither word tells us what an angel looks like.
It describes what an angel does.
The Bible often focuses more on an angel's mission than its appearance.
Many angels appeared so human that people initially did not realize they were looking at heavenly beings.
When Abraham was visited in Genesis 18, he saw what appeared to be men.
When Lot encountered angels in Sodom, they appeared as men.
"Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."
That statement only makes sense if angels can appear completely human.
Yet that is only part of the story.
Because there are other angels whose appearance is so astonishing that language itself struggles to describe them.
The Angel That Made Daniel Collapse
The prophet Daniel records one of the most detailed angelic encounters in Scripture.

"I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist. His body was like beryl, his face like the appearance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of burnished bronze, and the sound of his words like the sound of a multitude."
This is not a fragile figure.
The experience nearly destroyed him physically.
That reaction appears again and again throughout Scripture whenever humans encounter heavenly glory.
The Cherubim: Nothing Like Renaissance Paintings
Perhaps no angels have been misunderstood more than cherubim.
Today, the word cherub usually brings to mind a chubby baby with tiny wings.
The Bible presents something entirely different.
Cherubim first appear guarding Eden after humanity's fall.
Genesis 3:24 says God stationed cherubim and a flaming sword at the entrance of the Garden.
Already they are presented as guardians of divine holiness.
Ezekiel 1 describes beings with four faces.
Their legs gleam like polished bronze.
Their appearance is beyond ordinary categories.
Ezekiel repeatedly struggles to explain what he is seeing.
He is reaching for language because earthly vocabulary cannot fully contain heavenly realities.
They are symbols of divine authority.
All creation represented around the throne of God.
Another class of heavenly beings appears in Isaiah 6.
Isaiah sees them surrounding God's throne.
With two they cover their faces.
With two they cover their feet.
It is as though language itself reaches its limit before God's holiness.
Isaiah does not celebrate the experience.
One glimpse of God's holiness exposes every hidden impurity in the human heart.
The closer we come to God, the less impressed we become with ourselves.
Then comes perhaps the most astonishing vision in all Scripture.
Many scholars associate these mysterious beings with God's heavenly throne chariot imagery.
The God who sees all also judges all.
The God who sees all also loves completely.
The Eyes of Heaven Never Blink.
When John receives the Revelation of Jesus Christ, heavenly imagery reaches another level.
Revelation describes living creatures around God's throne.
John also sees mighty angels whose voices shake heaven and earth.
One angel places a foot on the sea and another on the land.
Another appears wrapped in cloud, crowned with a rainbow, with a face like the sun.
Again and again the descriptions communicate one truth:
These beings belong to a realm infinitely greater than our own.
The point is not to satisfy curiosity.
The point is to magnify God.
Every true angel points beyond itself.
One of the clearest signs of a genuine angel appears in Revelation 22.
They never redirect glory toward themselves.
The moment a spiritual experience elevates the creature above the Creator, something has gone terribly wrong.
The Most Important Truth About Angels
The greatest surprise in Scripture is not what angels look like.
The greatest surprise is how little the Bible focuses on them compared to Jesus.
Entire industries have been built around fascination with angels.
Meanwhile Scripture repeatedly redirects our attention.
Every road leads back to Christ.
The Bible is not an angel-centered story.
Many people spend their lives searching for angels while ignoring the Savior whom angels worship.
That is like becoming fascinated by the King's servants while refusing to meet the King.
For now, we see through a glass dimly.
But one day every believer will stand before realities that exceed imagination.
The redeemed gathered from every tribe and tongue.
And at the center of it all—not the angels.
The Savior whose scars purchased eternity.
But they are not the reason heaven is beautiful.
And perhaps that is why every true encounter with heaven ultimately leaves people talking less about angels and more about the One seated upon the throne.
Because when you finally see the glory of Christ, everything else becomes background.
One day the fear of the unknown will vanish, and the face you longed to see will be standing before you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PHARISEE INSIDE ALL OF US
paragraphs: THE PHARISEE INSIDE ALL OF US
The man stood in the temple with clean hands, polished theology, and a reputation everyone admired.
Beside him stood another man who could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
One thanked God that he was not like sinners.
The other simply whispered, "God, be merciful to me."
And Jesus shocked everyone by saying the broken man went home justified.
Two thousand years later, we still struggle to believe that story.
Because if we are honest, most of us do not see ourselves as the Pharisee.
We see ourselves as the tax collector.
Yet one of the most dangerous truths in Scripture is this:
The Pharisee is not merely a character in the story.
The Pharisee is a possibility living inside every human heart.
The Pharisee Inside All of Us
When modern readers hear the word "Pharisee," they usually picture a villain.
The Pharisees were respected religious leaders.
Many sincerely wanted to honor God.
The problem was not that they loved God's Law.
The problem was that they began loving their own righteousness more than God Himself.
What started as devotion slowly became self-exaltation.
What began as holiness slowly transformed into superiority.
What began as obedience slowly became pride.
That is why Jesus reserved some of His strongest rebukes not for prostitutes, tax collectors, or obvious sinners, but for religious people who believed they had no need for mercy.
The Greek word Jesus uses repeatedly for hypocrisy is ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs).
Originally, the word referred to an actor wearing a mask.
Someone appearing to be one thing while hiding another.
Jesus was not attacking sincere faith.
And if we are willing to look honestly into the mirror, we may discover how often we perform too.
The Hidden Addiction to Being Better Than Someone Else
The Pharisee spirit rarely announces itself.
It does not arrive saying, "I am prideful."
The human heart has an extraordinary ability to turn good things into idols.
Even biblical knowledge can become an idol.
Even ministry can become an idol.
Even serving Jesus can become an idol if it becomes a way of feeling superior to other people.
Notice the prayer of the Pharisee in Luke 18.
"I thank You that I am not like other men."
At first glance, it sounds spiritual.
The entire prayer is centered on himself.
The object of worship had quietly become the worshiper.
And before we judge him too quickly, we should ask ourselves difficult questions.
How often do we secretly compare ourselves to others?
How often do we feel relieved when someone else's failure makes us look better?
How often do we read stories of public scandals and think, "I would never do that"?
How often do we thank God for grace while secretly believing we deserve more credit than other people?
The Pharisee inside us feeds on comparison.
Grace starves comparison because grace reminds us that every person stands equally needy before the cross.
The Old Testament repeatedly emphasizes a Hebrew concept many believers overlook.
This word is often translated as lovingkindness, mercy, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness, or unfailing love.
Yet no single English word fully captures its depth.
Chesed describes God's relentless commitment to undeserving people.
Not people who earned His affection.
Not people who proved themselves worthy.
The Pharisee struggles with chesed because chesed destroys merit-based religion.
Chesed reminds us that salvation has always been God's initiative.
From Genesis to Revelation, God repeatedly chooses people nobody would have chosen.
People whose stories should have ended in failure.
Because grace is stronger than shame.
Because mercy is stronger than condemnation.
Because Jesus specializes in impossible redemption.
The Elder Brother We Rarely Notice
Many believers know the story of the prodigal son.
Fewer realize the older brother may be the more dangerous character.
The younger son ran into rebellion.
The younger son was lost far from the father.
The older son was lost near the father.
When the younger brother returned, the older brother became angry.
That is always the Pharisee's struggle.
Grace feels offensive when we secretly believe people should earn what God freely gives.
The older brother could tolerate obedience.
What he could not tolerate was mercy being extended to someone he considered less deserving.
Yet the Gospel stands upon this shocking truth:
Paul writes in Romans 3:23 that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
The Greek word translated "fall short" is ὑστεροῦνται (hysterountai).
It carries the idea of lacking, failing, coming behind, missing the standard.
Every human being stands in that condition.
The person reading these words right now.
Every one of us arrives at the same conclusion:
The Gospel remains scandalous because it destroys every human system of self-salvation.
The cross announces that our greatest problem was too severe for self-improvement.
If human goodness could save us, Jesus would not have needed to die.
The Aramaic language spoken by Jesus gives us a powerful glimpse into the intimacy of God's heart.
A deeply personal expression of relationship.
Jesus came not merely to improve behavior.
He came to reconcile people to the Father.
The Pharisee asks, "How good am I?"
Jesus asks, "Do you know My Father?"
There is coming a day when titles will not matter.
The Pharisee inside us dies only when we stop defending ourselves and start clinging to Jesus.
Only when we stop presenting our résumé and start confessing our need.
Only when we stop comparing ourselves with sinners and realize we are sinners rescued by grace.
This is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
It is not the story of good people earning heaven.
It is the story of guilty people being rescued by a perfect Savior.
The Bible is a library of rewritten lives.
The same Savior who transformed them still transforms people today.
That is why no failure is final when surrendered to Christ.
Including the Pharisee hidden inside each of us.
And perhaps that is the greatest scandal of all.
The very people who need mercy most are often the ones least aware of their need.
But when the Spirit opens our eyes, when pride collapses, when self-righteousness dies, when comparison finally loses its grip, we discover something breathtaking:
God was never asking us to impress Him.
He was inviting us to come home.
Someone you know is carrying invisible spiritual pride, religious exhaustion, secret shame, or crushing guilt. It may be the conversation God uses to bring them back to grace.
Because the moment we stop standing beside the Pharisee and start kneeling beside the tax collector is often the moment grace begins to feel real again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY ABIJAH SPOKE WITH COURAGE AGAINST A STRONGER KINGDOM
paragraphs: WHY ABIJAH SPOKE WITH COURAGE AGAINST A STRONGER KINGDOM
The battlefield was already decided in the minds of most people.
One king possessed overwhelming military advantage.
Everything visible suggested that Judah should lose.
Yet one man stepped forward and spoke as if Heaven itself stood behind him.
Few stories capture the collision between human strength and divine authority as powerfully as the confrontation between King Abijah of Judah and King Jeroboam of Israel recorded in 2 Chronicles 13.
This is not merely the story of a king facing impossible odds.
It is the story of what happens when truth stands before power.
It is the story of covenant confronting compromise.
It is the story of courage that can only be explained by faith.
And perhaps more importantly, it is the story many believers are living right now.
Some are standing in families where biblical truth is mocked.
Others work in environments where compromise is rewarded and conviction is punished.
Some are fighting private battles against addiction, fear, depression, shame, or spiritual exhaustion.
And yet the Spirit of God continues to ask the same question:
Will you trust what you see?
Or will you trust who I am?
The stage for Abijah's courage was set generations earlier.
After the reign of Solomon, the kingdom divided.
Ten tribes followed Jeroboam in the north.
Two tribes remained with the house of David in the south.
What followed was not merely political division.
Jeroboam feared that continued worship in Jerusalem would eventually turn people's hearts back toward the Davidic kingdom.
So he created an alternative religious system.
He invented worship practices that God had never commanded.
What began as political convenience became spiritual corruption.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly emphasize that true worship cannot be redesigned according to human preference.
God determines how He is worshiped.
This is why Abijah's speech becomes so significant.
Standing before a military force nearly twice the size of his own, he did not begin by discussing military strategy.
"Should you not know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingship over Israel forever to David and his sons by a covenant of salt?"
The Hebrew phrase is בְּרִית מֶלַח (Berith Melach), literally "covenant of salt."
In the ancient world, salt symbolized permanence, preservation, loyalty, and enduring faithfulness.
Abijah was reminding Israel that God's promises were not temporary political arrangements.
They were divine commitments established by God Himself.
His confidence was not rooted in troop numbers.
His confidence was rooted in God's faithfulness.
Many people today confuse faith with optimism.
Biblical faith is not positive thinking.
Biblical faith is confidence in the character and promises of God.
Optimism says things will probably work out.
Faith says God remains faithful regardless of the outcome.
That is why he could speak boldly when every visible circumstance suggested defeat.
When David faced Goliath, he did not focus on the giant's size.
When Moses stood before Pharaoh, he did not focus on Pharaoh's power.
When Daniel entered the lions' den, he did not focus on the lions.
When Peter stepped onto the water, he did not focus on the storm.
The greatest acts of courage in Scripture occur when people become more aware of God than their circumstances.
That is exactly what happened with Abijah.
His speech exposed a deeper issue.
"And now you think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD."
Abijah did not describe Judah merely as his kingdom.
He described it as the kingdom of the LORD.
Jeroboam was not merely opposing Judah.
He was opposing God's established purposes.
Many believers today are exhausted because they are fighting battles as if everything depends upon them.
Abijah reminds us that God's work ultimately belongs to God.
The burden becomes lighter when we remember whose battle we are actually fighting.
Yet Abijah's courage was not blind.
In fact, while Abijah was speaking, Jeroboam secretly positioned troops behind Judah's army.
From a human perspective, the situation was hopeless.
Then Scripture records one of the most powerful moments in the entire account.
"When Judah looked back, behold, the battle was before and behind them: and they cried unto the LORD."
This was not confidence in themselves.
The Hebrew concept behind crying out to God often carries the sense of desperate appeal, urgent trust, and complete reliance.
The people discovered something every believer eventually learns.
God often allows us to reach places where our own strength cannot save us.
Not because He wishes to destroy us.
Because He wishes to reveal Himself.
Many of the most beautiful testimonies begin at the point where human solutions end.
Then God stepped into the situation.
Not always according to our timing.
Not always according to our expectations.
But always according to His wisdom and faithfulness.
Scripture says God struck Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.
Because numbers do not determine outcomes when God intervenes.
This does not mean every believer will win every earthly battle.
What it does promise is something far greater.
The New Testament reveals the fullest expression of this truth through Jesus Christ.
The Roman Empire demonstrated its power.
The Son of God hung upon a cross.
To human eyes, evil had won.
Yet the greatest victory in history was unfolding.
The Greek word τετέλεσται (Tetelestai), spoken by Jesus in John 19:30, means "It is finished."
Three days later, the resurrection revealed what Heaven had known all along.
The stronger kingdom was never actually stronger.
The greater power belonged to God.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
That is why Abijah's story still matters.
Because every believer eventually stands before something that appears larger than their faith.
And in that moment, the question remains unchanged:
Or will we trust the God who has never broken a promise?
The Hebrew word often translated as faithfulness is אֱמוּנָה (Emunah).
It carries the idea of firmness, reliability, steadfastness, and trustworthiness.
God's faithfulness does not fluctuate according to circumstances.
Perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear today.
The battle in front of you may feel overwhelming.
But appearances have never limited God.
The same Lord who stood with David.
The same Lord who stood with Daniel.
The same Lord who stood with Abijah.
The same Lord who raised Jesus from the dead is still at work today.
Do not measure God's ability by the size of your problem.
Measure your problem by the greatness of your God.
Sometimes one share becomes the moment God uses to reach a struggling soul, restore a wandering believer, or introduce someone to Jesus Christ.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Your support helps expand the reach of biblical truth in a world starving for hope. It is one practical way to participate in spreading the Gospel and strengthening believers around the world.
The battle looked larger than Judah.
But Judah's God was larger than the battle.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Tertius Signed Paul’s Letter to the Romans
paragraphs:
Why Tertius Signed Paul’s Letter to the Romans
The Forgotten Name at the Bottom of Scripture That Reveals a Stunning Truth About Grace

They read Romans for its towering theology, its breathtaking vision of salvation, its deep explanations of grace, faith, justification, and the righteousness of God. They remember Paul. They quote Paul. They study Paul.
But near the end of the letter, almost hidden beneath the weight of eternity-changing doctrine, a different name suddenly appears.
A man most Christians have never heard sermons about.
A man whose name only appears once.
A man who quietly steps out from the shadows and writes a single sentence.
"I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, greet you in the Lord." (Romans 16:22)
Because that one sentence may reveal one of the most beautiful pictures of God's kingdom ever preserved in Scripture.
It is the story of an unseen servant.
A man whose hand helped deliver one of the greatest theological masterpieces ever written.
And it is a story that may completely change how you see your own place in God's plan.
The final chapter of Romans feels almost like the credits rolling after an epic film. Names appear one after another. Greetings are exchanged. Believers are honored. Co-workers are remembered.
Then suddenly comes this unexpected statement:
"I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord."
Ἐγὼ Τέρτιος ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολήν ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐν Κυρίῳ
Egō Tertios ho grapsas tēn epistolēn aspazomai hymas en Kyriō.
"I, Tertius, the one having written the letter, greet you in the Lord."
Tertius identifies himself as the one who physically wrote the letter.
In the ancient world this role was called an amanuensis.

Many authors dictated their words to trained scribes who recorded them with professional skill. This was common practice throughout the Roman Empire. Writing materials were expensive. Literacy levels varied. Professional scribes helped produce lengthy documents accurately and efficiently.
Paul appears to have frequently used this method.
"See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand."
That statement only makes sense if someone else had written most of the letter before Paul personally added a concluding section.
Likewise, in 2 Thessalonians 3:17 Paul mentions adding his own greeting as a mark of authenticity.
This strongly supports the understanding that Paul often dictated while trusted assistants wrote.
Romans appears to be one of those occasions.
And the man holding the pen was Tertius.
His name itself carries an interesting detail.
Many scholars believe it was likely a common Roman name, perhaps associated with a birth order or household designation.
We know almost nothing else about him.
Yet his hand helped preserve Romans.
Think about that for a moment.
When Paul dictated Romans, some of the most significant truths ever written flowed through the voice of an apostle and through the pen of an otherwise unknown servant.
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God..."
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us..."
As Paul explained justification by faith...
As Paul unfolded God's plan of redemption...
As Paul reached the soaring climax of Romans 8:
"For I am convinced that neither death nor life..."

The words that would shape churches, transform nations, fuel reformations, comfort martyrs, and lead countless souls to Christ passed through the faithful hands of a man most believers barely know exists.
And that should stop us in our tracks.
Because modern culture has trained us to believe significance belongs to visibility.
Jesus repeatedly overturned humanity's obsession with prominence.
The King born in a feeding trough.
The Savior who died between criminals.
Everything about Christ challenges worldly definitions of greatness.
In fact, the Hebrew concept behind faithful service carries a profound beauty.
The Hebrew word עֶבֶד (eved) means servant, bondservant, or devoted servant.
Many of God's greatest leaders were identified by this title.
Even the coming Messiah in Isaiah's Servant Songs.
In Scripture, servanthood is not humiliation.
The greatest people in God's kingdom are often those most willing to disappear so Christ can be seen.
That is difficult for modern hearts.
We live in a world chasing followers, impressions, engagement metrics, recognition, applause, influence, and personal platforms.
None of those things are inherently sinful.
But they become dangerous when they become our definition of worth.
Tertius reminds us that heaven measures differently.
The person setting up chairs matters.
The unseen saint faithfully serving Christ when nobody notices matters.
In Romans 12, Paul compares believers to parts of a body.
A hidden organ may be more vital than a visible hand.
Likewise, God's kingdom advances through countless faithful servants whose names never become famous.
Perhaps that is why his greeting feels so moving.
After sixteen chapters of profound doctrine, Paul allows this quiet servant one sentence.
One glimpse into the room where Romans was born.
And suddenly the masterpiece becomes personal.
There is another layer that makes this story even more beautiful.
The Gospel itself is the ultimate story of hidden grace.
Jesus did not come through the halls of imperial power.
He came through a humble virgin in an obscure village.
The King of kings entered history unnoticed by most of the world.
The scandal of the Gospel is that God repeatedly chooses what the world overlooks.
Paul understood this deeply when he wrote:
"God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise."
The Kingdom advances through surprising people.
That is where our theme becomes deeply personal.
The world says your value comes from recognition.
Jesus says your value comes from belonging to Him.
The world says your name must be known.
Jesus says your faithfulness is known by the Father.
The world says platform equals purpose.
The world says visibility creates significance.
Jesus says faithfulness creates eternal impact.
Tertius may have seemed insignificant to history.
Yet two thousand years later believers across the world still read words he faithfully recorded.
Imagine arriving in eternity and discovering how many lives were changed because of work you thought nobody noticed.
Imagine discovering that God was writing a story through your hidden obedience.
Imagine realizing that your unseen faithfulness was never unseen at all.
Perhaps you feel like Tertius today.
The God who saw Tertius sees you.
The God who remembered Tertius remembers you.
The God who included Tertius in Holy Scripture has never overlooked a single act of faithfulness done for His glory.
And perhaps that is the deepest lesson hidden in Romans 16:22.
The Gospel is not only about the famous apostle speaking.
It is also about the faithful servant writing.
Both became part of God's redemptive story.
Every effort to spread the Gospel becomes part of a much larger story that Jesus Himself is writing.
If our mission is helping people move from scandal to grace through the Gospel, supporting that mission is one practical way to participate in spreading biblical truth.
Because one day we may discover that the names earth forgot were written in heaven's boldest ink.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD MYSTERY OF THE PROPHET WHO SAW GOD'S THRONE ROOM
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD MYSTERY OF THE PROPHET WHO SAW GOD'S THRONE ROOM
There are moments in Scripture that feel less like reading history and more like standing on the edge of eternity.
Moments where heaven's curtain briefly opens.
Moments where human language struggles to describe what human eyes were never created to fully comprehend.
One of those moments belongs to a prophet most believers know by name, yet few truly understand.
His visions have inspired artists, terrified theologians, fascinated skeptics, and left generations of Christians staring at the pages of Scripture asking the same question:
And why did it change him forever?
Most people know Ezekiel as the prophet of dry bones.
But before he saw dead bones live again...
Before he spoke judgment and hope to a rebellious nation...
He witnessed something so overwhelming that he collapsed face-first into the dirt.
He saw the throne room of God.
Not in a dream created by his own imagination.
God opened heaven and allowed a captive prophet to glimpse divine glory.
And what he saw remains one of the greatest mysteries in all Scripture.
The story begins during one of Israel's darkest seasons.
Families were being carried into exile.
Everything they trusted seemed to be collapsing.
The temple still stood, but the nation's heart had already drifted far from God.
Then came a priest named Ezekiel.
In Hebrew his name is יְחֶזְקֵאל (Yechezqel).
What an extraordinary name for a man living among broken people.
Ezekiel sat among Jewish exiles near the Kebar River in Babylon.
"The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God."
And suddenly the prophet saw a storm approaching.
But this was no earthly storm.
The description sounds almost impossible to visualize.
Each reflected aspects of God's created order.
Ancient Jewish scholars often understood these creatures as representing the highest expressions of creation:
Later Scripture identifies these beings more clearly.
Not the harmless winged babies painted in Renaissance art.
These are mighty heavenly beings who dwell near the presence of God.
Servants of the King of Heaven.
Yet the creatures themselves were not the center of the vision.
Moving in every direction without turning.
Many modern readers attempt to force technological explanations onto the passage.
But Scripture itself points us elsewhere.
The mobility reveals something revolutionary for exiled Israel.
God was not trapped inside Jerusalem.
God was not limited to a temple.
Above the living creatures stood an expanse.
An immense heavenly platform shining like crystal.
And seated upon it was One whose glory surpassed description.
The prophet struggles to communicate the incomprehensible.
"Above the expanse over their heads was the likeness of a throne, in appearance like sapphire; and seated above the likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance."
This is one of the most profound moments in Scripture.
Ezekiel does not claim to see God's essence.
Scripture consistently teaches that God's fullness is beyond human comprehension.
Instead, he witnesses a visible manifestation of divine glory.
The Hebrew term later used is:
The word "Kevod" literally carries the idea of weight, substance, significance, majesty.
Then comes a detail many readers overlook.
The figure upon the throne possesses a human-like appearance.
Centuries before Christ walked the roads of Galilee.
A prophet sees a throne occupied by One appearing in human form.
Many conservative biblical scholars understand this as a theophany—a visible manifestation of God.
Others see a possible anticipation of the Messiah.
While Scripture does not explicitly identify the figure as the pre-incarnate Christ, Christians throughout church history have seen remarkable connections.
The God who would one day enter humanity was already revealing Himself in ways humanity could begin to understand.
"Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around."
Because even in judgment, God remembers mercy.
The rainbow first appeared after Noah.
A reminder that God's wrath never operates apart from His covenant faithfulness.
Even while Jerusalem moved toward destruction.
God was still a covenant-keeping God.
And then everything became too much.
This is the response repeated throughout Scripture whenever sinful humanity encounters divine holiness.
Modern culture often treats God casually.
But nobody who encounters God's holiness in Scripture remains casual.
His glory exposes every hidden motive.
And yet that same glory is also what heals us.
The throne room vision reveals something many believers desperately need to hear today.
God is still on the throne when your world falls apart.
Ezekiel saw the throne before he saw restoration.
Because everything else makes sense only when the throne comes first.
Maybe your life feels like exile right now.
Maybe you're carrying burdens nobody knows about.
Ezekiel's vision reminds us that heaven is not in crisis.
God has not surrendered His authority.
Nothing can remove Him from His throne.
The mystery of Ezekiel's vision is not ultimately about creatures, wheels, or heavenly architecture.
Why would a holy God reveal Himself to rebellious people at all?
Why would the King of eternity pursue those who repeatedly wander from Him?
The answer unfolds throughout the rest of Scripture.
Because God's ultimate goal was never merely to display His glory.
His goal was to bring sinners into relationship with Himself.
The throne room of Ezekiel ultimately points forward to Jesus Christ.
The One who left heavenly glory.
The One who entered human history.
The One who bore our sin.
The One who now sits enthroned forever.
The Apostle John later writes in Greek:
The glory Ezekiel glimpsed from afar would one day walk among humanity.
The King on the throne became the Savior on the cross.
And because of that cross, believers are no longer merely spectators of God's throne.
Through Christ, we are invited into His presence.
Hebrews 4:16 declares that we may approach the throne of grace with confidence.
The same throne that caused Ezekiel to collapse now becomes a throne of grace for those redeemed through Jesus Christ.
Maybe this article stirred something inside you.
Maybe you've drifted farther than you ever intended.
Maybe you've been pretending everything is fine while carrying battles nobody sees.
Maybe you've forgotten that the throne is occupied.
Be honest. This may have hit harder than you expected.
The throne was never empty... even on the day you thought heaven had gone silent.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: TAMAR AND JUDAH: THE STORY MOST PEOPLE SKIP
paragraphs: TAMAR AND JUDAH: THE STORY MOST PEOPLE SKIP
The Woman Hidden in the Shadows Who Became Part of the Line of Christ
Most people read past her name.
Others remember only enough to feel uncomfortable.
The story feels messy. Scandalous. Difficult to explain.
It sits in Genesis 38 like an interruption, wedged between the dramatic account of Joseph's betrayal and his rise in Egypt. At first glance it seems misplaced, almost unnecessary.
But God does not waste chapters.
And when the Holy Spirit preserved Tamar's story in Scripture, He was not preserving a scandal.
Because hidden inside one of the most uncomfortable stories in the Bible is one of the clearest pictures of the Gospel.
And ultimately, a story about Jesus.
God placed her in the family tree of Christ.
That should make us stop and ask why.
The story begins with Judah, one of the twelve sons of Jacob. This is the same Judah whose descendants would eventually produce King David and, generations later, Jesus Christ.
Yet Genesis 38 does not begin with Judah looking like a hero.
Judah leaves his brothers and settles among the Canaanites.
He marries outside the covenant family.
His firstborn son, Er, becomes so wicked that Scripture says:
In the ancient Near Eastern world, widowhood was devastating.
A woman without a husband often faced economic ruin, social vulnerability, and an uncertain future.
According to family obligation, Judah's second son, Onan, was supposed to provide offspring for his deceased brother through what later became known as levirate responsibility.
Instead, Onan selfishly exploited Tamar while deliberately preventing her from having children.
"What he did was wicked in the LORD's sight; so the LORD put him to death also." (Genesis 38:10)
Now Tamar has lost two husbands.
Neither tragedy was caused by her actions.
Many readers know exactly what that feels like.
People often suffer because of sins they never committed.
Faithful people suffer because others failed them.
The wounds may wear different clothing today, but injustice still exists.
Judah now has one remaining son, Shelah.
He promises Tamar that when the boy is older, she will be given to him as a wife.
But Judah has no intention of keeping his word.
She has been abandoned by the very man responsible for protecting her.
At this point many Bible readers are tempted to view Tamar only through the lens of what happens next.
But we cannot understand her actions without understanding her desperation.
Denied her rightful place in the family.
Denied the future she was promised.
Then comes the moment that has caused generations of readers to recoil.
Tamar disguises herself and positions herself where Judah will encounter her.
Not recognizing her, Judah propositions her.
The man who refused to honor righteousness now walks directly into his own exposure.
Before the encounter, Tamar requests collateral.
Judah gives her his seal, cord, and staff.
The ancient equivalent of a signature, legal authority, and identity combined.
Certain he will never hear about this again.
Sin often whispers the same lie.
Months later Tamar's pregnancy becomes known.
Suddenly Judah erupts with moral outrage.
"Bring her out and have her burned to death!" (Genesis 38:24)
The guilty man becomes the loudest accuser.
Humanity loves exposing sins it secretly excuses in itself.
Jesus would later confront this same spirit among religious leaders.
The one holding the stone is often hiding something too.
Then comes one of the most dramatic moments in all Scripture.
As Tamar is brought forward, she sends Judah his own seal, cord, and staff.
She does not launch an attack.
She does not deliver a speech.
Judah's response is one of the most important statements in Genesis:
This is not merely an admission of being caught.
A moment of genuine exposure before God.
And grace often begins exactly there.
Grace begins when truth finally wins.
The remarkable thing is that Judah's story does not end in shame.
Because God is not merely exposing Judah.
Years later, when famine strikes and Joseph tests his brothers in Egypt, Judah emerges as a different man.
The selfish brother becomes the sacrificial brother.
The man who once sold Joseph becomes the man willing to offer himself in Benjamin's place.
And this is where the story becomes astonishing.
When Matthew records the genealogy of Jesus, he includes a detail most ancient genealogies would have hidden.
"Judah the father of Perez and Zerah, whose mother was Tamar." (Matthew 1:3)
This matters because women were rarely included in ancient genealogies.
Because the genealogy of Jesus is not a list of perfect people.
It is a testimony to redeeming grace.
Yet all woven into God's redemptive plan.
The Greek word for Gospel is "εὐαγγέλιον" (euangelion).
News that God enters broken stories and redeems them.
News that sin does not have the final word.
News that failure is not the final chapter.
The deepest surprise in Tamar's story is that she was never the scandal.
The Bible repeatedly reveals a God who specializes in rescuing people from the chapters others would rather hide.
Perhaps that is why so many people avoid Tamar's story.
Because most people have chapters they wish were not there.
Yet Scripture refuses to hide the brokenness of God's people.
The Hebrew word often translated "grace" is "חֵן" (chen).
It carries the idea of favor freely given.
And every page of Scripture points toward the ultimate expression of that grace.
At the cross, God did not pretend sin was insignificant.
The One who was perfectly righteous carried the guilt of the unrighteous.
The One without scandal carried the shame of scandalized humanity.
The One without sin died for sinners.
That is why Tamar's story ultimately points beyond Tamar.
Because the Bible is not fundamentally about flawed people trying harder.
It is about a perfect Savior rescuing flawed people.
Maybe you opened this article carrying your own hidden chapter.
The same God who worked through Tamar's story is still rewriting stories today.
The same Savior who redeemed Judah still transforms hearts today.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Jesus writes endings that human beings never could.
What chapter of your life have you seen Jesus begin to rewrite?
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to hope.
Because sometimes the chapter we wish God would remove becomes the chapter He uses to reveal His glory.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF ENOS
paragraphs: His life occupies only a few lines of Scripture. No giant battle. No ark. No dream interpreted before kings. No slaying of giants. No dramatic confrontation with Pharaoh.
Just a name buried in a genealogy.
And yet hidden within those few verses is one of the most important turning points in human history.
Because Enosh appears in the aftermath of humanity's first scandal.
A scandal so devastating that it shattered paradise, fractured families, introduced death into creation, and left humanity wandering east of Eden carrying the weight of rebellion.
The story of Enosh is not simply the story of a forgotten man.
It is the story of what happens when broken people realize they cannot save themselves.
It is the story of humanity's first great awakening.
And it is the story of grace beginning to shine through the darkness.
The world Enosh inherited was drenched in grief.
The man who once walked with God in the Garden.
The man who heard the voice of the Creator without fear.
