Every spouse fighting for a broken marriage.
Every soul wondering why God seems silent.
The silence does not mean abandonment.
The prison does not mean God has forgotten.
The delay does not mean God has failed.
Those are not the same thing.
The irony is impossible to ignore.
The same Greek root behind "offended"—skandalon—is where we get the word scandal.
John faced the scandal of unmet expectations.
That is what Jesus always does.
He takes what appears to be failure and rewrites it into redemption.
He takes crosses and turns them into empty tombs.
He takes broken stories and turns them into testimonies.
He takes scandal and transforms it into grace.
Because that is who He is.
"Can I trust Jesus when He doesn't rescue me the way I expected?"
That question determines the shape of a person's faith.
Because mature faith is not trusting God only when miracles come.
Mature faith is trusting Him when prison doors remain closed.
Yet he trusted the One who would bring it.
And because of that, his story still speaks across centuries.
Not as a story of abandonment.
But as a story of unwavering faithfulness.
Perhaps someone reading this today feels trapped in a prison of grief, disappointment, confusion, betrayal, sickness, fear, or unanswered prayer.
The same Jesus who seemed absent from John's prison was still fully present in John's story.
And He is fully present in yours.
And Jesus has always been in the business of rewriting stories.
Your testimony may encourage someone else's faith journey.
Your support helps expand this ministry's mission of bringing people from scandal to grace through the power of the Gospel.
One day you may discover that the prayer God did not answer was the very path He used to bring you closer to Himself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND THE GIANT WITH SIX FINGERS AND SIX TOES
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND THE GIANT WITH SIX FINGERS AND SIX TOES
Most Christians know the story of David and Goliath.
Few know the story of the giant who came after.
A giant so unusual that Scripture pauses long enough to record a chilling detail.
He had six fingers on each hand.
And then, almost as quietly as he appears, he dies on a battlefield forgotten by most believers.
At first glance, it sounds like a strange biblical footnote.
An oddity tucked away in the historical records of Israel.
But the deeper you go, the more this giant becomes a window into one of the Bible's most fascinating themes: the long war between the kingdom of God and the seed of rebellion.
And once you see it, you cannot unsee it.
The story begins in a single verse.
"There was yet a battle in Gath, where was a man of great stature, that had on every hand six fingers, and on every foot six toes, four and twenty in number; and he also was born to the giant."
The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 20:6 repeats the same detail.
This was a real man remembered by God Himself in inspired Scripture.
And God thought it important enough to preserve one remarkable fact about him.
Because biblical details are rarely accidental.
To understand this giant, we must first understand where he came from.
Gath was one of the five major Philistine cities and the hometown of the most famous giant in Scripture.
The very place that once produced Israel's greatest enemy was still producing giants decades later.
These warriors belonged to a remnant connected to the Rephaim.
The Hebrew term רְפָאִים (Repha'im) appears throughout the Old Testament describing ancient giant clans who occupied parts of Canaan before Israel's conquest.
Deuteronomy, Joshua, Samuel, and Chronicles all preserve traces of these formidable peoples.
By the time of David, most had been destroyed.
The giant with twenty-four digits belonged to the final generation of these enemies.
The last echoes of a dying rebellion.
The Bible tells us that after Goliath's death, several other giant warriors emerged.
Each was eventually defeated by David's mighty men.
The giant with six fingers and six toes represents the final chapter of a story that had stretched across generations.
The kingdom of God was advancing.
The enemies of God were retreating.
The giants were disappearing from history.
This is often how God works.
The victories we celebrate publicly are often only the beginning.
Others had to finish the war.
The Number Six and Human Rebellion
Many readers immediately notice something intriguing.
The giant's unusual anatomy centers around the number six.
The number six in Scripture often carries associations with humanity.
Man was created on the sixth day.
The infamous number associated with the Beast in Revelation is 666.
Scripture never explicitly states that the giant's twenty-four digits symbolize the number of the Beast.
Any claim beyond what Scripture reveals becomes speculation.
Yet the repeated emphasis on six naturally invites reflection.
Throughout Scripture, humanity apart from God continually attempts to exalt itself.
The rulers who claimed divine status.
Again and again, human strength rises against God.
Again and again, God humbles it.
The giant's extra digits may simply be an accurate physical description.
And still falling before the purposes of God.
Some skeptics assume this detail proves the story is legendary.
It is a genuine genetic variation in which individuals are born with extra fingers or toes.
Some individuals possess fully functional extra digits.
What once sounded impossible now sounds medically recognizable.
The Bible's credibility is strengthened rather than weakened.
Scripture records exactly what one might expect from an eyewitness account.
Ancient Hebrew writers did not obsess over physical abnormalities the way modern readers often do.
When Scripture records a detail, it usually serves a narrative purpose.
The giant's unusual anatomy amplified one central reality.
The sort of enemy people would talk about for years.
The kind of warrior who could make ordinary men tremble.
Yet despite all his advantages, he dies in a single verse.
The Bible's focus is never the greatness of the giant.
The focus is always the greatness of God.
A Gospel Hidden in the Battlefield
The giant with six fingers and six toes is more than ancient history.
Because every believer eventually faces a giant that seems abnormal.
The giant always looks larger than you expected.
They make ordinary people feel small.
Yet Scripture repeatedly teaches a stunning truth.
The story was never about the giant.
It was always about the God who stands behind His people.
When Israel looked at Goliath, they saw a giant.
When David looked at Goliath, he saw a target too large to miss.
That same perspective echoes through every giant story in Scripture.
The giant with twenty-four digits is not killed by David.
He is defeated by Jonathan, the son of Shimea, David's brother.
The courage David demonstrated had multiplied.
This is how the kingdom grows.
The next generation finishes the work.
One believer says yes to God.
The giant's death is not merely a military victory.
It is proof that faith reproduces itself.
Every giant in Scripture eventually falls.
The giant with six fingers and six toes fell.
The Greek word for enemy is ἐχθρός (echthros).
Yet even that giant has an expiration date.
Jesus Christ stepped into humanity's battlefield and confronted the greatest giant mankind had ever known.
And through His death and resurrection, He secured victory forever.
Every giant story in the Old Testament points ultimately to Him.
Every fallen enemy foreshadows His triumph.
The giant with six fingers and six toes stood taller than ordinary men.
Your giant may feel impossible today.
But it still answers to the King of Kings.
And giants have never survived an encounter with the purposes of God.
Maybe that is why this strange detail remains preserved in Scripture thousands of years later.
Not to make us marvel at the giant.
But to remind us how temporary giants really are.
One day every enemy will be gone.
And the only kingdom standing will belong to Jesus Christ.
The giant was remembered because of his twenty-four digits.
But history remembers the God who brought him down.
The giant looked unforgettable until he met the God who never loses.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE IS THE ONLY AND FINAL AUTHORITY
paragraphs:
THE BIBLE IS THE ONLY AND FINAL AUTHORITY
Let Scripture Speak for Itself
There is a question that has haunted every generation of believers.
The loudest voice on social media?
Everything ultimately comes down to authority.
Because the authority you trust becomes the foundation upon which you build your life.
Jesus warned that two houses can look identical from the outside while standing on completely different foundations. One survives the storm. The other collapses when the winds begin to roar.
The tragedy of our age is not merely that people reject Scripture.
It is that many claim to believe Scripture while quietly placing something else above it.
Something else becomes the lens through which God's Word is filtered.
Instead of Scripture shaping us, we begin shaping Scripture.
And whenever humanity attempts to edit God's voice, confusion follows.
The Bible repeatedly presents itself not as one authority among many but as the very Word of God, possessing divine authority because its ultimate source is God Himself.
When the Apostle Paul wrote to Timothy, he used language that leaves no room for uncertainty:
Not inspired in the modern sense of artistic inspiration.
Scripture proceeds from the mouth of God.
This is why Scripture possesses authority.
Not because the Church gave it authority.
Scripture possesses authority because God spoke it.
The prophet Isaiah captured this permanence with breathtaking clarity:
"The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever."

וּדְבַר־אֱלֹהֵינוּ יָקוּם לְעוֹלָם
(U'devar Eloheinu yakum le'olam)
"The Word of our God stands forever."
That truth becomes even more astonishing when we consider Jesus Himself.
When Satan confronted Jesus in the wilderness, the Son of God could have responded with displays of divine power.
Instead, He repeatedly answered with Scripture.
Something written in the past that remains authoritative in the present.
If the eternal Son of God submitted Himself to Scripture's authority, what arrogance exists in us when we attempt to stand above it?
Many people imagine that the greatest threat to biblical authority comes from unbelievers.
Historically, that has rarely been the greatest danger.
The greater danger often comes from people who claim to honor Scripture while quietly redefining it.
The serpent's first recorded words in Genesis reveal the strategy:
The attack began with God's Word.
Because if confidence in God's Word collapses, everything else eventually follows.
Thousands of years later, the strategy remains unchanged.
The question is still being asked.
Can we trust what God said?
Shouldn't we update what God said?
Yet Scripture consistently points believers back to itself as the final standard.
When the Bereans heard Paul's preaching, they did something remarkable.
Acts 17 praises them because they searched the Scriptures daily to verify what they were hearing.
They examined the teachings of an Apostle.
They did not treat even Paul as the ultimate authority.
The Bible never teaches blind allegiance to human leaders.
It teaches submission to God's Word.
This distinction is desperately needed today.
We live in an era overflowing with voices.
But Scripture repeatedly reminds believers that truth is not determined by popularity.
"The sum of Your word is truth."
"The entirety of Your Word is truth."
This is why Scripture must interpret Scripture.
Clear passages must illuminate difficult passages.
Personal opinions must bow before the full counsel of God's Word.
The Bible is not a collection of disconnected inspirational sayings.
It is one unified revelation centered upon one glorious Person.
From Genesis to Revelation, Scripture tells a single unfolding story.
Every promise finds fulfillment in Christ.
Every shadow finds substance in Christ.
Every prophecy reaches its destination in Christ.
The authority of Scripture and the authority of Christ cannot be separated.
To reject Scripture is ultimately to reject the One who gave it.
To love Christ is to treasure His Word.
"If you love Me, you will keep My commandments."
Love and obedience were never enemies.
Truth and grace were never enemies.
Authority and freedom were never enemies.
The modern world often portrays authority as oppression.
Scripture presents God's authority as liberation.
Because the Creator understands reality better than His creation.
A fish experiences freedom in water.
A train experiences freedom on tracks.
Human beings experience true freedom when living according to God's design.
The authority of Scripture is not a prison.
"Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path."
And history repeatedly demonstrates the consequences.
Whenever cultures abandon God's Word, confusion multiplies.
But where God's Word reigns, clarity emerges.
Not because every question instantly disappears.
But because God's voice becomes louder than the noise.
The Bible does not claim to answer every curiosity.
It reveals the God who saves sinners.
At the center of Scripture is not merely information.
The greatest authority question is not whether we agree with God.
The greatest question is whether we will surrender to Him.
Because Scripture reveals an uncomfortable truth about every one of us.
The Bible diagnoses the human condition with devastating accuracy.
Yet it also announces the greatest news the world has ever heard.
Lived the perfect life we could never live.
And now offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life to all who repent and believe.
This message is not man's invention.
And it comes to us through Scripture.
That is why the Bible must remain the final authority.
Because without Scripture, we do not merely lose guidance.
But because the living God has chosen to reveal Himself through His written Word.
The question before every generation remains unchanged.
Or will we kneel beneath it?
Will we demand that God's Word conform to us?
Or will we allow God's Word to transform us?
Perhaps that is why the most dangerous words a believer can ever speak are not, "I don't understand."
Everything after that sentence is a battle for authority.
And eternity hangs on the outcome.
If this stirred something in your spirit, don't keep it to yourself.
What passage of Scripture has carried you through your darkest season?
When everything else changes, the voice of God remains unchanged.
The world keeps rewriting its truth. Heaven never has to revise its own.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY JESUS REFUSED CERTAIN WINE
paragraphs: The crowd had seen blood before.
Crucifixions were public warnings, public humiliations, public spectacles of fear. The condemned did not simply die; they were displayed. Broken bodies became billboards of imperial power.
Yet on a hill called Golgotha, something happened that continues to perplex historians, theologians, skeptics, and believers alike.
A dying man was offered wine.
At first glance, the detail feels insignificant. Almost forgettable. Buried beneath the nails, the thorns, the darkness, the earthquake, and the cry that split history itself.
Especially when the detail concerns Jesus Christ.

The refusal of that cup reveals something astonishing about the heart of our Savior. It exposes the depth of His love, the cost of redemption, and the scandalous grace that would flow from His suffering.
To understand why Jesus refused certain wine, we must first walk into the dust, blood, and agony of Golgotha itself.

"And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it."
(Mark 15:23)

"They offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it."
(Matthew 27:34)
The Greek text of Mark uses the phrase:

Myrrh was a fragrant resin commonly used in perfumes, burial preparations, and medicinal applications. Ancient sources indicate that mixtures of wine and narcotic substances were sometimes given to condemned prisoners to dull pain before execution.
The Babylonian Talmud later references a practice in which women of Jerusalem provided an intoxicating drink to those being led to execution.
Or at least a form of mercy.
The drink could numb the senses, cloud awareness, and lessen the torment.
The answer reaches into the very center of the Gospel.
Many people imagine salvation happened merely because Jesus died.
But Scripture repeatedly emphasizes something deeper.

"He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth."
(Isaiah 53:7)
A word carrying the idea of being humbled, oppressed, or subjected to suffering.
The Messiah would not escape suffering.
The wine mixed with myrrh represented relief.

"And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross."
(Philippians 2:8)
The Greek word for obedient is:
Meaning one who listens under authority and fully submits.
Jesus was not seeking the easiest path.
He was fulfilling the Father's will completely.
This is what makes the scene so heartbreaking.
The One who turned water into wine refused wine when it could have eased His pain.
The One who supplied joy at Cana accepted agony at Calvary.
The One who fed thousands denied Himself even a measure of comfort.
Many of us spend our lives looking for ways to numb pain.
Humanity has always looked for cups that help us forget.
He looked directly at the horror awaiting Him.
This becomes even more powerful when we consider what happened in Gethsemane.
There, Jesus spoke of another cup.

"My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will."
(Matthew 26:39)
Throughout the Old Testament, the cup often symbolized God's judgment.
The cup represented divine wrath against sin.
Jesus refused one cup on Golgotha because He was committed to drinking another.
The other would bear the punishment humanity deserved.
You hear the religious leaders sneering.
Then you see Him reject the wine.
You realize He is choosing to feel everything.
The scandal of the Gospel is not merely that sinners can be forgiven.
The scandal is that the innocent Son of God willingly absorbed what guilty people deserved.

"He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree."
(1 Peter 2:24)
A sacrificial term often associated with carrying an offering to an altar.
Jesus was not merely a victim.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Because if Jesus had sought escape, we would have no salvation.
If He had chosen comfort over obedience, we would still be condemned.
If He had turned away from suffering, humanity would remain separated from God.
Even the timing of the wine in John's Gospel reveals profound meaning.
Later, after the work was nearly complete, Jesus accepted wine.
A sour wine was lifted to Him.
The narcotic mixture that dulled suffering had been rejected.
The sour wine received near the end helped fulfill prophecy and precede His final declaration.
Then came the words that shook eternity:
The refusal of the first wine makes the triumph of the final cry even more powerful.
And because He carried it, we do not have to.
That truth reaches beyond theology and into the deepest wounds of human experience.
Many readers know what it feels like to carry shame.
To wonder whether God could possibly love someone with your history.
The Gospel answers with a cross.
And on that cross stands a Savior refusing relief because He was determined to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
Your worst chapter is not stronger than His grace.
Your deepest failure is not greater than His mercy.
Your scandal is not beyond His redemption.
The same Jesus who refused the numbing wine now offers living water.
The same Jesus who embraced suffering now offers peace.
The same Jesus who bore judgment now offers forgiveness.
The same Jesus who died now lives.
This is why the Gospel continues to transform lives across centuries.
Because Christianity is not the story of humanity climbing toward God.
It is the story of God descending toward broken humanity.
The hill of Golgotha proves it.
And perhaps today, someone reading these words feels exhausted from running, hiding, pretending, or carrying guilt that Christ already paid for.
Maybe you have spent years reaching for your own versions of numbing wine.
Maybe you have tried everything except surrender.
Not because your story is clean.
Because His grace is greater than your mess.
The rejected cup at Golgotha became part of the greatest rescue mission in history.
The Savior refused temporary relief so He could secure eternal redemption.
That is not merely a theological detail.
That is love with nail-scarred hands.
He refused the cup that could numb His pain so He could become the cure for yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JUDAS DIDN'T BETRAY JESUS FOR MONEY ALONE
paragraphs: JUDAS DIDN'T BETRAY JESUS FOR MONEY ALONE
That is the number most Christians remember.
Thirty reasons, we assume, that Judas Iscariot sold the Son of God.
But what if the money was never the real story?
What if the silver was only the symptom?
What if the greatest betrayal in human history began long before the coins ever touched Judas' hands?
Because if we reduce Judas to greed, we may miss the terrifying truth hiding in his story.
And if we miss that truth, we may fail to recognize pieces of Judas in ourselves.
The Greek text preserves the question:
"Τί θέλετέ μοι δοῦναι;" (Ti thelete moi dounai?)
"What are you willing to give me?"
The question reveals more than a transaction.
It reveals a heart that had already shifted.
A disciple who no longer saw Jesus as priceless.
A follower who had begun calculating value.
A man who had started measuring devotion by personal return.
Long before Judas sold Jesus, Judas had reduced Jesus.
That is where betrayal always begins.
Many imagine Judas as a villain from the beginning.
The Gospels paint a more unsettling picture.
For years Judas walked where the other disciples walked.
Yet proximity to Jesus did not automatically produce surrender to Jesus.
That reality should shake every churchgoer.
Judas reminds us that a person can be near Christ without belonging fully to Christ.
The Hebrew Scriptures contain a word that captures covenant loyalty:
It is often translated as lovingkindness, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness.
God continually demonstrates chesed toward His people.
Yet covenant love can be resisted.
The tragedy of Judas is not that God withheld grace.
The tragedy is that Judas repeatedly rejected what grace was offering.
"Judas, who had charge of the moneybag, used to help himself to what was put into it." (John 12:6)
The betrayal did not begin with thirty silver coins.
Private sins nobody else could see.
A heart that slowly learned how to justify disobedience.
Few people wake up one morning and commit catastrophic betrayal.
Most spiritual collapses begin with tiny permissions.
The enemy rarely destroys faith in a moment.
One neglected conviction at a time.
One ignored warning at a time.
One secret surrender at a time.
Eventually Judas encountered a Jesus who was not becoming the Messiah he expected.
Many scholars note that first-century Jews longed for political deliverance from Roman oppression.
The Hebrew term מָשִׁיחַ (Mashiach) means "Anointed One."
Yet Jesus arrived announcing a Kingdom unlike anything many expected.
Instead of overthrowing Rome, He preached repentance.
Instead of seizing power, He embraced servanthood.
Instead of destroying enemies, He loved them.
Instead of ascending a throne, He moved toward a cross.
Perhaps Judas wanted a Messiah who would fulfill his plans.
When Jesus refused to become that Messiah, disappointment began hardening into disillusionment.
This may be one of the most dangerous spiritual conditions in existence.
The kind that follows Jesus as long as Jesus cooperates with our expectations.
The kind that worships until obedience becomes costly.
The kind that remains loyal until God's will conflicts with personal ambition.
Many people have not abandoned Jesus because they stopped believing He exists.
They have abandoned Jesus because He did not become who they wanted Him to be.
A healer who did not heal fast enough.
A provider who did not provide the way they expected.
The distance between admiration and betrayal is often shorter than we think.
Then comes one of the most haunting moments in Scripture.
At the Last Supper Jesus identifies the betrayer.
The question in Greek is astonishing:
"Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, κύριε;" (Mēti egō eimi, kyrie?)
Every disciple recognized his own capacity for failure.
That humility is missing in many modern believers.
We often read Judas and see someone else.
Jesus intends us to see ourselves.
Not because we have committed his exact sin.
But because every heart contains the potential for betrayal when surrenderedness is replaced by self-rule.
The symbol of affection became the instrument of betrayal.
How many betrayals still wear the disguise of devotion?
How many people sing worship songs while refusing God's authority?
How many know Christian language but resist Christian surrender?
How many honor Christ with their lips while protecting idols in their hearts?
Judas did not merely hand Jesus over.
He used the appearance of intimacy to conceal rebellion.
That is why his story remains terrifying.
"When Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind..." (Matthew 27:3)
The Greek word used here is μεταμεληθεὶς (metamelētheis).
But it is not the same word used for true repentance.
The New Testament often uses another word:
A transformation of mind and heart leading toward God.
Only one ran back to Jesus.
Many people live trapped between those two realities.
But instead of running toward Christ, they run from Him.
That is exactly where Satan wants them.
Because shame whispers that failure is final.
The Gospel declares that failure can become the beginning of redemption.
Yet the Cross demonstrates that no sin is greater than the mercy of God for those who repent.
The Aramaic name Jesus likely heard throughout His earthly ministry was יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua).
Not "The Lord saves those who never failed."
Judas stands forever as a warning.
Peter stands forever as an invitation.
One believed his sin was bigger than God's mercy.
The other discovered God's mercy was bigger than his sin.
Every reader eventually chooses between those paths.
This is where the story becomes personal.
Maybe your betrayal was not thirty pieces of silver.
Maybe it was years of hidden compromise.
Maybe it was building a version of Jesus who served your agenda instead of surrendering to His.
The question is not whether you have failed.
The question is what you will do next.
The Gospel is not the story of people who never fell.
It is the story of a Savior who restores those who return.
Because the Cross was already anticipating every failure before it happened.
Before you reached the end of yourself.
And He still went to Calvary.
The kind of grace that rewrites destinies.
The kind of grace that takes failures and turns them into testimonies.
The kind of grace that transforms the worst chapters into the beginning of redemption.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
Because every share extends the reach of the Gospel.
Every save preserves truth for another difficult day.
Every follow keeps people connected to biblical encouragement.
But the blood of Christ still saves sinners today.
The most dangerous betrayal was never selling Jesus for silver—it was believing there was nowhere left to run after failing Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF EGLAH
paragraphs: Some names in Scripture thunder across history.
Others appear almost unnoticed, like a single footprint in the sand before the tide comes in.
Eglah is one of those names.
She appears only briefly in the biblical record, mentioned almost as an afterthought among King David's wives:
"His sixth son was Ithream, by Eglah David's wife." (2 Samuel 3:5)
And yet Scripture never wastes words.
Every name preserved by the Holy Spirit exists for a reason.
Some stories are written in paragraphs.
This is the untold story hidden behind one of the Bible's quietest women.
And it may be far more relevant to your life than you realize.
Because many people know exactly what it feels like to be an Eglah.
Standing in the shadows while everyone else seems to occupy center stage.
Yet throughout Scripture, God repeatedly reveals a stunning truth:
He specializes in seeing the people nobody else notices.
The Hebrew name עֶגְלָה (Eglah) literally means "heifer" or "young cow."
To modern ears, that sounds strange.
But within the ancient Hebrew world, names often carried symbolic beauty, vitality, fertility, strength, and value.
They reflected hopes, circumstances, character, or prophetic significance.
What we know with certainty is remarkably little.
Eglah was one of David's wives.
She is listed sixth among the wives mentioned during David's reign in Hebron.
That is the extent of the biblical record.
And perhaps that silence itself carries a lesson.
Modern culture teaches us that significance is measured by visibility.
The Kingdom of God measures differently.
Heaven has never confused prominence with importance.
Many of God's most treasured servants occupy only a few verses.
Yet they remain eternally known by God.
One of the most beautiful titles of God appears in the story of Hagar.
After being abandoned and afflicted, she encounters God in the wilderness and declares:
Not merely a God who sees nations.
Not merely a God who sees kings.
The Hebrew verb רָאָה (ra'ah) means to see, perceive, understand, notice, and attend to.
God's seeing is never passive observation.
This truth changes everything about Eglah.
History may know almost nothing about her.
Some people reading this are exhausted from living unseen lives.
The God who saw Hagar also saw Eglah.
Eglah's story becomes even more intriguing when viewed within the complicated realities surrounding David's family.
The years in Hebron were not simple years.
David was a man after God's own heart, yet he was also a deeply flawed man.
The household surrounding him reflected both divine blessing and human brokenness.
This is one reason Scripture feels so real.
The Bible never airbrushes its heroes.
And that honesty points us directly toward the Gospel.
Because Scripture is not ultimately about impressive people.
It is about a perfect Savior.
The Bible repeatedly exposes human weakness so that divine grace shines brighter.
From Genesis to Revelation, the message remains astonishingly consistent:
This brings us to the heart of the biblical story.
The greatest scandal in history is not human sin.
The Hebrew word חֵן (chen) means grace, favor, undeserved kindness.
In the Greek New Testament, the word becomes χάρις (charis).
A gift that cannot be earned.
A mercy that cannot be purchased.
A love that cannot be deserved.
The entire Bible moves toward the arrival of Jesus Christ.
The Redeemer who would step into humanity's scandal and rewrite it forever.
When Jesus arrived, He consistently moved toward the people society ignored.
The Greek text repeatedly describes Jesus being moved with compassion.
A profound emotional stirring from the deepest part of one's being.
Jesus did not merely tolerate broken people.
Most readers race past names like Eglah.
We hurry toward the stories we recognize.
Yet these names remind us that God's kingdom contains countless faithful people whose impact remains largely unseen.
History often celebrates the visible few.
One day eternity will reveal stories never told on earth.
The Lord who records every sparrow's fall has never misplaced a single faithful life.
Perhaps the greatest lesson from Eglah is that she was never the main character.
The modern world tells us to build our own kingdoms.
Scripture invites us to participate in Christ's.
The modern world tells us to make our names great.
Jesus tells us to make His name great.
The modern world tells us to pursue visibility.
Jesus calls us to pursue faithfulness.
Because in the end, salvation was never found in being remembered by history.
It is found in being known by Christ.
"I know my own and my own know me." (John 10:14)
The Greek word for "know" here is γινώσκω (ginōskō).
It describes intimate, personal, relational knowledge.
Not that the world knows your name.
But that the King of Heaven does.
Maybe Eglah's greatest contribution to Scripture is her reminder that God's story includes people who seem insignificant.
People who occupy only a verse.
People who wonder if they matter.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to save famous sinners.
At Calvary, all stand equally in need of grace.
And at the empty tomb, all who trust Christ receive the same mercy.
That is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
But because it reveals a Savior who enters human scandal and transforms it into redemption.
A Savior who takes broken stories and rewrites them with grace.
A Savior who takes forgotten people and makes them beloved children of God.
And perhaps that is why Eglah's brief appearance remains preserved forever in the Word of God.
But because she mattered to God.
And if you have ever felt unseen, forgotten, overlooked, or insignificant, remember this:
The God who remembered Eglah has not forgotten you.
The God who saw Hagar sees you.
The God who redeemed David's broken household can redeem your story.
The God revealed in Jesus Christ is still rewriting lives today.
Maybe your name is not known by the world.
But if you belong to Christ, it is written where it matters most.
If this story stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Have you ever felt unseen by people but seen by God?
The names the world forgets are often the very names God remembers forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A Leader Can Be Popular and Wrong
paragraphs: A Leader Can Be Popular and Wrong
Voices rose like thunder. Approval flowed. The people were united. The leader stood at the center of it all, celebrated, admired, affirmed.
That may be one of the most uncomfortable truths in all of Scripture.
Popularity has never been proof of righteousness.
Applause has never been evidence of truth.
A leader can be admired by millions and still be walking in rebellion against God.
A leader can have influence, charisma, authority, talent, intelligence, vision, success, and a devoted following while simultaneously leading people away from the heart of the Lord.
We live in an age where numbers are often mistaken for anointing. Followers become substitutes for faithfulness. Visibility becomes confused with holiness. Influence becomes confused with obedience.
Yet the Bible repeatedly confronts us with a sobering reality:
God does not measure leaders the way people do.
The prophet Samuel learned this lesson when searching for Israel's next king.

“Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
(1 Samuel 16:7)
The Hebrew word for heart here is לֵבָב (levav), meaning the inner person, the true center of thoughts, desires, motives, and character.
Human beings often evaluate what can be seen.
That truth should shake every leader.
Because sometimes the most dangerous leader is not the obviously corrupt one.
The one whose popularity becomes a shield against accountability.
Yet when the people demanded an idol, Aaron gave them one.
Exodus records one of the most shocking leadership failures in Scripture.
The people wanted a visible god.
Instead of standing firm, Aaron surrendered to public pressure.
And led the people into sin.
Leadership is tested not when people agree with you.
Leadership is tested when obedience to God becomes unpopular.
Anyone can stand with truth when truth is celebrated.
Faithful leaders stand with truth when truth costs them something.
During His earthly ministry, crowds followed Him everywhere.
Thousands gathered to hear Him teach.
Yet Jesus refused to shape His message around public approval.
In John 6, after delivering difficult teaching, many followers walked away.

ἀπῆλθον εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω
(apēlthon eis ta opisō)
Jesus did not change the message to keep the audience.
Because truth was more important than popularity.
Faithfulness was more important than influence.
Obedience was more important than acceptance.
That principle is almost foreign in modern culture.
Today leaders are often tempted to tell people what they want to hear.
The prophet Jeremiah warned about this danger centuries ago.
They comforted people without confronting sin.
Not every comforting voice is a godly voice.
Not every popular message is a biblical message.
Not every admired leader is leading people toward Christ.
Sometimes people follow leaders because they make them feel good.
Jesus calls us to follow leaders who help us become holy.
Those are not always the same thing.
The Lord repeatedly warned Israel about leaders who gathered followers while drifting from God.
Ezekiel spoke against shepherds who fed themselves rather than the flock.
Micah rebuked leaders who distorted justice.
Isaiah confronted rulers who honored God with their lips while their hearts remained far away.
Again and again Scripture reminds us that leadership is not measured by popularity.
The greatest example is Jesus Himself.
No leader in history was more righteous.
Yet no leader in history was more rejected.
The same crowd that cried “Hosanna” eventually shouted “Crucify Him.”
The Messiah remained the Messiah whether people applauded Him or condemned Him.
That reality should deeply challenge us.
Many believers spend enormous energy asking:
The Apostle Paul understood this tension.
Writing to the Galatians, he asked:
“Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God?”
The Greek word for approval is πείθω (peithō), carrying the idea of winning favor or persuading others.
Paul understood something every Christian leader must learn.
The pursuit of human approval eventually collides with obedience to God.
Sooner or later a choice must be made.
And every leader reveals whom they truly serve by what they choose when that collision occurs.
This is not merely a warning for pastors, teachers, or public figures.
Every one of us leads someone.
And every one of us faces the temptation to exchange truth for approval.
The frightening reality is that crowds can be wrong.
“The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.”
Perhaps the most dangerous question a leader can ask is:
“How can I remain faithful to Christ?”
That is the voice every believer should long to hear.
Because there is coming a day when followers, influence, likes, status, recognition, titles, awards, and public admiration will all disappear.
And on that day, no leader will be evaluated by popularity polls.
No one will be judged by audience size.
No one will stand before God carrying social influence as a defense.
The only question that will matter is faithfulness.
Were we faithful to Christ when obedience was costly?
Were we faithful when truth was unpopular?
Were we faithful when compromise seemed easier?
Were we remain loyal to Jesus when the crowd moved in another direction?
That question reaches beyond leadership and into every human heart.
Because each of us follows someone.
And before we follow any leader, we must first follow Christ.
The greatest scandal in history was not that sinful humanity rejected Jesus.
The greatest scandal was that God used that rejection to accomplish salvation.
At Calvary, what appeared to be defeat became redemption.
What looked like failure became victory.
What looked like the end became a new beginning.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
This is the beauty of grace.
This is why every broken story can be rewritten.
Because Jesus specializes in taking what seems ruined and transforming it into something redeemed.
Maybe this article exposed something uncomfortable.
Maybe it revealed places where approval has become more important than obedience.
Maybe it uncovered leaders you've followed too closely.
Maybe it exposed areas where you've been leading for applause instead of faithfulness.
If so, don't ignore that conviction.
His grace is greater than your failure.
His mercy is deeper than your compromise.
His cross is sufficient for your repentance.
And His resurrection power is still transforming hearts today.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
Someone you know may desperately need this reminder today.
Supporting the mission helps expand Gospel-centered content that reaches hearts, strengthens believers, and points people to Jesus Christ around the world.
One day the crowd's voice will disappear, but the voice of Jesus will still be calling your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Did Jacob Bury the Household Idols?
paragraphs:
Why Did Jacob Bury the Household Idols?
The Forgotten Grave That Exposed a Family's Hidden Sin—and Why It Still Speaks to Every Heart Today
There are moments in Scripture that seem so small we almost read past them without slowing down. A few verses. A brief command. A handful of objects buried beneath an ordinary tree.
Yet hidden beneath the soil of Shechem lies one of the most powerful pictures of repentance in the entire Old Testament.
Not a mountain covered in fire.
That single act would forever mark the turning point of Jacob's household, revealing that before God transforms our future, He often asks us to bury the things we've secretly been carrying.
Perhaps that is why this story still reaches into our generation with unsettling clarity.
Many of us profess faith while quietly protecting idols no one else can see.
Most are carved inside the human heart.
And before Jesus can rewrite everything, something must first be buried.

The story begins after one of the darkest chapters in Jacob's family history. Genesis 34 records violence, revenge, deception, and bloodshed after Dinah's tragic defilement. Jacob's sons answered sin with even greater sin, slaughtering an entire city under the appearance of covenant faithfulness.
The covenant family had become almost indistinguishable from the pagan nations surrounding them.
Genesis 35 opens with God speaking again.
"Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there. Make an altar there to God, who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau." (Genesis 35:1)
God does not begin with punishment.
No one walks back to Bethel while still carrying the gods of Shechem.
He turns toward his family and gives one of the strongest calls to repentance recorded in Genesis.
"So Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, 'Put away the foreign gods that are among you and purify yourselves and change your garments.'" (Genesis 35:2)
The Hebrew phrase translated "put away" is הָסִרוּ (hāsîrû), meaning remove completely, turn aside, take away. It is not merely hiding sin. It is separating from it.

The "foreign gods" are called אֱלֹהֵי הַנֵּכָר ('elohei hanekhar), literally "the gods of foreigners" or "alien gods." They represented the beliefs, loyalties, and identities of the surrounding pagan cultures. These were not harmless decorations. They embodied spiritual allegiances that violated Israel's covenant with the one true God.
Many readers naturally ask: Where did these idols come from?

Years earlier, Rachel had stolen her father Laban's household gods, called תְּרָפִים (terāphîm), in Genesis 31. Scholars have long debated their exact function. They may have represented family deities, symbols of inheritance rights, or objects consulted for divination. Whatever their role, Scripture consistently portrays them as illegitimate substitutes for trusting God.

Additional idols likely came from the spoils taken after the destruction of Shechem (Genesis 34). In the ancient Near East, conquering armies often seized religious objects alongside valuables. Without realizing it, Jacob's household had accumulated visible reminders of invisible compromise.
How often do believers do the same?
We remove ourselves from obvious sin while quietly preserving smaller compromises that seem harmless.
We keep bitterness because it feels justified.
We keep pride because it feels earned.
We keep secret addictions because no one knows.
We keep materialism because everyone else does.
We keep self as king while still calling Jesus Lord.
The Apostle John would later conclude his first epistle with a surprisingly direct warning:
"Little children, keep yourselves from idols." (1 John 5:21)
Because idols are never merely external.
They are whatever competes for the affection, trust, fear, hope, security, or worship that belongs to God alone.

Timothy Keller famously summarized this biblical truth by describing an idol as anything more fundamental to your happiness, identity, or security than God Himself. While that phrasing is modern, the principle is deeply rooted in Scripture.
Jacob's family then does something astonishing.
"They gave to Jacob all the foreign gods that they had, and the rings that were in their ears. Jacob hid them under the oak that was near Shechem." (Genesis 35:4)
The text has puzzled readers for centuries.

Many scholars believe these earrings functioned as pagan amulets connected to idol worship, magical protection, or religious rituals. In the ancient Near East, jewelry often carried spiritual significance beyond simple ornamentation. Jacob removes not only the idols themselves but also the accessories associated with false worship.
Sometimes even the reminders must go.
The Hebrew verb translated "hid" is טָמַן (ṭāman), meaning to bury, conceal permanently, or place out of sight. This was not temporary storage.
He never intended to retrieve them.
The oak near Shechem became a silent cemetery for false gods.
Centuries later, Jesus would speak words that echo this same spiritual reality:
"If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me." (Luke 9:23)

The Greek word translated "deny" is ἀπαρνησάσθω (aparnēsasthō), meaning to utterly renounce, to disown, or to refuse association with. It is the same family of language used when Peter denied knowing Jesus—but here Christ calls believers to deny the old self instead.
Biblical repentance is not adding Jesus to our existing loyalties.
It is burying every rival king.
Notice what happens immediately after Jacob's obedience.
"And they journeyed, and a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob." (Genesis 35:5)

This does not teach that repentance guarantees an easy life. Scripture consistently rejects such a conclusion. Instead, it demonstrates that walking in covenant faithfulness places God's people under His gracious care according to His sovereign purposes.
At Bethel, God reaffirmed Jacob's covenant promises, reminding him once again that his identity rested not in his failures but in God's faithfulness.
Jacob's story ultimately points beyond itself.
Every buried idol whispers toward another hill outside Jerusalem.

At the cross, Jesus Christ bore not only our sins but every false god that enslaved us. Paul writes in Colossians 3:5, "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you..." The Greek expression νεκρώσατε (nekrōsate) literally means "put to death," not merely suppress. Sin is not managed; it is mortified through union with Christ.

Three days after His burial, Jesus rose victorious, proving that death does not have the final word. Because He lives, those who trust Him can leave the graves of their former idols behind and walk in newness of life.
The scandal of Jacob's household was real.
The God who called Jacob back to Bethel is the same God who, through Jesus Christ, still calls sinners home today.
Perhaps the most dangerous idols are not the ones sitting on shelves but the ones sitting on thrones inside our hearts.
Anything we cannot surrender has already become our master.
The question is not whether we possess idols.
The question is whether we are willing to bury them.
Maybe you've been carrying one so long that it feels like part of your identity.
Maybe you've learned to worship on Sundays while quietly protecting it the rest of the week.
Jacob's story reminds us that genuine revival begins not with louder worship but with deeper repentance.
And before resurrection came a cross.

If this message exposed something God has been quietly speaking to your heart, don't ignore His voice today. Be honest before Him. Your testimony may become the encouragement another weary soul desperately needs.
Sometimes God uses a single story from Scripture to awaken a heart that has grown spiritually numb.
Because when the Gospel changes one life, that transformed life often becomes the beginning of someone else's journey home.
Some idols are buried beneath trees. Others must be buried beneath the cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY ARE CHRISTIANS SO DIVIDED ONLINE?
paragraphs: WHY ARE CHRISTIANS SO DIVIDED ONLINE?
Somewhere between a Bible verse and a comment section, something went terribly wrong.
A third arrives with a theological thread.
A fourth declares everyone else deceived.

Within minutes, brothers and sisters who claim allegiance to the same crucified and risen Christ are tearing each other apart before an audience of believers, skeptics, seekers, atheists, and wounded souls watching silently from the shadows.
Many of them came looking for Jesus.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question is not why the world is confused about Christianity.
Perhaps the question is why Christians are becoming confused about Christianity.
Because the internet did not create division.
It revealed what was already living in the human heart.
The problem is older than Facebook.
The first family on earth experienced division.
The first disciples argued over greatness.
The first churches wrestled with factions.
The first century believers had disputes over doctrine, leadership, traditions, ethnicity, and spiritual gifts.
But the speed, scale, and visibility of division have become unprecedented.
The Apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians:
“I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree and that there be no divisions among you.”
The word Paul used for “divisions” is the Greek word σχίσματα (schismata).
It literally means tears, splits, or fractures.
The image is not two people discussing truth.
The image is a garment being ripped apart.
Paul understood something many Christians online forget.
Not every disagreement creates a schism.
The Real Enemy Is Not Who You Think
Many believers speak as though their greatest enemy is another denomination.
Yet Scripture presents a radically different picture.
The Greek phrase is οὐκ ἔστιν ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα.
“Our struggle is not toward blood and flesh.”
The enemy is not another believer.
The enemy is not a Christian who interprets secondary issues differently.
The enemy is not someone whose worship style differs from ours.
Yet online environments reward us for behaving as though fellow believers are the opposition.
And suddenly Christians become experts at attacking each other while forgetting how to rescue the lost.
The internet did not invent this temptation.
One of the most fascinating discoveries in biblical language is the word Paul uses for humility.
In the ancient world it was frequently despised.
Choosing to take the lesser place.
The shocking reality is that Christianity transformed humility from a weakness into a virtue.
Then he describes the Son of God descending into humanity, suffering, rejection, humiliation, and death.
The One who created galaxies willingly lowered Himself.
Yet many Christians online cannot endure a disagreement without launching a public war.
The contradiction should make all of us uncomfortable.
Including every person reading these words.
Because division often begins where humility ends.
The internet has created unprecedented access to biblical knowledge.
This can be a tremendous blessing.
But Scripture warns about a danger many overlook.
The Greek verb for “puffs up” is φυσιοῖ (physioi).
It paints the picture of something inflated.
Knowledge without love produces spiritual inflation.
A person may know Greek grammar and still lack grace.
Know doctrine and still lack gentleness.
Know theology and still lack Christlike character.
Yet many stood face-to-face with the Messiah and failed to recognize Him.
Being right is not the highest Christian calling.
Being transformed into the image of Christ is.
The Tower of Babel Has Returned
In Genesis 11 humanity gathered around a single ambition.
“Let us make a name for ourselves.”
The Hebrew phrase is נַעֲשֶׂה־לָּנוּ שֵׁם (na'aseh lanu shem).
“Let us make for ourselves a name.”
The original sin beneath Babel was not architecture.
And online Christianity often falls into the same trap.
Even ministry can become self-promotion dressed in spiritual language.
When personal brands become more important than Christ's reputation, Babel is quietly being rebuilt.
One viral controversy at a time.
Before His crucifixion, Jesus prayed one of the most profound prayers recorded in Scripture.
Just as a body contains many parts yet remains one body.
Jesus understood there would be differences.
But His prayer reveals God's heart.
Unity rooted in truth and love.
One of the most tragic realities of online Christian division is that unbelievers are watching.
The wounded former church member is watching.
The broken woman searching for hope at two in the morning is watching.
Many are not reading theological papers.
And what they observe often becomes their perception of Christ.
“By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”
Not if you win every debate.
Not if you dominate every argument.
Love remains the unmistakable evidence of genuine discipleship.
The Mirror We Do Not Want to Face
Perhaps the reason this conversation feels uncomfortable is because every Christian has contributed to the problem at some level.
Some through pride disguised as discernment.
The deepest challenge is not identifying who is causing division.
The deepest challenge is allowing God to reveal where division lives inside us.
The Hebrew word for search is חָקַר (chaqar).
Maybe that prayer is exactly what online Christianity needs.
Because revival has never started with winning debates.
Imagine what could happen if Christians became known online not merely for defending truth but for displaying Christ.
Imagine believers who refused to treat fellow Christians as enemies.
Imagine comment sections that reflected heaven more than culture.
Imagine followers of Jesus who cared more about God's glory than personal victory.
Perhaps then the world would once again see what made Christianity so powerful in the first place.
Jesus remains the answer to what divides us.
The same blood that forgives our sins also destroys the walls that separate us.
The cross is not merely where we are reconciled to God.
It is where we are reconciled to one another.
Maybe that is why the enemy works so hard to keep Christians fighting.
Because a united Church is dangerous.
And a Christ-centered Church changes the world.
So before typing the next comment...
One day every argument will fall silent, every denomination will disappear, every platform will fade, and only one name will remain standing.
Jesus never asked His Church to be famous. He asked us to be faithful.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN ALL CHRISTIANS CAST OUT DEMONS?
paragraphs:
CAN ALL CHRISTIANS CAST OUT DEMONS?
The Question That Divides Churches, Terrifies Believers, and Reveals What Jesus Actually Taught
There are few subjects that create as much fascination, fear, controversy, confusion, and curiosity among Christians as the subject of demons.
Some believers have never seen what they believe to be demonic activity.
Others claim to have witnessed dramatic deliverances.
Some churches avoid the subject completely.
Others make it the center of nearly everything.
And somewhere between fear and sensationalism sits an uncomfortable question that many sincere believers quietly ask:
Can all Christians cast out demons?
The answer matters because it forces us to confront a deeper question:
What exactly did Jesus intend His followers to do?
Have we misunderstood spiritual authority because we have forgotten spiritual intimacy?
The debate is not ultimately about demons.
It is about what happens when ordinary believers begin taking Jesus seriously.
And it is about the beautiful truth that runs through every page of Scripture:
Imagine standing in a first-century village.
The air is thick with dust.
The demons recognize Him before the crowd does.
They know exactly who He is.
The Gospels repeatedly record an astonishing reality:
The kingdom of darkness fears Jesus.
Not because He is merely a teacher.
Not because He is merely a prophet.
But because He is God incarnate.
When Jesus commands demons to leave, they leave.
The Greek word frequently used regarding authority is ἐξουσία (exousia).
It means delegated authority, lawful power, the right to act.
It belongs to Him because He is Lord.
This becomes the foundation for understanding everything else.
The question is never whether believers have power in themselves.
The question is whether Christ chooses to share His authority with His followers.
Scripture answers that question with a resounding yes.
In Luke 10:19, Jesus tells His disciples:
"Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy..."
The disciples operate under His authority.
Because whenever believers begin focusing more on demons than on Jesus, they become vulnerable to error.
The New Testament never presents deliverance ministry as a celebration of human power.
Instead, it is a testimony to Christ's victory.
"Jesus gave that authority only to the apostles."
Scripture should never be approached casually.
But the biblical evidence extends beyond the Twelve.
In Luke 10, Jesus sends seventy-two disciples.
When they return, they rejoice that demons submitted to them in Jesus' name.
Authority over demons was not restricted solely to the Twelve.
The kingdom was advancing through ordinary followers.
"And these signs will accompany those who believe: in My name they will cast out demons..."
The phrase "those who believe" is broad.
The focus is not an elite class of Christians.
The focus is believers acting in Christ's name.

While scholars continue discussing textual considerations surrounding the longer ending of Mark, the broader New Testament witness consistently demonstrates believers exercising spiritual authority through Christ.
The doctrine does not stand or fall on one passage.
It is woven throughout the fabric of the New Testament.
But then we encounter one of the most sobering moments in Scripture.
Seven men attempt to cast out demons using Jesus' name.
"Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?"
Because they treated authority like a formula.
They wanted Jesus' authority without Jesus Himself.
And that mistake is still being repeated today.
The kingdom does not operate through magic words.
It operates through genuine union with Christ.
The Hebrew concept behind true spiritual authority is deeply connected to covenant relationship.
In the Old Testament, God's people were never empowered independently from Him.
The same principle remains true under the New Covenant.
Authority flowing from relationship becomes ministry.
This is why some believers become confused.
They have seen bizarre demonstrations online.
They have watched self-proclaimed deliverance experts turn spiritual warfare into entertainment.
But Scripture repeatedly directs attention back to Christ.
Deliverance was never intended to become a stage performance.
It was intended to reveal the King's victory.
The Gospel remains greater than any demon.
The resurrection remains greater than any darkness.
Jesus remains greater than every spiritual enemy.
Can all Christians cast out demons?
Biblically speaking, the answer appears to be yes—in the sense that authority belongs to Christ and can be exercised by believers acting under His lordship.
However, that answer requires careful qualification.
Not every believer is called to the same ministry expression.
Not every believer possesses the same spiritual gifts.
Not every believer will encounter the same situations.
The New Testament recognizes diversity within the body of Christ.
Yet nowhere does Scripture teach that ordinary believers are powerless against demonic forces.
Believers share in that authority because they belong to Him.
Perhaps the more important question is not:
Perhaps the more important question is:
Because demons fear Christ far more than they fear human confidence.
Spiritual authority is not measured by volume.
It is measured by genuine submission to the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
The Aramaic language spoken during Jesus' earthly ministry carried profound relational depth.
When Jesus taught His followers to pray, He addressed God as Father.
This pattern appears throughout the New Testament.
The disciples who exercised authority were first disciples who followed.
Before public ministry came private surrender.
And perhaps this is where many readers find themselves today.
Not battling a demonized man in a distant village.
The greatest miracle may not be casting out a demon.
The greatest miracle may be realizing that Jesus has not given up on you.
The same Savior who commanded demons also welcomed sinners.
The same Lord who rebuked darkness also restored failures.
The same Christ who defeated hell also forgave Peter.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Maybe you've spent years believing God could use everyone except you.
Maybe you've carried the weight of past failures.
Yet Scripture repeatedly tells the story of a God who specializes in rewriting lives.
Yet grace wrote a new ending.
But because Christ redeemed what seemed beyond redemption.
That is still what Jesus does today.
So can all Christians cast out demons?
The biblical evidence points toward believers sharing in Christ's authority.
But the deeper truth is even more beautiful.
The greatest evidence of Christ's authority is not merely demons leaving.
It is broken hearts becoming healed hearts.
It is dead souls becoming alive.
And perhaps that miracle is happening in your life right now.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is one encounter with Jesus away from a completely rewritten story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why God Told Ezekiel to Do Something Bizarre
paragraphs:
Why God Told Ezekiel to Do Something Bizarre
The Shocking Prophetic Sign That Reveals Humanity's Hidden Rebellion—and Why Jesus Is the Only Hope
What if the strangest command God ever gave one of His prophets was never meant to entertain your curiosity—but to expose your own heart?

Some passages in Scripture make us uncomfortable. Others confuse us. But then there are those that stop us in our tracks because they seem almost impossible to understand. The book of Ezekiel contains several of these moments, and perhaps none is more startling than when God commanded His prophet to perform actions so bizarre, so humiliating, and so emotionally exhausting that many readers wonder, "Why would God ask anyone to do this?"
Or was something much deeper unfolding before the eyes of a nation that had stopped listening?

This is not merely the story of an eccentric prophet. This is the story of a holy God pursuing a rebellious people with relentless love. It is a story that begins with scandal and ends with grace, because that is what God has always done. He takes shattered lives, impossible situations, and hopeless sinners and rewrites everything through His redeeming mercy.

If you have ever wondered whether God still speaks to people who have ignored Him, whether He still pursues those who have wandered far away, or whether your own failures have become too great to redeem, then Ezekiel's story is also your story.

The year was around 593 BC. Jerusalem still stood, but spiritually it had already collapsed. The people continued offering sacrifices while their hearts bowed before idols. They claimed God's covenant while rejecting God's authority. Religion continued, but repentance disappeared.

The Hebrew word used repeatedly throughout Ezekiel for idols is גִּלּוּלִים (gillûlîm), a deliberately insulting term often translated "idols," but carrying the sense of "worthless things," "filthy objects," or even "dung idols." God was exposing not merely false worship but the disgusting spiritual corruption hidden beneath outward religion.
His very name, יְחֶזְקֵאל (Yeḥezqē'l), means "God strengthens."
He would need every bit of that strength.
Unlike many prophets who simply preached, Ezekiel became God's living sermon.

God instructed him to lie on his left side for 390 days representing Israel's years of guilt (Ezekiel 4:4–5). Then he was to lie on his right side for forty days representing Judah's guilt (Ezekiel 4:6). He was commanded to ration food and water as a picture of the coming siege upon Jerusalem.
Then came perhaps the most disturbing command.
"You shall eat it as a barley cake, having baked it in their sight over human dung." (Ezekiel 4:12)
At first glance, this shocks nearly every modern reader.
Was God actually commanding His prophet to violate the Law?
"Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I have never defiled myself..." (Ezekiel 4:14)
Unlike Israel, Ezekiel had carefully obeyed God's dietary laws all his life. His response was not rebellion but reverence.
Instead of human waste, the Lord permitted him to use cow dung.
"So I will let you bake your bread over cow's dung instead of human excrement." (Ezekiel 4:15)
God was not delighting in humiliation.

Throughout the ancient Near East, dried animal dung was commonly used as cooking fuel. Human waste, however, represented ceremonial defilement and utter disgrace. God's message was that Israel's rebellion would drive them into foreign lands where they would experience shame, scarcity, uncleanness, and separation from the blessings they had long taken for granted.
The point was never the fuel.
The point was the consequences of sin.
God was allowing Ezekiel's daily life to become visible prophecy.
People who ignored sermons could not ignore what they saw.
Then God commanded something even more heartbreaking.
Ezekiel was told to shave his head and beard (Ezekiel 5:1).

For an Israelite priest, this was deeply shameful. According to the Law, priests were forbidden from disfiguring their beards as pagan mourning rituals (Leviticus 21:5). Yet here God instructed Ezekiel to shave as a prophetic sign—not of paganism—but of the coming disgrace awaiting Jerusalem.
The hair was divided into three parts.
Each action represented God's coming judgment through famine, war, and exile.
Still the people refused to repent.
Perhaps the most emotionally crushing command came later.
Without warning, God told Ezekiel that his beloved wife would die.
"The desire of your eyes I am about to take from you at a stroke." (Ezekiel 24:16)
"But you shall not mourn or weep..." (Ezekiel 24:16)
Imagine losing the person you love most.
Imagine being forbidden to grieve publicly.
Because Ezekiel's silence would mirror what was about to happen to Jerusalem.
The Temple—the very heart of Israel's national identity—would soon fall.
The people's grief would become so overwhelming they would scarcely know how to express it.
His obedience became a sermon no one could ignore.
The Hebrew word often translated "sign" throughout Ezekiel is מוֹפֵת (môp̄ēṯ)—a miraculous sign, wonder, or prophetic symbol that points beyond itself to God's greater purpose.
Everything Ezekiel did pointed somewhere beyond Ezekiel.
Every strange command exposed something far deeper than unusual behavior.
God was revealing that external religion without transformed hearts always ends in destruction.
Centuries later another man would come whose life also became God's living message.
Unlike Ezekiel, He would not merely symbolize judgment.
The Greek Gospel of John introduces Him with breathtaking simplicity:
Ἰδοὺ ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ (Idou ho amnos tou Theou)
Jesus Christ became the final living sign.
Where Ezekiel pointed toward judgment, Jesus absorbed judgment.
Where Ezekiel warned of exile, Jesus opened the way home.
Where Ezekiel carried symbolic suffering, Christ carried real suffering.
Isaiah had foretold it centuries earlier:
"He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities..." (Isaiah 53:5)
On the cross, scandal reached its climax.
The perfectly innocent Son of God hung between criminals.
Yet what appeared to be history's greatest scandal became heaven's greatest rescue.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Your shame does not have the final word.
Your failures do not have the final word.
Your addiction does not have the final word.
None of them have the authority to rewrite your future.
"If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." (2 Corinthians 5:17)
The Greek phrase is καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis)—not repaired, not patched, not improved, but an entirely new creation.
God never asked Ezekiel to perform bizarre signs for shock value.
Every action revealed God's holy justice and His relentless mercy.
Even judgment itself was ultimately meant to call people back before it was too late.
The tragedy was never God's severity.
The tragedy was the people's refusal to listen.
Today, many still dismiss God's warnings while assuming tomorrow is guaranteed.
Every breath is another invitation to come home.
Perhaps today, your own story feels beyond repair.
Perhaps you have convinced yourself that your failures are too great.
The God who pursued rebellious Israel is the same God who pursued the world through His Son.
The cross declares what Ezekiel's signs only foreshadowed.
But God's mercy is greater still.
If this message strengthened your faith and helped you see the beauty of God's Word more clearly, would you prayerfully consider helping us continue this ministry?
One simple way to glorify God is by sharing biblical truth so that more people encounter the Gospel. You never know whose eternity God may touch through a simple act of faithfulness.
If this article spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
The same God who turned Ezekiel's strange obedience into a message of eternal significance is still writing stories today—and He delights in turning scandal into grace through His Son.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF FORTY DAYS IN SCRIPTURE
paragraphs: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF FORTY DAYS IN SCRIPTURE
There are seasons when God seems silent.
Prayers rise but answers do not come.
Doors close. Waiting stretches longer than expected. The heart grows restless. Faith begins asking questions it never imagined asking.
Why is God taking so long?
It echoes through deserts, storms, wildernesses, mountains, prison cells, caves, and empty tombs.
And surprisingly, throughout Scripture, God repeatedly answers that question with a number.

Again and again, whenever God was preparing people for transformation, exposing what was hidden, reshaping identity, testing loyalty, purifying faith, revealing His glory, or preparing the world for a new chapter of redemption, forty appears.
Because before God changes circumstances, He often changes hearts.
In Hebrew, the number forty is אַרְבָּעִים (arba'im).
Throughout the Old Testament, arba'im repeatedly appears during periods of testing, judgment, preparation, purification, transition, and divine revelation.
In Greek, the New Testament uses the word τεσσαράκοντα (tessarakonta).
The biblical writers were not presenting a mystical formula. They were revealing a divine rhythm.
Forty became the language of preparation.
God was not merely delaying outcomes.
The Flood: Forty Days That Exposed a Corrupt World
The first major appearance of forty emerges during one of humanity's darkest moments.
"So the rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights." (Genesis 7:12)
Humanity had descended into violence, rebellion, corruption, and spiritual darkness.
God's judgment came through the Flood.
Yet even here, judgment was not God's final word.
Beyond the waters stood a covenant.
The Flood was not merely about ending a wicked chapter.
It was about beginning a redeemed one.
This theme will repeat throughout Scripture.
God removes what destroys so He can restore what gives life.
Noah entered the ark as a survivor.
He emerged as the beginning of a new humanity.
The wilderness between those realities lasted forty days of rain.
Moses: Forty Days on the Mountain
When Israel arrived at Mount Sinai, Moses ascended into God's presence.
"Moses entered the cloud as he went on up the mountain. And he stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights." (Exodus 24:18)
The Hebrew Scriptures describe God revealing His covenant during this forty-day encounter.
While Moses was receiving divine revelation, Israel was creating a golden calf below.
One man was climbing toward God.
An entire nation was drifting away.
Human nature has not changed much.
We still manufacture substitutes when God seems distant.
We still prefer visible idols over invisible faith.
Yet Moses emerged carrying the Law.
God was preparing a leader capable of carrying the weight of a nation's future.
Few moments feel more relatable than Elijah's collapse.
After experiencing one of the greatest victories in biblical history on Mount Carmel, Elijah ran for his life.
He did not begin with correction.
"Forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God." (1 Kings 19:8)
Sometimes the greatest miracle is not fire from heaven.
Sometimes the greatest miracle is God refusing to abandon a weary servant.
The forty days were not punishment.
The journey reminds every exhausted believer that God's grace often arrives before God's instructions.
Israel's Forty Years: A Nation Being Reshaped
The most famous period involving forty is Israel's wilderness journey.
Because of unbelief, the people wandered for forty years.
The Hebrew text repeatedly emphasizes that God was testing and teaching them.
"And you shall remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that He might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart."
God already knew what was in their hearts.
The wilderness reveals things prosperity often hides.
The wilderness was not merely where Israel wandered.
It was where God revealed them to themselves.
Many believers discover the same truth.
The season they wanted to escape became the season God used to transform them.
Jesus and the Forty Days of Testing
Every previous forty-pointed journey ultimately leads to Christ.
Before beginning His public ministry, Jesus entered the wilderness.
The Greek text uses τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέρας καὶ τεσσαράκοντα νύκτας (tessarakonta hēmeras kai tessarakonta nyktas).
The Son of God enters the wilderness where Israel had failed.
Yet where Adam failed, Jesus stands.
Every temptation is met with Scripture.
Every attack is answered with truth.
Every lie is defeated by obedience.
The wilderness was not proof that God had abandoned Jesus.
The wilderness was preparation for ministry.
Some readers need to hear that today.
Your wilderness may not be evidence of God's absence.
It may be evidence of His preparation.
Perhaps the most overlooked forty-day period occurs after the Resurrection.
"presented Himself alive after His suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God." (Acts 1:3)
They needed undeniable proof that Jesus truly lived.
For forty days, Christ restored confidence, strengthened faith, clarified truth, and prepared His followers for the mission ahead.
The Gospel did not spread because people embraced wishful thinking.
It spread because witnesses became convinced that Jesus Christ had risen from the dead.
The Pattern Hidden Inside Every Forty
When all these events are placed together, a remarkable pattern emerges.
Every forty-day or forty-year season contains the same movement.
Then God launches people into a greater purpose.
Forty is not ultimately about waiting.
This pattern reaches its climax in the Gospel itself.
The greatest scandal in human history was not political corruption, public failure, or moral collapse.
It was humanity's rebellion against its Creator.
The Bible declares that all have sinned.
Every heart carries evidence of the Fall.
Yet God did not abandon His creation.
Jesus Christ stepped into human history, bore our sin, carried our shame, endured our judgment, died on the cross, and rose again victorious.
The scandal of sin became the stage for grace.
That is the heartbeat of Scripture.
Every biblical forty points toward God's ability to take what appears hopeless and transform it into something glorious.
The wilderness is not the destination.
The mountain is not the destination.
The flood is not the destination.
The testing is not the destination.
Perhaps you are living inside your own forty right now.
A season where God feels quieter than expected.
The God who met Noah, Moses, Elijah, Israel, the disciples, and ultimately revealed Himself in Jesus Christ is still writing stories.
And He still specializes in turning scandal into grace.
If this message stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Faithful support helps expand the reach of biblical truth, create more Gospel-centered content, and place Scripture before people who may never otherwise encounter it.
One day you may discover that the season you begged God to end was the very season He used to prepare you for everything He promised.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Absalom's Hair
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From Absalom's Hair
There are some tragedies in Scripture that begin long before the moment everyone remembers.
Most people remember Absalom hanging from a tree.
Few remember how he got there.
Fewer still realize that the very thing he celebrated became the thing that destroyed him.
And if we're honest, that's not just Absalom's story.
Because sometimes the gifts God gives us become idols we worship.
Sometimes the blessings we receive become the source of our pride.
Sometimes the thing that makes us feel important becomes the thing that slowly pulls us away from the One who gave it.
But what happened in his heart was.
The son who looked like a king
The Bible introduces Absalom in a way that feels almost cinematic.
"Now in all Israel there was no one who was praised as much as Absalom for his good looks. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him." (2 Samuel 14:25)
Absalom possessed the kind of appearance that immediately commanded attention.
He carried the presence of royalty.
And then Scripture gives us a fascinating detail.

"When he cut the hair of his head—he used to cut his hair from time to time when it became too heavy for him—he would weigh it, and its weight was two hundred shekels by the royal standard." (2 Samuel 14:26)
The biblical writer could have skipped that detail.
Because the Holy Spirit was showing us something important.
Absalom's hair had become part of his identity.
Part of the thing that made him stand out.
Part of what made him feel powerful.
The Hebrew text repeatedly highlights his physical excellence.
