Not because God delights in our suffering.
Not because He has abandoned us.
But because there are dimensions of His character that can only be discovered in deep waters.
You learn He is Provider when resources disappear.
You learn He is Healer when sickness arrives.
You learn He is Comforter when grief overwhelms you.
You learn He is Savior when you realize you cannot save yourself.
The storm introduces us to aspects of Christ we might never encounter on calm seas.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel itself.
Humanity was caught in a storm far greater than wind and waves.
But Jesus stepped into our boat.
He carried our sin to the cross.
He bore the wrath we deserved.
He died the death we should have died.
And through His resurrection, He spoke peace over the greatest storm humanity has ever faced.
The Hebrew word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) means far more than the absence of conflict.
This is why our mission remains simple:
The sinner becomes a child of God.
Perhaps as you read these words, your own storm feels overwhelming.
Maybe the waves are already crashing over the edge of your boat.
Maybe you've wondered whether God has forgotten you.
The presence of a storm is not evidence of the absence of God.
The same Jesus who slept in the boat remains sovereign today.
The same voice that silenced Galilee still reigns over every circumstance.
The same Savior who calmed the sea still calms hearts.
And if He is in your boat, your storm does not get the final word.
What storm has Jesus carried you through?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone desperately needs to keep going.
Or if you're still in the middle of the storm:
We read every testimony and prayer request.
One day you will realize the storm that almost broke you was the very thing Christ used to reveal Himself to you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF TERAH
paragraphs: The Man History Forgot… But Grace Did Not
They know the father of faith.
They know the man who left everything behind when God called.
But hidden behind Abraham stands a man whose story is rarely told.
A man who started a journey he never finished.
And if we are honest, his story feels far more like ours than Abraham's ever did.
The Bible gives Terah only a handful of verses, yet those verses contain one of Scripture's most haunting portraits of unfinished purpose.
A grief too heavy to carry.
Yet even there, grace was already writing a better ending.
Genesis 11:26 introduces Terah as the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
At first glance, he appears to be little more than a genealogical footnote.
Behind every name is a story.
Behind every story is a soul.
And behind Terah's soul lies a tragedy most readers overlook.
"Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldeans."
No parent is designed to bury a child.
The wound cuts against creation itself.
Parents expect children to stand over their graves.
Some grief changes a person forever.
The Hebrew text says Haran died "עַל־פְּנֵי אָבִיו" (al-penei aviv).
A father staring into a grave that should never have existed.
We often rush past that verse.
Years later, the memory likely still followed him.
Anyone who has lost someone understands this language.
Not because it is written in Hebrew.
Because it is written in tears.
"Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law... and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldeans, to go into the land of Canaan."
Most Christians assume Abraham initiated everything.
Terah walked away from the familiar.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us.
But later revelation gives us a clue.
"Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nahor: and they served other gods."
Terah was not a spiritual giant.
He was not a hero of faith.
Like so many stories in Scripture, grace begins before repentance is complete.
God often starts moving people long before they fully understand who He is.
Long before they have perfect theology.
Long before they have perfect obedience.
Long before they have perfect faith.
Some readers need to hear that.
You may still be carrying confusion.
Yet God may already be drawing you toward Himself.
The journey often starts before understanding arrives.
Then comes one of the saddest sentences in Genesis.
"And they came unto Haran, and dwelt there."
The city carried the same name as Terah's dead son.
Whether coincidence or providence, Scripture leaves us staring at a painful possibility.
A grieving father leaves one Haran behind.
Only to stop permanently in another.
How many lives have done the same?
How many people begin moving toward God's future only to settle in yesterday's pain?
How many believers survive but never truly continue?
Some stop because life broke them in places nobody can see.
And wounded people often build houses where they were only supposed to rest.
Genesis 11:32 delivers the final earthly summary:
"And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years: and Terah died in Haran."
From a human perspective, the story feels heartbreaking.
Because immediately after Terah's death comes Genesis 12.
The chapter that changes history forever.
"Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country..."
God speaks to Abram where Terah stopped.
The story continues where the father ended.
This is one of the most beautiful realities in all of Scripture.
God's purposes are bigger than human failure.
God still brought Abraham to Canaan.
The Gospel echoes this truth even louder.
Every one of us has a little Terah inside.
Places where disappointment became permanent residence.
But as the One who finishes what humanity cannot.
This is why the Gospel is not ultimately about human achievement.
The Bible is not a collection of perfect people reaching God.
It is the story of a perfect Savior reaching imperfect people.
Terah reminds us what broken humanity looks like.
Jesus reveals what redeeming grace looks like.
Perhaps that is why Terah's brief story remains so powerful.
Because many readers see themselves in him.
The person who wonders if the story is already over.
The Gospel answers with a resounding no.
Because Jesus specializes in unfinished stories.
Maybe it is disappointment with God.
Maybe it is a wound nobody else knows exists.
Whatever your Haran may be, Christ is still calling:
There is more ahead than behind.
The most devastating thing about Terah's story is not that he stopped.
The most hopeful thing about the Gospel is that Jesus never does.
The Savior who carried a cross can carry your unfinished story too.
And the same God who continued His covenant after Terah's death is still writing redemption beyond every human limitation today.
The enemy wants you to believe your failure is final.
If this article exposed a place where you have settled in your own Haran, be honest.
Jesus still leads people to Canaan.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Was Jesus Sleeping?
paragraphs:
Why Was Jesus Sleeping?
The Hidden Meaning of the Storm That Reveals Who Is Really Panicking
And somehow, in the middle of all of it, Jesus was asleep.

That detail is so shocking that many readers move past it too quickly. But if we slow down and step into the boat with the disciples, we begin to realize that this moment may be one of the most revealing pictures of Jesus in the entire Gospel narrative.
Because this story is not merely about weather.
And it is about the God who remains at peace while everything around us appears to be falling apart.
The account is recorded in Mark 4:35-41, Matthew 8:23-27, and Luke 8:22-25. Mark, who provides the most vivid details, writes:
"καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ἐν τῇ πρύμνῃ ἐπὶ τὸ προσκεφάλαιον καθεύδων"
(kai autos ēn en tē prymnē epi to proskephalaion katheudōn)
"And He was in the stern, upon the cushion, sleeping."
Mark includes details an eyewitness would remember forever.
While the boat was filling with water.
While experienced fishermen believed they might die.
And that single image confronts every anxious heart that has ever asked:
"God, don't You care what I'm going through?"
The disciples eventually shook Him awake and cried:
"Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing?"
That question is still being asked today.
Many people do not immediately question God's power.
The disciples knew Jesus could do miracles.
What terrified them was that He appeared unconcerned.
Because the sleeping Christ was not an indifferent Christ.
To understand this moment, we must first understand something astonishing about Jesus.
Yet He was also fully man.
The Scriptures never portray Jesus as pretending to be human.
The prophet Isaiah foretold this reality centuries earlier:
"He was despised and rejected by men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief."
After days of ministry, teaching crowds, healing the sick, confronting opposition, and serving people continuously, Jesus was physically exhausted.
The Creator of the universe entered our humanity so completely that He experienced weariness just as we do.
The One who never slumbers according to Psalm 121 entered human flesh and slept.
The Greek word used for sleeping here is "καθεύδων" (katheudōn).
The Son of God was truly human.
And because He became truly human, He understands every weakness we face.
"For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses."
Jesus understands exhaustion because He experienced it.
He understands tears because He shed them.
He understands pain because He carried it.
He understands storms because He stood in them.
Yet there is something even deeper happening.
The Sea of Galilee is known for violent storms.
Surrounded by hills and valleys, sudden winds can rush downward and create dangerous conditions within minutes.
For them to panic suggests the situation was genuinely severe.
Because He trusted the Father completely.
Long before this storm, the Psalms had already described the security of those who trust God.
"In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety."
The Hebrew word for peace here is:
But shalom means far more than the absence of conflict.
The storm outside the boat did not create a storm inside His heart.
That may be one of the greatest lessons in the entire passage.
Many people spend their lives trying to control external circumstances so they can have internal peace.
Internal peace rooted in the Father remains stable regardless of external circumstances.
The disciples had calm seas inside the boat before the storm.
Jesus had a storm outside the boat.
The difference was not the storm.
Then comes one of the most dramatic moments in Scripture.
"He rebuked the wind and said to the sea, 'Peace! Be still!'"
Jesus speaks to the storm as though speaking to an unruly force that must submit to authority.
"The wind ceased, and there was a great calm."
Only Jesus can transform one into the other.
Then He asks a question that cuts directly into the human heart:
"Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?"
The issue was never ultimately the weather.
It was whether they trusted the One in the boat.
Because faith is not believing storms will never come.
Faith is believing Jesus remains Lord when they do.
This moment becomes even more powerful when viewed through the lens of the Gospel itself.
The sleeping Christ in the storm points forward to another moment.
Another situation where God seemed absent.
Another moment when hope appeared lost.
As Jesus hung upon Golgotha, many believed the story was ending in failure.
Yet what looked like defeat was becoming redemption.
What looked like scandal was becoming salvation.
What looked like an ending was becoming a beginning.
This is the recurring pattern of the Gospel.
God often works most powerfully when His presence appears hidden.
The disciples interpreted sleeping as indifference.
The world interpreted the Cross as defeat.
Many believers interpret waiting as abandonment.
And storms are not proof that Jesus has left the boat.
Perhaps that is why this story continues to grip hearts nearly two thousand years later.
Because every generation finds itself somewhere in this boat.
Some are battling hidden struggles nobody else sees.
And all of them eventually ask the same question:
The answer stands at the center of Christianity.
He cared enough to enter our broken world.
He cared enough to rise again.
The sleeping Savior became the crucified Savior.
The crucified Savior became the risen Savior.
And the risen Savior still speaks peace into storms today.
Maybe the greatest miracle in this passage is not that Jesus calmed the sea.
It is that He revealed a kind of peace the storm could not touch.
A peace available to every believer who trusts Him.
A peace purchased through His sacrifice.
A peace rooted in His sovereignty.
A peace that survives even the darkest night.
If this message stirred something in your spirit, do not keep it to yourself.
What storm has challenged your faith recently?
The Gospel spreads when believers refuse to keep God's truth to themselves.
Because sometimes the greatest evidence that God is working is not the absence of the storm—but the presence of Christ within it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY GOD SENT FIERY SERPENTS AMONG HIS PEOPLE
paragraphs: WHY GOD SENT FIERY SERPENTS AMONG HIS PEOPLE
The Judgment That Was Actually Mercy
Most people read the story once and move on.
But if that is all we see, we have missed one of the most emotionally devastating, spiritually revealing, and prophetically beautiful moments in all of Scripture.
Because this story is not ultimately about snakes.
It is about what happens when people grow tired of God's provision.
It is about what happens when blessings become ordinary.
It is about what happens when hearts become poisoned long before bodies are bitten.
And most importantly, it is about how God transformed a symbol of death into a symbol of salvation that would one day point directly to Jesus Christ.
Israel had witnessed miracles most people only dream of seeing.
Manna fell from heaven every morning.
A pillar of cloud guided them by day.
A pillar of fire led them by night.
Yet somehow, it still was not enough.
The wilderness revealed what prosperity often conceals.
The condition of the human heart.
"And the people became impatient on the way. And the people spoke against God and against Moses."
The Hebrew text uses the phrase:
"The soul of the people became short."
This describes spiritual exhaustion that has transformed into resentment.
Unable to see beyond present discomfort.
How many believers today are surrounded by evidence of God's faithfulness while simultaneously questioning His goodness?
How many prayers have already been answered while new complaints continue to rise?
How many miracles have become normal?
"Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless bread."
That statement should stop us cold.
The manna they despised was literally bread from heaven.
Every morning God proved His faithfulness.
The provision had become an entitlement.
The problem was never the manna.
The problem was the heart consuming it.
"Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people."
The word "seraphim" comes from the Hebrew root:
The bites likely produced an intense burning sensation.
The same root gives us the word "seraphim" used in Isaiah 6 for the burning angelic beings surrounding God's throne.
The judgment itself carried imagery connected to holiness.
God was exposing a deeper poison.
The venom in the snakes merely revealed the venom already living inside the camp.
Because before the snakes ever arrived, another poison was spreading.
The serpents exposed externally what already existed internally.
This is one of the most uncomfortable truths in Scripture.
Sometimes God's judgments reveal rather than create.
Sometimes He allows hidden conditions to become visible.
Sometimes the wound must be exposed before healing can begin.
Yet genuine repentance often begins there.
The Hebrew concept behind repentance is often connected to the word:
Repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
The people begged Moses to intercede.
And this is where the story becomes astonishing.
God could have simply removed the snakes.
He could have instantly healed everyone.
He could have spoken a word and ended the crisis.
Instead, He gave a strange command.
Lift it up on a pole.
Anyone who looks at it will live.
At first glance this seems bizarre.
Why use the image of the very thing causing death?
The Hebrew word for bronze is:
A word that sounds remarkably similar to:
The linguistic connection creates powerful symbolism.
The image represented the judgment they deserved.
Yet God transformed that image into the means of healing.
Those bitten were not healed through medicine.
Trusting God's provision when it made little sense.
Believing God's promise when death was already in their veins.
Looking upward when every circumstance screamed hopelessness.
Then, nearly fifteen centuries later, Jesus shocked a religious leader named Nicodemus by connecting Himself directly to this story.
"And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life."
Καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν
Jesus was declaring that the bronze serpent had always been about Him.
The wilderness story was a shadow.
The Apostle Paul later wrote in 2 Corinthians 5:21:
"He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us."
Jesus became the place where judgment and mercy collided.
The Cross became the place where holiness and grace embraced.
The One without venom absorbed the poison of the world.
The innocent One carried the guilt of the guilty.
The spotless Lamb bore the consequences of rebellious sheep.
This changes how we read Numbers 21.
The fiery serpents were not merely punishment.
The bronze serpent revealed the solution.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story still grips us today.
Because we recognize ourselves in it.
We know what it means to complain while blessed.
We know what it means to forget God's faithfulness.
We know what it means to become spiritually numb.
We know what it means to carry hidden poison.
We know what it means to need mercy.
And that is why the story remains breathtaking.
The God who sent judgment also provided salvation.
The God who exposed the wound also provided healing.
The God who revealed sin also provided a Savior.
The wilderness was never the end of the story.
Maybe you have been bitten by something invisible lately.
You have tried everything to fix it.
Everything except looking fully at Christ.
The Israelites were not healed by understanding the serpent.
And many people today know facts about Jesus without ever truly looking at Him.
The same God who provided healing in the wilderness still offers healing today.
And maybe that is why this story continues to echo across thousands of years.
Because every human being eventually discovers the same terrifying truth:
The greatest danger was never the serpent outside us.
It was the poison inside us.
And every human being is invited into the same breathtaking hope:
The Savior has already been lifted up.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
The same Cross that exposed your sin is the Cross that proved you were worth saving.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jonah Obeyed… But His Heart Didn’t
paragraphs:
Jonah Obeyed… But His Heart Didn’t
The Most Dangerous Place to Be Is Not Outside God’s Will—It’s Doing God’s Will Without God’s Heart
There are people reading this right now who are exhausted.
Not because they walked away from God.
They are exhausted because they never stopped.
Yet somewhere deep beneath the surface, something hardened.
And maybe the most terrifying part is this:
The Book of Jonah is often taught as the story of a runaway prophet swallowed by a great fish.
But that is not the climax.
The fish is not the point.
The storm is not the point.
The real scandal of Jonah is that after God corrected his behavior, He still had to confront his heart.
The book begins with God's command:
"The word of the LORD came to Jonah."
Nineveh was not just another city.
It was the capital of Assyria.
Assyria was notorious for violence, cruelty, conquest, and terror.
People he did not want God to forgive.
Not because he doubted God's power.
He ran because he feared God's mercy.
"...that You are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abundant in lovingkindness."
The very attributes that give us hope were the attributes Jonah hated seeing applied to his enemies.
The prophet wasn't afraid God would destroy Nineveh.
How many of us are more like Jonah than we want to admit?
We celebrate grace when it reaches us.
We struggle when it reaches people who hurt us.
We sing about forgiveness until God asks us to forgive.
We love mercy until mercy is given to someone we believe doesn't deserve it.
When Jesus would later walk among sinners, tax collectors, prostitutes, outcasts, and rebels, the religious elite would be scandalized.
Because grace is always scandalous to people who secretly think they earned their place.
The Gospel has never been about deserving.
It has always been about rescue.
After Jonah's rebellion, God sends a great fish.
"וַיְמַן יְהוָה דָּג גָּדוֹל" (Vayeman YHWH dag gadol)
"And the LORD appointed a great fish."
Everything in creation responded to God's voice.
And yet God never gave up on him.
Because somebody reading this needs to hear that.
You may have fought God's calling.
You may have buried conviction beneath years of excuses.
Yet the God of Jonah is still pursuing people.
The fish was never punishment alone.
It was rescue disguised as discipline.
Many of us call it abandonment when God is actually preserving us.
Many of us call it failure when God is redirecting us.
Many of us call it disaster when God is saving us from ourselves.
A picture that would later point forward to Christ Himself.
"For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth."
Jonah emerged from darkness to preach repentance.
Jesus emerged from death to offer salvation.
Jonah was angry when enemies were spared.
Jesus died so enemies could become family.
When Jonah finally enters Nineveh, something astonishing happens.
The nation humbles itself before God.
One of the greatest revivals in Scripture unfolds.
Churches would write books about it.
Conferences would be built around it.
Social media would explode with testimonies.
Yet Jonah sits outside the city angry.
Imagine witnessing hundreds of thousands turning toward God and becoming furious about it.
That is how deep heart-level rebellion can go.
A person can stand in the center of a miracle while refusing to celebrate it.
A person can witness God's power while resenting God's mercy.
A person can obey externally while remaining distant internally.
And suddenly this ancient prophet doesn't seem so ancient anymore.
How many marriages have survived externally while hearts remain distant?
How many Christians attend worship every week while secretly nurturing bitterness?
How many leaders serve faithfully while carrying hidden resentment?
How many believers know God's commands but resist God's compassion?
This is why the final chapter of Jonah is so important.
God appoints a plant to give Jonah shade.
And God asks a devastating question.
Then God contrasts Jonah's concern for a temporary plant with His own compassion for an entire city full of people.
Because Jonah's answer is not the final answer.
God intentionally leaves the story open.
Will we rejoice when grace reaches people we dislike?
Will we celebrate when God forgives those who hurt us?
Will we trust His justice while embracing His mercy?
Will we allow God not only to direct our behavior but transform our hearts?
The Greek word often used throughout the New Testament for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It means a change of mind that produces a change of direction.
Many people think repentance is merely stopping bad behavior.
That is why Jesus repeatedly addressed motives, attitudes, pride, hypocrisy, self-righteousness, and hidden sins.
External obedience without internal surrender was never God's goal.
The Gospel is not behavior management.
Maybe that's where this article finds you today.
Maybe you are Jonah sitting outside Nineveh.
Secretly struggling with disappointment toward God.
Jesus did not merely come to change your actions.
He came to change your heart.
The same grace that saved you is the same grace that can soften what life has hardened.
The same mercy that pursued Jonah is pursuing you.
The same Savior who died for sinners died for the people you struggle to forgive.
And the same God who rewrote Jonah's story is still rewriting stories today.
Maybe the person you least expect.
Maybe the person you believe deserves it least.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
That is the scandal of grace.
That is why the cross remains the greatest reversal in human history.
Be honest. This may have hit harder than you expected.

If we truly desire to glorify God and help spread biblical truth in a world desperate for hope, one of the most practical ways is by helping sustain Gospel-centered content that points people to Christ.
One day we may discover that the greatest miracle in Jonah was never the fish or the city—it was God's refusal to stop pursuing a stubborn heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Forgotten Widow Who Protected a King
paragraphs: The Forgotten Widow Who Protected a King
Scripture remembers the people who protected them.
Most believers can instantly recognize the names David, Solomon, Elijah, Peter, Paul, or Mary. Entire sermons are built around them. Books are written about them. Paintings immortalize them.
Yet buried in the pages of Scripture is a woman most Christians have never heard preached about.
No crown rested upon her head.
No army marched under her command.
And yet God used her to protect the future of a kingdom.
Her name was the woman of Zarephath.
And without her obedience, one of the most important prophets in biblical history might not have survived.
The world often assumes significance belongs to those standing on stages.
Sometimes heaven's greatest victories happen in kitchens.
Sometimes kingdoms are preserved through ordinary acts of faith.
Sometimes history changes because a widow decides to trust God one more day.
The story begins during one of Israel's darkest spiritual collapses.

King Ahab ruled the northern kingdom of Israel. Scripture describes him as one who "did more to provoke the LORD God of Israel to anger than all the kings of Israel that were before him" (1 Kings 16:33).
The nation was drowning in idolatry.
Truth was being exchanged for deception.
The prophet Elijah stood almost alone against a culture racing toward judgment.
The Hebrew text records Elijah's declaration:
"As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives..." (1 Kings 17:1)
For years the skies remained closed.
But God was already preparing an unlikely rescue.
After first sustaining Elijah through ravens at the Brook Cherith, God gave a surprising command.
This was not an Israelite city.
The very place one would least expect God to demonstrate His power.
While Israel abandoned God, a Gentile widow would become an example of faith.
When Elijah arrived, he found her gathering sticks.
She was collecting fuel for one final meal.
Her response is one of the most heartbreaking statements in Scripture.
"I have only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug" (1 Kings 17:12).
Many readers miss the emotional weight of this moment.
This was not a woman wondering how next month would go.
This was a mother looking at starvation.
This was a parent carrying the unbearable burden of watching hope disappear.
Many know exactly how that feels.
Through nights spent staring at ceilings wondering how much more can be endured.
The widow was standing at the edge of human possibility.
He simply told her to trust God's promise.
The command sounds impossible because faith often does.
God frequently asks people to move before they see provision.
Abraham walked before knowing the destination.
Moses stretched out the staff before the sea parted.
The widow baked bread before the miracle appeared.
Faith is not pretending the problem isn't real.
Faith is believing God is greater than the problem.
The miracle that followed remains one of the most beautiful pictures of divine provision in Scripture.
The flour did not run out.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say God filled a warehouse.
It does not say God delivered abundance all at once.
Many believers desperately want God to reveal the entire roadmap.
Often He provides only the next meal.
Because dependence grows where certainty disappears.
Then the story becomes even more shocking.
Many believers understand this chapter far too well.
There are seasons when God's faithfulness seems undeniable.
The widow cried out in anguish.
Elijah carried the child and prayed.
"O LORD my God, let this child's life return to him" (1 Kings 17:21).
Scripture records one of the earliest resurrections in biblical history.
The God of Israel was not merely stronger than drought.
Centuries later, Jesus Himself would reference this widow.
That fact alone should stop us.
Out of countless Old Testament stories, Christ chose to mention her.
In Luke 4:25-26, Jesus reminded His audience that during Elijah's famine many widows existed in Israel.
Yet Elijah was sent to a widow in Zarephath.
Because God's grace often appears where pride least expects it.
The Greek word Jesus used for grace-filled divine favor throughout the New Testament is χάρις (charis).
That truth still changes lives today.
You serve faithfully but receive little recognition.
You pray quietly while others occupy platforms.
You sacrifice while others receive applause.
The widow's story whispers a truth modern culture desperately needs.
God does not measure importance the way people do.
He sees prayers nobody else hears.
He sees tears nobody else notices.
And He uses ordinary people to accomplish extraordinary purposes.
The widow likely never understood the full significance of her obedience.
She simply gave a prophet a meal.
Yet in doing so she protected the very messenger God was using to confront kings.
She helped preserve a prophetic voice that would shake nations.
She became part of God's redemptive story.
This is the scandal of grace.
And ultimately this widow points us toward Someone greater.
"For by grace you have been saved."
At the cross, Jesus took our sin.
At the resurrection, He defeated our death.
What no king could accomplish, the King of Kings accomplished forever.
This is why the widow's story still matters.
Because every rescue in Scripture points toward the greater rescue found in Christ.
Every miracle points toward the Savior.
Every act of provision points toward the Bread of Life.
Every resurrection points toward the empty tomb.
And every forgotten person points toward a God who never forgets.
Perhaps today you feel like the widow.
Running on a handful of flour.
Do not overlook what God can do with what seems insufficient.
The God who sustained the widow.
The God who raised her son.
If this story stirred something in your spirit, do not keep it to yourself.
What part of the widow's journey felt most personal to you?
Because sometimes the people who change history never wear crowns.
They simply trust God when they have one meal left.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: UNDERSTANDING THE DEEP MEANING OF PSALM 139:23–24
paragraphs: UNDERSTANDING THE DEEP MEANING OF PSALM 139:23–24
The Dangerous Prayer That Can Change Everything
There are prayers that comfort us.
There are prayers that protect us.
There are prayers we whisper when life falls apart.
And then there are prayers so dangerous that if God answers them, nothing in us can remain the same.
Psalm 139 ends with one of those prayers.
Not even a prayer for deliverance.
Instead, David asks God to expose him.
To search places inside him that even he cannot see.

"Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting."
(Psalm 139:23–24)
Far fewer dare to pray them.
Because this prayer invites God into the darkest rooms of the human soul.
And once He enters, everything changes.
The Weight of the Original Hebrew

חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
(Chaqreni El, v'da levavi)
"Search me, God, and know my heart."
The Hebrew verb חָקַר (chaqar) means much more than a casual search.
A careful exploration beneath the surface.
This is the language of a miner digging beneath rock.
A king examining every detail before rendering judgment.
David is not asking God for a quick glance.
He is inviting God to conduct a complete excavation.
This is remarkable because Psalm 139 has already established that God knows everything.
The Hebrew there uses the same root.
Because David is not asking for God's information.
He is asking for God's intervention.
He wants God to expose what remains hidden from his own eyes.
The Heart We Cannot Fully See
Scripture repeatedly warns us about trusting it.
The Hebrew word for heart is לֵב (lev).
It represents far more than emotion.
In biblical thought, the heart is the control center of the human person.
"Lord, expose the true reasons behind everything I do."
Because many sins are easy to recognize.
The sins that destroy us most effectively are often the sins we can no longer see.
That is why he does not merely ask God to forgive him.
He asks God to reveal him.
Test Me and Know My Anxious Thoughts
The word בָּחַן (bachan) means to test metal by fire.
Ancient refiners used intense heat to separate precious metals from impurities.
David asks God to do the same with him.
The Hebrew word translated "thoughts" can also refer to troubling inner anxieties.
"Lord, expose what controls me when nobody is watching."
Every believer knows the public version of faith.
The dangerous prayer concerns the private version.
Who are we when applause disappears?
Who are we when ministry success fades?
Who are we when no one notices our sacrifice?
Who are we when no one sees our obedience?
Perhaps the most shocking phrase comes next.

וּרְאֵה אִם־דֶּרֶךְ־עֹצֶב בִּי
(U're'eh im derekh otzev bi)
"See if there is any wicked way in me."
David is asking God to identify every pattern within him that leads away from life and toward destruction.
"See if they have a wicked way."
"See if there is any wicked way in me."
Revival often begins where blame ends.
Many people want transformation around them.
The Gospel Revealed in David's Prayer
Here is where Psalm 139 becomes even more beautiful.
David's prayer reveals a problem humanity cannot solve on its own.
If our hearts are hidden from us...
If sin runs deeper than behavior...
Then self-improvement can never be enough.
This is where Psalm 139 quietly points forward to Jesus Christ.
The Son of God entered humanity not merely to improve us but to save us.
Not merely to modify behavior but to transform hearts.
The New Testament uses the Greek word καρδία (kardia) for heart.
Jesus repeatedly addressed the heart because He knew the real issue was never merely external conduct.
At the cross, Christ carried not only visible sins but hidden ones.
Not only failures but the broken nature producing those failures.
Through His death and resurrection, believers receive more than forgiveness.
The dangerous prayer of Psalm 139 becomes possible because of the grace of Calvary.
The God who searches us is the same God who loves us.
The God who exposes sin is the same God who paid for it.
The God who reveals our wounds is the same God who heals them.
Many people fear God's examination because they assume exposure leads to rejection.
The greatest scandal in your life is not stronger than the grace of Christ.
The deepest secret in your heart is not beyond His mercy.
The most painful chapter in your story is not the final chapter.
Mary Magdalene carried a shattered past.
That is the heartbeat of Scripture.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
And that is the heartbeat of Psalm 139.
The prayer is dangerous because it destroys illusions.
But it is beautiful because it leads to freedom.
David ends with one final plea:
God never exposes merely to shame.
An invitation away from destruction and into life.
An invitation away from self-deception and into truth.
An invitation away from darkness and into Christ.
Perhaps that is why Psalm 139 has survived thousands of years.
Because every generation discovers the same reality.
The greatest danger is not what others know about us.
The greatest danger is what remains hidden within us.
And the greatest miracle is that Jesus loves us enough to search those places anyway.
So before you move on, pause for a moment.
Do I truly want God to answer this prayer?
Because if He does, your comfort may disappear.
But something far greater will emerge.
A heart increasingly surrendered to Christ.
A soul increasingly transformed by grace.
A life increasingly led in the everlasting way.
And perhaps that is the miracle David understood all along.
The God who searches us completely is the God who loves us completely.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
One day you will thank God for every prayer He answered—and especially for the ones that first broke your heart before He healed it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Warrior History Forgot
paragraphs:
The Warrior History Forgot
The Untold Story of Jaribai, One of David’s Forgotten Warriors
Most people dream of being remembered.

A name engraved on a monument.
A story preserved in history.
A legacy passed from generation to generation.
Yet Scripture quietly preserves the memory of men whose names are almost never spoken from pulpits, rarely studied in Bible classes, and nearly forgotten by the modern church.
One of those men was Jaribai.
His story occupies only a few words in Scripture.
Yet those few words reveal something breathtaking about the Kingdom of God.
Because while history celebrates kings, God remembers servants.
While nations preserve the names of rulers, heaven records the names of faithful warriors.
And hidden among David's mighty men stands a forgotten name that still speaks to every believer who has ever wondered if their faithfulness matters.
And his story may be more important than you realize.
The first mention appears in the list of David’s warriors:
"And among the mighty men were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem..." (1 Chronicles 11:26)
Further into the list we find:
"...Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah, that pertained to the children of Benjamin..." (1 Chronicles 11:31)
Many scholars identify Ribai (sometimes rendered Jaribai in historical traditions and textual discussions) as one of the fathers connected to David’s elite warriors.
Though Scripture gives few details, the preservation of his name inside the inspired record reveals something profound.
Nothing in God's Word is accidental.
The Holy Spirit did not waste ink.
Every remembered servant carries a lesson.
And the lesson hidden inside Jaribai's forgotten legacy may be exactly what the modern believer needs to hear.
Because our culture is obsessed with visibility.
The Kingdom of God answers differently.
Jesus never measured significance the way the world does.
The Greek word often translated as servant is:

A bondservant.
One wholly devoted to another.
In the Roman world, a doulos possessed no personal glory.
Yet Jesus repeatedly elevated servants above celebrities.
Heaven celebrates loyalty more than visibility.
This truth runs through the entire story of David’s mighty men.
Yet many of their stories occupy only a single verse.
From a human perspective that seems unfair.
From God's perspective it is glorious.
Because heaven keeps records that earth cannot erase.
The prophet Malachi gives us a remarkable glimpse into God's heart:
"Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him..." (Malachi 3:16)
People whose names may never trend.
People who never build massive platforms.
Jaribai reminds us that obscurity before men does not mean obscurity before God.
In fact, some of heaven's greatest heroes may be completely unknown on earth.
The scandal of grace is that God often chooses the overlooked.
The Gospel repeatedly demonstrates that God writes redemption stories from broken material.
This is why our ministry theme matters so deeply:
The entire Bible is a testimony to divine rewriting.
The Hebrew word for grace is:
In the Greek New Testament, grace becomes:
The unearned favor of God poured out through Christ.
Grace takes failures and rewrites them into testimonies.
Grace takes obscurity and fills it with eternal significance.
Grace takes forgotten names and places them inside God's eternal story.
Jaribai may be forgotten by history.
But he is not forgotten by God.
Perhaps you are raising children who do not yet appreciate your sacrifices.
Perhaps you faithfully serve in a church ministry few people notice.
Perhaps you pray for loved ones year after year without visible answers.
Perhaps you work a job that feels insignificant.
Perhaps your acts of obedience seem invisible.
"And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only... he shall in no wise lose his reward." (Matthew 10:42)
On the day Jesus died, the world saw a failed Messiah.
Religious leaders saw a problem solved.
What looked insignificant was actually history's greatest victory.
That is often how God works.
He hides eternal significance inside ordinary faithfulness.
Jaribai's name survives because God wanted future generations to understand something essential:
The Gospel itself is built upon this truth.
Jesus Christ entered human history not as an earthly celebrity but as a servant.
"He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him." (Isaiah 53:2)
Yet through that humble Servant, salvation came to the world.
The Aramaic-speaking disciples who followed Jesus witnessed something astonishing.
The One who washed feet became the King of Kings.
The One rejected by men became the cornerstone.
The One crucified in shame became the Savior of the world.
That is the power of divine rewriting.
That is the power of grace.
That is the story hidden behind every forgotten servant in Scripture.
And that is the invitation extended to every reader today.
Perhaps that is why Jaribai's name remains preserved after thousands of years.
Not because of what history remembers.
But because of what God remembers.
And if God remembers a forgotten warrior whose story occupies only a few words, imagine how carefully He remembers those redeemed by the blood of His Son.
Maybe you needed to hear that today.
Maybe you've been measuring your life by earthly visibility instead of heavenly faithfulness.
Maybe you've been waiting for recognition when God has been building reward.
Maybe you've mistaken silence for abandonment.
The God who remembered Jaribai remembers you.
The God who recorded forgotten names records faithful obedience.
The God who transformed scandal into grace through Jesus Christ is still rewriting stories today.
And perhaps the greatest legacy is not being known by the world.
Perhaps the greatest legacy is hearing these words from Christ:
Those words will matter long after every earthly platform disappears.
Long after every human monument crumbles.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Many believers around the world are searching for deeper biblical understanding rooted in Scripture, historical context, original languages, and Christ-centered discipleship.
Supporting this work is more than funding content. It is helping spread biblical truth, strengthen believers, reach the lost, and proclaim the Gospel to a generation hungry for hope.
Because sometimes the names history forgets are the names heaven never stops remembering.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Do You Want Me to Do for You?
paragraphs:
What Do You Want Me to Do for You?
The Question That Exposes Every Heart, Reveals Every Wound, and Changes Every Life
There are moments in Scripture that seem so simple we almost miss their terrifying depth.
Then comes a question that feels almost unnecessary.
A question so obvious it almost sounds absurd.
Yet hidden inside it is one of the most life-changing conversations ever recorded.
A blind beggar named Bartimaeus sits beside the road outside Jericho. Dust fills the air. Crowds move around him. Voices rise and fall like waves. He cannot see faces, but he hears rumors.
Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.
For years Bartimaeus had likely heard stories.
And now Hope was walking past him.
"Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!"
The crowd immediately does what crowds often do.
They tell him to be quiet.
But pain that has met possibility cannot stay silent.
So he cries out even louder.
"Son of David, have mercy on me!"
The Creator of the universe halts His journey because one desperate voice refuses to stop calling His name.
The One holding galaxies together pauses for a blind beggar.
The One who sustains creation listens to a forgotten man sitting in the dirt.
The crowd may have ignored him.
The same people who were rebuking Bartimaeus moments earlier suddenly become messengers.
"Take heart. Get up. He is calling you."
Bartimaeus throws aside his cloak and runs toward Jesus.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
In Greek, the phrase appears as:

Τί σοι θέλεις ποιήσω;
(Ti soi theleis poiēsō?)
"What do you desire that I should do for you?"
At first glance the question seems unnecessary.
Because Jesus was never merely interested in fixing symptoms.
Jesus already knew what Bartimaeus needed.
The question was not for Jesus.
God often asks questions not because He lacks information but because we lack revelation.
Not because God could not find Adam.
Jesus asks questions that uncover the soul.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
For perhaps the first time in years, Bartimaeus is invited to speak his deepest desire aloud.
Not what others think he should want.
"Rabboni, that I may regain my sight."
Bartimaeus is not approaching Jesus as a magician.
Faith is not merely believing Jesus can do something.
Faith is trusting who He is.
"Go your way; your faith has made you well."
And he follows Jesus on the road.
But the deeper miracle is often overlooked.
The healing happened after the confession.
This is where the story collides with us.
Because Jesus still asks the same question today.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
Many of us would rather answer with religious clichés.
And while surrender is biblical, Jesus often presses deeper.
Because beneath our church language are hidden realities.
Many believers have become experts at pretending.
We know how to look strong.
We know how to sound spiritual.
We know how to smile while bleeding internally.
But Jesus does not heal the version of us we perform.
He heals the version of us we surrender.
That is why this question can feel uncomfortable.
If Jesus stood before you right now and asked:
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
Would you ask Him to heal your marriage?
Restore your relationship with your children?
Or would you stand silent because you have lived with your pain so long that you no longer believe healing is possible?
Many people stop asking because disappointment taught them to stop expecting.
Yet Bartimaeus teaches us something profound.
Faith keeps calling even when crowds keep criticizing.
Faith keeps believing when circumstances remain unchanged.
Faith keeps crying out when silence seems louder than answers.
The story becomes even more powerful when we notice something remarkable.
Just a few verses earlier, Jesus asked the exact same question to James and John.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
The identical question exposed radically different priorities.
When Jesus asks us what we want, our answer often reveals what truly rules our hearts.
The question is not merely about receiving blessings.
Because the greatest miracle in the story was not eyesight.
Many people can see physically and remain spiritually blind.
The greatest miracle was that Bartimaeus recognized who Jesus truly was.
Bartimaeus saw the Son of David.
The blind man saw more than the sighted crowd.
And perhaps that is the scandalous beauty of grace.
The people society overlooks often recognize Jesus more clearly than those who think they have everything together.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Every one of us is Bartimaeus.
But because mercy heard our cry.
This is why the cross changes everything.
At Calvary, Jesus took the blindness of humanity upon Himself.
The judgment we deserved fell on Him.
The grace we did not deserve flowed to us.
The Gospel is not a story about good people finding God.
It is a story about a holy God stopping for broken people.
This is why no scandal is too great.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The woman at the well carried a broken history.
And perhaps today Jesus is stopping for you.
As you read these words, He asks the same question He asked Bartimaeus.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
The miracle often begins when the mask finally comes off.
And if this message exposed something hidden inside you, be honest.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Through your support, more souls hear about Jesus, more believers are strengthened, and more lives are impacted by biblical truth.
One desperate cry stopped the Savior on the road to Jerusalem—and your cry is not too small for Him to hear today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN DEMONS READ YOUR MIND?
paragraphs: The Question That Keeps Millions Awake at Night
There is a moment almost every believer has experienced but few talk about.
You hate it the moment it appears.
And almost immediately another fear follows:
"Did a demon put that thought there?"
Then a second question emerges, even more disturbing:
"If demons can put thoughts into my mind... can they read my mind too?"
For centuries Christians have wrestled with that question.
Fueled movies, myths, superstitions, and spiritual paranoia.
But what does Scripture actually say?
And the answer is both comforting and deeply sobering.
The Bible never portrays believers as living in a spiritually neutral world.
The apostles warned about spiritual warfare.
The Greek word translated "wrestle" is πάλη (palē).
The Christian life is not a playground.
But the battlefield is not what many people imagine.
The greatest spiritual battles are often invisible.
A sudden urge to give up.
Most demonic warfare occurs not through dramatic possession but through deception.
Not necessarily access to your thoughts.
Only God Searches the Human Heart
One of the clearest biblical truths is that God possesses knowledge no created being possesses.
The hidden center of human existence.
God alone searches that place perfectly.
Likewise, when Solomon dedicated the Temple he prayed:
"You alone know the hearts of all the children of mankind." (1 Kings 8:39)
"You alone know the heart of all humanity."
This theme appears repeatedly throughout Scripture.
The ability to fully know the thoughts, motives, intentions, and inner workings of the human heart belongs uniquely to God.
It is one of His divine attributes.
An attribute demons do not possess.
Demons Are Powerful—but They Are Not Omniscient
One of Satan's greatest victories has been convincing people he possesses abilities that belong only to God.
The Bible never presents Satan as omniscient.
The Greek New Testament repeatedly portrays demonic beings as intelligent observers.
After thousands of years observing humanity, demons understand human behavior extraordinarily well.
Far better than most people understand themselves.
A seasoned poker player can predict another player's hand.
That does not mean he can read minds.
Likewise demons often appear to know what someone is thinking because they have spent years studying human reactions.
What seems supernatural may often be highly informed observation.
The Difference Between Suggestion and Knowledge
One reason people become confused is because Scripture clearly shows demons influencing people.
But influence is not the same thing as mind reading.
"The devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot to betray Him."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Satan read Judas's thoughts.
The same strategy appears in Genesis.
The serpent never reads Eve's mind.
The devil's greatest weapon is rarely raw power.
He wins by convincing people to cooperate with lies.
This is why Scripture repeatedly emphasizes renewing the mind.
Because the battlefield is often fought through competing voices.
This is where many believers desperately need freedom.
An intrusive thought does not automatically reveal demonic possession.
Nor does it prove demonic mind reading.
Sometimes intrusive thoughts arise from stress.
The mere appearance of a thought is not sin.
The issue is not whether a thought appears.
The issue is whether it is embraced.
"You cannot keep birds from flying over your head, but you can keep them from building a nest in your hair."
A passing thought is not ownership.
Many Christians spend years condemned over thoughts they never wanted in the first place.
And that should bring enormous comfort.
The One Place Demons Cannot Enter
There is a reality many believers forget.
The Holy Spirit dwells within God's people.
"Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?" (1 Corinthians 3:16)
The Greek word for temple is ναός (naos).
That does not eliminate spiritual warfare.
But it radically changes the battlefield.
But he does not own what Christ has purchased.
And he does not possess the divine ability to search the secret depths of the redeemed heart.
The Fear That Reveals Something Beautiful
Ironically, many people who fear demons can read their minds reveal something important.
They care deeply about their relationship with God.
The very anxiety often comes from a sincere desire to honor Christ.
But fear can become its own trap.
The enemy loves believers who are obsessed with him.
Because distracted Christians rarely focus on Jesus.
Scripture never commands believers to become experts on demons.
It commands believers to fix their eyes on Christ.
The more you stare at darkness, the larger darkness appears.
The more you stare at Jesus, the smaller darkness becomes.
The New Testament's emphasis is not demon awareness.
Scripture gives us no reason to believe they can.
The Bible consistently reserves perfect knowledge of the human heart for God alone.
But omniscience belongs exclusively to God.
That truth should bring both comfort and conviction.
Comfort because your deepest thoughts are not open territory for demonic invasion.
Conviction because the One who truly knows every thought is not a demon.
The One who knows every secret.
And astonishingly, He loves you anyway.
Not after you clean yourself up.
The question was never whether demons can read your mind.
What will you do with the God who already knows your heart completely and still stretched out His hands on a cross for you?
Maybe that's why this subject feels so personal.
Because beneath every fear of darkness is a deeper longing to know whether we are truly seen.
The Gospel answers with a resounding yes.
The God who knows everything about you is the same God who chose not to walk away from you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WHEELS WITHIN WHEELS
paragraphs:
THE WHEELS WITHIN WHEELS
The Most Misunderstood Vision in the Bible — And Why It Might Explain What God Is Doing When Your Life Makes No Sense
Most people encounter Ezekiel's vision and immediately get lost.
Some see strange prophetic symbolism too mysterious to understand.
And wheels within wheels moving in every direction without turning.
It feels more like a scene from an apocalyptic film than a message from God.
But what if one of the strangest visions in Scripture contains one of the most comforting truths ever given to suffering people?
What if the wheels within wheels are not primarily about mystery?
What if they are about control?
What if God gave this vision to people whose world had completely fallen apart because they desperately needed to know something many believers still struggle to believe today:
God is still reigning when life appears chaotic.
The prophet Ezekiel was not standing in Jerusalem when he received this revelation.
Many wondered if God had abandoned them.
Many wondered if Babylon's gods had defeated Israel's God.
Many wondered if history had slipped out of God's hands.
Not over a place of victory.
The God of Israel was showing His people that His presence was never confined to a building.
He was not trapped inside Jerusalem.
He was not defeated by empires.
He was not limited by geography.
What follows is one of the most breathtaking revelations in all Scripture.
The imagery immediately communicates divine majesty.
Throughout Scripture, storms often accompany God's appearance.
God arrives not as a passive observer but as the sovereign ruler of creation itself.
Then Ezekiel sees four living creatures.
Later Scripture identifies them as cherubim.
These are not cute angelic decorations.
Heavenly attendants associated with the very presence of God.
The lion represented majesty among wild animals.
The ox represented strength among domesticated animals.
The eagle represented supremacy among birds.
The human face represented intelligence and moral responsibility.
Together they portray the fullness of God's created order serving His throne.
Beside each living creature stood a wheel.
The Hebrew phrase is particularly striking.
This design allowed movement in every direction.
"When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went."
God's government is never forced to recalculate.
History does not create problems God must solve.
History unfolds according to purposes God already understands completely.
Then Ezekiel notices another shocking feature.
The wheels are covered with eyes.
"Their rims were tall and awesome, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around."
The New Testament echoes this reality.
The Greek text of Hebrews 4:13 says:
"All things are naked and laid open."
Then Ezekiel's vision reaches its climax.
And seated upon that throne is the likeness of a man.
This is one of the most astonishing moments in the Old Testament.
God reveals Himself in a form anticipating the ultimate revelation of Jesus Christ.
Centuries later, the apostle John would see the glorified Christ seated in heavenly glory.
The One above the wheels is not chaos.
The One above the wheels is not fate.
The One above the wheels is not chance.
The One above the wheels is King.
The Wheels Are Not the Point
This is where many readers get distracted.
People become fascinated with the mechanics.
Yet Ezekiel was never trying to make people obsessed with wheels.
He was trying to make them look above the wheels.
When your life feels like wheels spinning in impossible directions...
One of the greatest comforts in this vision is mobility.
Ancient people often viewed gods as territorial.
Their power was tied to regions.
The wheels reveal a God whose throne chariot moves anywhere He chooses.
And the same remains true today.
There is no hospital room He cannot enter.
No prison cell He cannot reach.
The Gospel Hidden in the Vision
The greatest fulfillment of Ezekiel's vision is ultimately found in Christ.
Humanity looked at the cross and saw apparent chaos.
Yet above every visible wheel turning beneath history sat the throne of God.
The crucifixion was not an accident.
The resurrection was not a recovery plan.
The Gospel was the eternal purpose of God unfolding exactly as He intended.
Acts 2:23 declares that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.
Even the darkest moment in human history remained under divine sovereignty.
Your story may currently look like intersecting wheels moving in directions you do not understand.
You may be standing in your own Babylon.
You may be staring at circumstances that seem impossible to explain.
You may wonder whether God has forgotten.
Ezekiel's vision answers with thunderous clarity.
And above every wheel sits a throne occupied by the King who was crucified, risen, and coming again.
Maybe that is why this vision has survived thousands of years.
Because every generation eventually finds itself standing in Babylon asking the same question:
And every time Ezekiel's wheels answer:
Be honest. Did this vision hit differently after seeing its true meaning?

The wheels never promised you understanding.
The throne promised you a King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN WHO SAVED MOSES BEFORE PHARAOH'S DAUGHTER DID
paragraphs: THE WOMAN WHO SAVED MOSES BEFORE PHARAOH'S DAUGHTER DID
Most people know the dramatic scene. A helpless infant floating among the reeds of the Nile. A compassionate royal daughter discovering him. A child destined to confront kings and split seas.
But long before Pharaoh's daughter ever laid eyes on Moses, another woman stood between him and death.
A woman whose name is often spoken quietly.
A woman whose courage changed the history of redemption.
A woman whose faith protected a deliverer before the world even knew he existed.
And if we are honest, her story feels painfully familiar.
Because there are moments when every believer finds themselves standing where Jochebed stood—trapped between impossible circumstances and impossible promises.
Egypt had become a place of terror for God's covenant people. What began as a season of favor under Joseph had become generations of oppression. Fear ruled the throne.
Pharaoh looked upon the growing Hebrew population and saw not neighbors but threats.
Exodus 1 records one of the most horrifying decrees in Scripture:
"Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river."
This was not merely political oppression.
It was an attack against the covenant promises God had given to Abraham centuries earlier.
The enemy knew something was coming.
The enemy always attacks what God intends to use.
And somewhere in the middle of that national nightmare, a Hebrew woman discovered she was carrying a child.
Imagine feeling life move inside your womb while knowing the government had already signed your son's death warrant.
Imagine hearing stories of babies stolen.
Imagine counting the months until birth while wondering whether your child would survive.
Yet Scripture introduces her with stunning simplicity.
"And the woman conceived, and bare a son: and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months."
The Greek translation of the Old Testament, known as the Septuagint, uses language emphasizing that the child was beautiful and remarkable.
Hebrews 11:23 later explains what was really happening:
"By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents."
The Greek word used here is πίστις (pistis), meaning trust, confidence, and unwavering reliance upon God.
Jochebed looked at circumstances that screamed death and chose to trust a God who promised life.
Faith simply believes God has the final word about reality.
For three months she hid her son.
Every knock on the door could end everything.
Most of the time it looks like surviving another day.
It looks like praying another prayer.
It looks like obeying when your hands are shaking.
It looks like trusting God while your heart is breaking.
Eventually she could hide him no longer.
This is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Exodus says she prepared an ark of bulrushes.
The Hebrew word used is תֵּבָה (tevah).
Remarkably, this exact word appears only one other time in the entire Old Testament.
When judgment covered the earth, God preserved Noah through an ark.
When death threatened Moses, God preserved him through an ark.
The same God who saved Noah was saving Moses.
The same God who preserved the covenant before was preserving it again.
Jochebed coated the basket with pitch.
And carried him toward the Nile.
Try to imagine the weight of those steps.
Every mother understands that some moments break your heart simply because love is involved.
She could no longer protect him herself.
So she entrusted him to the One who could.
That is often the hardest faith of all.
Not trusting God when you still have options.
Trusting God when your options have run out.
Many believers are standing at their own Nile River right now.
And like Jochebed, they are discovering that sometimes faith means placing what you love most into God's hands.
The Nile was supposed to be a place of death.
Instead it became a pathway to destiny.
What the enemy designs as destruction often becomes divine transportation.
The river Pharaoh intended to kill Hebrew sons became the very river that carried Israel's future deliverer into the palace.
God often defeats evil using the very mechanisms evil created.
Then comes the moment everyone remembers.
Her heart is moved with compassion.
And in one of Scripture's most astonishing reversals, Moses' own mother is hired to raise him.
Only God could write a story like that.
The woman who surrendered her son receives him back.
The woman who trusted God is entrusted with the very child she feared losing.
The woman who risked everything watches God do what she never could.
This is not merely a story about motherhood.
It is a story about redemption.
Because Jochebed's story points beyond Moses.
Every great story in Scripture eventually leads us to Christ.
Moses would lead people out of slavery.
Jesus would lead humanity out of sin.
Moses would guide Israel through water.
Jesus would open the way to eternal life.
And just as God preserved Moses to accomplish salvation history, God preserved the line through which the Messiah would eventually come.
Nothing could stop God's redemptive plan.
The Gospel is filled with this same pattern.
What looks like defeat becomes victory.
What looks like scandal becomes grace.
What looks like an ending becomes a beginning.
The cross itself appeared to be history's greatest failure.
Yet three days later the empty tomb revealed what heaven knew all along.
The very instrument of execution became the symbol of salvation.
The place of shame became the place of redemption.
That is why Jochebed's story still matters.
Because every believer eventually discovers that God does some of His greatest work in moments that feel completely out of control.
The Nile was never outside God's sovereignty.
The thing keeping you awake at night is not bigger than the God who carried Moses through the reeds.
The chapter confusing you is not beyond the Author's ability to rewrite.
The wound is not beyond healing.
The failure is not beyond redemption.
The shame is not beyond grace.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You have been staring at a river and calling it the end.
You have been staring at a basket and calling it loss.
You have been staring at uncertainty and calling it fear.
You have been staring at a scandal.
If this story stirred something deep inside you, don't keep it to yourself.
What is the "Nile River" in your life that you are struggling to place into God's hands?
Someone else may find hope through your testimony.

Faithful support helps spread biblical truth, create more Christ-centered resources, and reach people who desperately need the Gospel. If we truly desire to glorify God with what He has entrusted to us, supporting Gospel-centered work and sharing it publicly becomes part of that stewardship.
Because somewhere right now, another Jochebed is praying through tears.
And somewhere right now, God is already moving through the reeds.
The river never had the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Man Who Ran Before the News
paragraphs:
The Man Who Ran Before the News
The Untold Story of the Messenger Running Ahead of Absalom’s News
There are moments in Scripture that seem so small we almost run past them.
Then he disappears from the biblical narrative forever.

Yet hidden inside one brief moment during one of Israel's darkest family tragedies is a lesson that speaks directly into modern hearts obsessed with recognition, platforms, influence, visibility, and applause.
The story unfolds in the shadow of betrayal, rebellion, heartbreak, and a father's shattered soul.
And at the center of it all is a man most Christians have never noticed.
A man who arrived before the news.
And perhaps, without realizing it, a picture of every believer called to carry the message of a King.
The account is found during the rebellion of Absalom against his father, King David.
Absalom was not merely a rebellious son.
He was a son who stole hearts.
"Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." (2 Samuel 15:6)
The Hebrew word used for "stole" is לָקַח (laqach), carrying the sense of taking, seizing, or capturing.
Absalom did not simply gain popularity.
He captured loyalty that belonged to another.
He took hearts that should have remained devoted to the king.
David's own son became his enemy.
The rebellion exploded into civil war.
And David carried a burden few parents can understand.
When the battle finally came, David gave a strange command.
"Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom." (2 Samuel 18:5)
But he wanted mercy even more.
The father still loved the son who had tried to destroy him.
Long before the cross, another shadow of grace was already appearing.
Because this is how God loves rebels.
This is how God loves sinners.
This is how God loves us.
Yet His heart still runs after us.
Someone had to carry news that would simultaneously save a kingdom and break a father's heart.
The first messenger selected was a Cushite servant.
He was entrusted with the truth.
The son of Zadok the priest.
Again and again he pleaded for permission.
"You shall not take the news this day." (2 Samuel 18:20)
Joab understood something many modern believers forget.
Not everyone who wants to carry a message is prepared for the weight of that message.
"Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite." (2 Samuel 18:23)
Yet he did not carry the complete message.
But he carried what David truly needed to hear.
The faster runner was not the fuller messenger.
And suddenly the story becomes painfully relevant.
But heaven has never been impressed by who arrives first.
Heaven cares about who faithfully carries the King's message.
Some believers spend their lives trying to outrun everyone else.
Yet the Kingdom has never been built by the fastest runners.
It has always been built by faithful messengers.
Jesus never commanded His disciples to become famous.
He commanded them to become faithful.
The Greek word translated "faithful" throughout the New Testament is πιστός (pistos).
One who can be trusted with what belongs to another.
That is the heart of biblical success.
One day every earthly platform will disappear.
Every human achievement will be forgotten.
The tragedy of modern Christianity is that many want the influence of Ahimaaz but not the responsibility of carrying truth.
We want to be seen running.
We want people to notice our effort.
We want recognition for our activity.
But the Kingdom is not advanced by appearances.
The most powerful servants of God are often the least visible.
The mother teaching Scripture to her children.
The father quietly leading his family.
The disciple sharing Christ without cameras.
The saint whose name never trends but whose faithfulness shakes eternity.
David's story also reveals another deeper Gospel reality.
When news finally reached him, the victorious king did not celebrate.
The Scripture records one of the most heartbreaking cries in the Bible:
"O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would God I had died for thee." (2 Samuel 18:33)
David wanted to die in Absalom's place.
A human king could wish it.
Only the King of Kings could accomplish it.
David's cry points forward to another King.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ did what David could never do.
The Son of God actually died for rebels.
Actually died for those who stole their hearts away from their rightful King.
The Gospel is not the story of good people finding God.
It is the story of a holy King pursuing rebels who deserve judgment and offering grace through His Son.
The Greek word χάρις (charis), translated "grace," means undeserved favor.
A gift that cannot be purchased.
A blessing that cannot be deserved.
Every believer was once an Absalom.
Every believer stole loyalty from God.
Yet Christ stepped into our place.
The cross became the meeting point of justice and mercy.
The place where scandal became grace.
The place where broken stories were rewritten forever.
That is why this forgotten messenger matters.
Because his story asks a question every believer must answer.
Or are you carrying the King's message?
Those are not always the same thing.
And when eternity finally arrives, nobody will care who ran fastest.
Everyone will care who carried the truth.
The Lord sees every faithful step.
Nothing done for Christ is ever wasted.
Nothing surrendered to Christ is ever lost.
Nothing entrusted to Christ remains unchanged.
Because that is what Jesus does.
He takes rebels and makes them sons.
He takes shame and creates testimony.
He takes ruins and builds redemption.
He takes scandal and turns it into grace.
And He is still rewriting stories today.
If this message stirred something in your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Have you ever felt forgotten while trying to remain faithful to God?
Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs today.
Because one faithful step in obedience may matter more in eternity than a lifetime spent chasing applause.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Eli's Blind Spot
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Eli's Blind Spot
When a faithful man lost what mattered most—not because he stopped serving God, but because he stopped seeing what was happening in his own house.
There are stories in Scripture that comfort us.
There are stories that inspire us.
Then there are stories that quietly dismantle every illusion we've built about ourselves.
The story of Eli belongs to the last category.

Eli spent decades ministering before the LORD. He wore the sacred garments. He knew the sacrifices. He judged Israel for forty years (1 Samuel 4:18). Generations looked to him for wisdom. If anyone appeared spiritually successful, it was Eli.
Yet one sentence exposes the tragedy behind an otherwise honorable life.
At first, it sounds like nothing more than old age.

"...his eyesight had begun to grow dim so that he could not see."
—1 Samuel 3:2

וְעֵינָו הֵחֵלּוּ כֵהוֹת לֹא יוּכַל לִרְאוֹת
ve'enav hechellu kehoth lo yukhal lir'ot
"His eyes had begun to grow dim; he was unable to see."
Certainly, Eli's physical vision was fading.
But the narrative quickly reveals something far more devastating.
His greatest blindness was not in his eyes.
And that is where this story begins to confront every believer.
Because spiritual blindness almost never announces itself.
It quietly settles into familiar routines.
Meanwhile, things that should concern you stop alarming you.
His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, served as priests alongside him.
Exploiting women serving at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (1 Samuel 2:22).
The text describes them with shocking honesty:
Many English translations soften it as "worthless men" or "scoundrels."
It describes people who have become morally bankrupt.
Men who rejected God's authority while pretending to represent Him.
The high priest's own sons were destroying the worship of Israel.
Scripture never says he was unaware.
"My sons, it is not a good report that I hear..."
Parents often confuse warning with correction.
Leaders often confuse conversation with accountability.
Christians often confuse conviction with repentance.
The issue wasn't that Eli lacked affection.
The issue was that he loved peace more than painful obedience.
God's indictment comes through an unnamed prophet.
"Why then do you honor your sons above Me?"
Those words should make every reader stop.
Notice what God did not say.
He didn't accuse Eli of hating God.
He didn't accuse Eli of abandoning ministry.
He didn't accuse Eli of worshipping idols.
Instead, He revealed a hidden hierarchy.
Every heart has something it gives the greatest weight.
Because idolatry doesn't always bow before statues.
Sometimes it smiles across the dinner table.
Sometimes it sits in the living room.
Sometimes it wears the face of someone we love.
Sometimes the greatest rival to God's glory is not evil.
This is why Jesus later says:
"Whoever loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me."
But because family is safest only when Christ remains first.
The consequences spread across an entire nation.
Eli himself collapsed backward after hearing the news.
It had been unfolding for years.
Blind spots rarely destroy lives overnight.
One excuse repeated until it feels normal.
Perhaps that's why the next chapter introduces someone who could actually hear God.
An old priest losing spiritual sensitivity.
A young servant hearing God's whisper.
God wasn't looking for the most experienced.
He was looking for the most responsive.
When the LORD called Samuel, the Hebrew says:
That one word echoes throughout Scripture.
Before God entrusts people with great assignments...
He first looks for surrendered hearts.
Maybe that's the lesson Eli forgot.
Years of ministry can never replace daily surrender.
Every generation must answer God's call with its own "Hineni."
This story is not preserved to shame parents.
Nor is it written merely to criticize leaders.
It exists because every human heart has blind spots.
Others ignore compromise because confronting it feels costly.
Blind spots are called blind because we cannot see them ourselves.
That is why we desperately need Scripture.
But because David understood something we often forget.
The most dangerous sins are usually the ones we no longer recognize.
The Greek New Testament later gives us a similar warning.
Spiritual vision requires continual dependence upon Christ.
The moment we believe we see clearly apart from Him...
And this is where Eli's story becomes our own.
Every believer has moments when serving God becomes easier than listening to God.
When protecting appearances becomes easier than pursuing holiness.
When preserving comfort becomes easier than obeying Christ.
Yet the Gospel interrupts that cycle.
Unlike Eli, Jesus never failed to honor His Father.
Jesus created a new family through grace.
This is why the Gospel is not merely advice.
The cross exposes every blind spot while simultaneously providing forgiveness for those who repent.
Our failures do not have the final word.
That is why our theme remains true:
The greatest miracle is not that God exposes our blindness.
The greatest miracle is that He opens blind eyes.
The Greek word Jesus often uses when healing is:
A life finally able to see reality through God's truth.
Perhaps today the Holy Spirit is gently revealing an area you've ignored.
Grace has never been permission to remain blind.
Grace is God's invitation to finally see.
