They are wondering if God is still working in their own lives.
They are wondering if their mistakes have disqualified them.
They are wondering if their story can still be redeemed.
The answer of Scripture is a resounding yes.
The Gospel is filled with people who should have been forgotten.
Mary Magdalene carried a painful past.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
And that is the heartbeat of Elijah's story.
The whirlwind was not merely transportation.
A declaration that God finishes what He starts.
A reminder that heaven belongs to those whom God redeems.
A picture pointing forward to Jesus Christ, who would conquer sin, death, and the grave for all who believe.
The greatest mystery is not where Elijah went.
The greatest miracle is that sinners like us can be welcomed into God's family through Christ.
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (charis).
Elijah's departure reminds us that salvation has always been God's work from beginning to end.
The same God who carried Elijah is the same God who carries believers today.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
But God still calls people by grace.
Your scandal is not greater than His mercy.
Your failure is not greater than His forgiveness.
Your past is not stronger than His cross.
And your future is not determined by what happened to you but by Who redeemed you.
Have you ever experienced a season where you thought God was finished with you, only to discover He was still working?
Your testimony may become someone else's encouragement.
Most importantly, your support helps expand the reach of the Gospel so more people can encounter biblical truth and the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
One day, every mystery about heaven will be answered, but the greatest answer has already been given at the cross.
The same God who carried Elijah is still carrying those who belong to Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: UNDERSTANDING THE DEEP MEANING OF PSALM 90:12
paragraphs: UNDERSTANDING THE DEEP MEANING OF PSALM 90:12
The Prayer Most People Never Pray
Most people pray for opportunities, breakthroughs, open doors, financial relief, restored relationships, and freedom from pain.
But there is one prayer buried in Scripture that many believers read, few understand, and even fewer genuinely pray.
It is a prayer so dangerous that if God answers it, your priorities will change.
And perhaps most unsettling of all...
"So teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom."
At first glance, the verse appears simple.
But beneath those words is a profound cry that cuts through human pride, self-deception, and the illusion that tomorrow belongs to us.
This is not merely a prayer about counting time.
It is a prayer about learning how to live before it is too late.
Psalm 90 is unique among the Psalms because it is attributed to Moses.
Long before David sang songs of worship, Moses stood between a holy God and a rebellious people.
He watched an entire generation die in the wilderness.
He experienced disappointment, heartbreak, rebellion, and loss.
He understood something most people spend their lives trying to avoid:
"The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years..."
Moses was not obsessed with death.
The Hebrew language reveals something powerful.

The phrase "teach us" comes from the Hebrew root יָדַע (yada) in its instructional sense, involving more than intellectual knowledge. It points toward experiential understanding—knowledge that transforms behavior.
Moses is not asking God for information.
He is asking God for transformation.
"Help me know how many days I have."
"Help me live as if my days matter."
"To number our days, thus make us know."
The word לִמְנוֹת (limnot) comes from the Hebrew verb מנה (manah), meaning:

to count,
to assign,
to reckon,
to appoint,
to evaluate carefully.
Moses is asking God to help him see every day as a divine stewardship.
"What am I doing with the life I've been given?"
Modern culture constantly trains people to live as though death belongs to someone else.
We assume there will always be another opportunity.
But Psalm 90 destroys the illusion of unlimited tomorrows.
James echoes the same truth centuries later:

"What is your life? It is even a vapor, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away."
(James 4:14)
The Greek word translated "vapor" is ἀτμίς (atmis).
The Bible is not trying to depress us.
It is trying to wake us.
Because people who believe they have endless time often waste the little time they actually possess.
The verse does not end with numbering days.
"That we may gain a heart of wisdom."
The Hebrew word for wisdom is:
Chokmah refers to skill in living according to God's design.
A person may have degrees and still lack wisdom.
A person may have wealth and still lack wisdom.
A person may have influence and still lack wisdom.
Wisdom is seeing life from God's perspective and responding accordingly.
The prayer of Psalm 90 is ultimately:
"Lord, help me see life the way You see life."
One of the greatest tragedies in Scripture is how often people squandered God's gifts.
The Samaritan woman carried a scandalous past.
Their stories should have ended differently.
According to human standards, their failures should have defined them forever.
But Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
This is why Psalm 90 is not merely about mortality.
Because every numbered day becomes another opportunity for grace.
The Gospel transforms Psalm 90 from a funeral reflection into an invitation.
Because the Christian does not merely count days.
The Greek phrase ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν (exagorazomenoi ton kairon) literally carries the idea of buying back opportunities.
Making every moment count for eternity.
No one understood numbered days better than Jesus.
Every step toward Jerusalem moved Him closer to the cross.
He lived with complete awareness of His mission.
He perfectly invested every moment in the Father's will.
And then, on the cross, He carried the weight of every wasted day we have ever lived.
And through His resurrection, He offered something astonishing:
Not merely a better use of time.
But eternal life beyond time itself.
This is why the Gospel is the ultimate answer to Psalm 90.
Because numbering our days reveals our need.
The Prayer Most People Never Pray
Many people ask God to lengthen their lives.
Few ask Him to deepen them.
The greatest tragedy is not dying.
The greatest tragedy is reaching the end of life and discovering you never truly lived for what mattered most.
One day every calendar will stop.
Only what was done for the glory of God remains.
So perhaps Psalm 90:12 is not a prayer about death after all.
Perhaps it is a prayer about finally learning how to live.
Maybe today is the day to stop assuming tomorrow is guaranteed.
Maybe today is the day to forgive.
To follow Christ more deeply than ever before.
Maybe today is the day to pray the prayer most people never pray:
"Lord, teach me to number my days."
And if He answers, your life may never look the same again.
If this message stirred something deep within your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What would change in your life if you truly lived as though every day was a gift from God?
One day you will realize life was never measured by how many days you received, but by what you surrendered to Christ within them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHERE YOUR TREASURE LIVES
paragraphs: The quiet idol nobody talks about.
Jesus never said your god would always sit on a carved throne.
He never said idolatry would always look like golden statues, pagan temples, or ancient rituals.
In fact, some of the most dangerous idols wear modern clothes.
Some masquerade as hobbies, entertainment, investments, political loyalties, personal brands, success, comfort, or endless distraction.
The tragedy is that many people who would never bow before a physical idol unknowingly bow before these every day.
Because whatever receives your greatest affection, deepest trust, highest loyalty, and continual sacrifice eventually becomes your god.
And Jesus exposed this reality with frightening clarity.
"For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."
Ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου.
(Hopou gar estin ho thēsauros sou, ekei estai kai hē kardia sou.)
"Where your treasure exists, there your heart will be."
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say your treasure follows your heart.
He said your heart follows your treasure.
Most people believe their money follows their passions.
Jesus says your passions eventually follow your investments.
Your heart migrates toward whatever you continually pour your resources into.
Your money is not merely revealing your heart.
Your attention is not merely exposing your loves.
Your time is not merely measuring your priorities.
The things we repeatedly invest in become the things we cannot imagine living without.
That is why Jesus spoke so frequently about money.
Not because He wanted people's wallets.
And worship always reveals the true god sitting on the throne.
The Hebrew Scriptures understood this long before the New Testament.
The Hebrew word often translated "heart" is לֵב (lev).
But the biblical concept is much deeper than modern emotion.
The lev represents the center of thought, desire, decision-making, affection, loyalty, and will.
The heart in Scripture is not merely where you feel.
It is where your deepest loyalties are anchored.
When God spoke through the prophet Ezekiel, He diagnosed humanity's deepest problem:
"I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh."
Because the problem was never merely external behavior.
Something other than God kept occupying the seat reserved for Him alone.
That truth becomes painfully personal when we examine our own lives.
Look honestly at your last seven days.
What stole your attention the moment you woke up?
What did you run to when anxiety appeared?
Those answers often reveal our true god more clearly than our church attendance.
The rich young ruler discovered this reality face-to-face with Jesus.
Yet when Jesus instructed him to surrender his wealth, everything was exposed.
The issue was never money itself.
Scripture never teaches that wealth is inherently sinful.
Money had become his functional savior.
And when Jesus touched the idol, the man walked away grieving.
Because money had become his god.
"For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil."
The Greek word used is φιλαργυρία (philargyria).
This is why Jesus said something that still unsettles modern readers:
"You cannot serve both God and Mammon."
It represented wealth personified as a master.
Jesus was presenting a stark reality.
The only question is who occupies it.
The human heart was created for worship.
If we do not worship God, we will inevitably worship something else.
And that "something else" always demands sacrifice.
It promises life but leaves emptiness.
It promises freedom but creates bondage.
It promises significance but produces exhaustion.
That is the scandal humanity has lived with since Eden.
We were created to worship God.
Yet we continually hand our hearts to lesser things.
But this is where the Gospel explodes into the story.
Because Christianity is not primarily the story of people finding God.
It is the story of God pursuing idolaters.
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we dismantled every idol.
The cross is where every false god is exposed.
And where every repentant sinner can find freedom.
At Calvary, Christ paid the debt we could never pay.
The idols that enslaved us no longer need to define us.
The chains that controlled us no longer need to rule us.
The shame that haunted us no longer needs to own us.
Because Jesus does not merely forgive sinners.
This is why genuine discipleship is not simply behavior modification.
And when the treasure changes, the heart follows.
People often ask how they can know whether God truly occupies first place in their lives.
Eventually they will lead you directly to your throne.
And if what you find there is not Christ, His invitation remains open.
Because the Gospel is not about perfect people maintaining flawless devotion.
It is about a perfect Savior rescuing imperfect worshipers.
Maybe this article exposed something uncomfortable.
Maybe you recognized a rival god hiding in plain sight.
Do not run from that conviction.
The One who reveals idols is also the One who breaks their power.
The One who exposes hearts is also the One who heals them.
The One who confronts sin is also the One who offers mercy.
And perhaps today is the day your heart finally comes home.
What has God been exposing in your heart lately?
Your testimony may encourage someone who is quietly struggling.
One day every investment will be revealed, and every throne will be occupied by its true king.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Were There Giants After the Flood?
paragraphs:
Why Were There Giants After the Flood?
The Mystery That Shakes Genesis, Challenges Traditions, and Reveals a Greater Story of Grace
They read Genesis, see the Flood destroy the world, and assume every trace of the ancient corruption disappeared beneath the waters.
And suddenly, centuries later, giants are standing in the Promised Land.
If the Flood destroyed everything outside Noah's Ark, why were there giants after the Flood?
Did some of the Nephilim board the Ark?
Or is there something deeper happening in Scripture that many believers have overlooked?
What if the answer is not merely about giants?
What if it is about the relentless war between corruption and redemption...
and the even greater truth that no scandal, no rebellion, and no darkness can stop God's plan to bring salvation through Jesus Christ?
The story begins in one of the most mysterious passages in the entire Bible.
"When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose."
"The Nephilim were on the earth in those days—and also afterward..."
That final phrase is impossible to ignore.
The Bible itself anticipates the question.
The Nephilim existed before the Flood...
and somehow there were giant clans after it.
Its exact meaning is debated, but it is often connected to the root נפל (naphal), meaning "to fall."
Many scholars understand Nephilim as "fallen ones."
Others understand them as mighty warriors or tyrannical giants.
Whatever interpretation one adopts, Scripture presents them as extraordinary figures connected with widespread corruption before the Flood.
The Bible does not provide every detail modern readers wish it did.
But God did not write Scripture to satisfy every curiosity.
He wrote it to reveal Himself.
The first theory people often hear is that some Nephilim somehow survived the Flood physically.
Yet Scripture repeatedly emphasizes the total destruction of the pre-Flood world.
"Every living thing that was on the face of the ground was wiped out."
The language leaves little room for secret survivors.
The biblical record consistently teaches that only Noah, his family, and the animals preserved on the Ark survived.
That is why many biblical scholars reject the idea that pre-Flood Nephilim physically survived.
A second explanation is that similar events occurred again after the Flood.
Those who hold the supernatural interpretation of Genesis 6 suggest that whatever produced the Nephilim before the Flood happened again later.
This view attempts to explain why giant clans appear centuries afterward.
Groups such as the Anakim, Rephaim, Emim, and Zamzummim are described as unusually large people.
Numbers 13:33 records the fearful report of Israel's spies:
The Bible never directly calls the Anakim descendants of pre-Flood Nephilim.
The frightened spies make that connection.
Whether their assessment was completely accurate is another question entirely.

A third explanation, held by many conservative scholars, is that the word Nephilim became a broader term for powerful warriors or giant peoples rather than referring exclusively to the beings of Genesis 6.
In this view, later giants were not survivors of the original Nephilim but distinct groups whose great size reminded people of those ancient legends.
The truth is that Scripture does not settle every detail beyond dispute.
Because when we become obsessed with giants, we can miss the greater story standing directly in front of us.
The giants are not the heroes.
The giants are not even the point.
Genesis says the thoughts of people's hearts were continually evil.
The Flood was not merely judgment.
It was a response to a world consumed by corruption.
"But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD."
The Hebrew word translated favor is:
Noah's story was never ultimately about a boat.
And that pattern continues throughout Scripture.
Yet God keeps writing a different ending.
When Israel encountered giants in Canaan, fear spread through the camp.
Everyone saw the size of the enemy.
Few remembered the size of God.
Then a shepherd boy named David walked onto a battlefield.
But David understood something Goliath did not.
Victory never belonged to the strongest man.
But because the Lord was faithful.
The same pattern reaches its climax at the Cross.
Humanity's greatest giant was never Goliath.
The giant was separation from God.
Every human being eventually stands before those giants.
And that is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
Jesus Christ stepped into humanity's battlefield and confronted the giant none of us could defeat.
At the Cross He carried our sin.
At the empty tomb He conquered death.
What looked like scandal became salvation.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like the end became a new beginning.
That is the heartbeat of Scripture.
The New Testament captures this beautifully.
When Jesus cried from the Cross:
He declared that the debt of sin had been paid in full.
The greatest enemy had been defeated.
And because of that, your story does not have to end where your failures began.
Maybe you came here curious about ancient giants.
But perhaps the real giant standing before you today is something else.
The Gospel declares that Jesus Christ still rewrites stories.
He is still turning scandals into testimonies.
Still turning rebels into sons and daughters.
Still turning broken people into new creations.
That is why our mission exists.
Not merely to answer difficult Bible questions.
But to help people encounter the Savior who stands behind every page of Scripture.
What giant has God helped you overcome?
Your testimony may encourage someone who is struggling in silence right now.
They are helping spread the Gospel.
They are helping place biblical truth into more homes, more devices, more hearts, and more lives.
Because one day, nobody will remember how large the giants were.
But eternity will remember what Jesus Christ did with the people who trusted Him.
The giant is never the final chapter when Christ is holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHO WAS OG, KING OF BASHAN?
paragraphs:
WHO WAS OG, KING OF BASHAN?
The Giant Everyone Feared… and the Forgotten Story That Proves No Scandal, No Giant, and No Past Is Bigger Than Jesus
Some names in Scripture make people stop.
But then there is a name hidden deep inside the pages of the Old Testament that feels almost mysterious.
A man whose reputation was so terrifying that God Himself had to tell Israel not to be afraid before the battle even began.
Yet most believers know almost nothing about him.
Who was Og, King of Bashan?
Why does Scripture mention his enormous bed?
Why did Moses record his defeat so carefully?
And why does his story still matter for every person carrying shame, fear, addiction, failure, regret, or a past they believe can never be overcome?
Because the story of Og is not ultimately about a giant.
It is about a greater King.
It is about the God who specializes in taking impossible situations and rewriting them through His grace.
The first time we encounter Og, he appears as one of the final obstacles standing between God's people and their inheritance.
“Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan: and Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.” (Deuteronomy 3:1)
Israel had already experienced miraculous victories.
And Og himself belonged to a remnant of giants.
“For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of the Rephaim.” (Deuteronomy 3:11)
Throughout the Old Testament, the Rephaim are described as a race of unusually large and powerful people.
Whether every detail of their stature can be measured precisely is debated among scholars, but Scripture leaves no doubt about the central point:
These were individuals whose size and strength inspired fear.
Og represented the last major remnant of that terrifying legacy east of the Jordan.
Not because the threat was imaginary.
But because God had already determined the outcome.
“And the LORD said unto me, Fear him not: for I will deliver him, and all his people, and his land, into thy hand.” (Numbers 21:34)
This is one of the most repeated commands in all Scripture.
Not because giants do not exist.
But because God remains greater than every giant.
That truth reaches far beyond Bashan.
Many people reading this are fighting giants right now.
The giant of a scandal that still haunts your name.
Some have spent years believing those giants are too large to defeat.
The battle itself was surprisingly short in the biblical record.
God delivered Og into Israel's hands.
The obstacle that looked impossible became another testimony of God's faithfulness.
Then Moses includes a detail that has fascinated readers for centuries.
“Behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron; is it not in Rabbah of the children of Ammon? Nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it.” (Deuteronomy 3:11)
The measurements translate to approximately thirteen and a half feet long and six feet wide.
Some scholars argue the measurement reflects the bed itself rather than Og's exact height.
Others suggest it was a royal display object emphasizing his enormous stature.
Either way, Moses was making a point.
Because faith is not pretending problems are small.
Faith is believing God remains bigger.
Biblical courage is not denying reality.
Biblical courage is acknowledging reality while trusting God more.
That is exactly what happened at Bashan.
But there is something even deeper hidden beneath the story.
Throughout Scripture, giant enemies often symbolize humanity's impossible condition.
No human being can defeat those enemies through personal effort.
The Greek word for sin is ἁμαρτία (hamartia).
It literally carries the idea of missing the mark.
Every person carries a story that contains brokenness.
That is where the Gospel enters.
Because Jesus confronted the giant nobody else could defeat.
At the cross, Christ faced sin.
At the cross, Christ faced death.
At the cross, Christ faced the judgment we deserved.
Then three days later, He walked out of the tomb.
The greatest giant in history fell before the greatest King in history.
This is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
Jesus does not merely help people fight giants.
And perhaps that is why Og's story continues to resonate thousands of years later.
Every human heart knows what it feels like to stand before something larger than itself.
Yet the entire Bible points toward one breathtaking reality:
The New Testament word for grace is χάρις (charis).
The kind of mercy that rewrites stories.
The kind of mercy that takes persecutors like Paul and turns them into apostles.
The kind of mercy that takes adulterers, thieves, doubters, addicts, outcasts, failures, and broken people and transforms them into testimonies.
The kind of mercy that takes your story and rewrites it too.
That is the heartbeat of everything we do at Gospel Warrior.
Because every day people arrive carrying giants.
Some arrive carrying wounds they have hidden for years.
Some arrive convinced God could never use them.
And every day we point them to the same answer:
The Savior who still rewrites stories.
The Savior who still turns scandals into testimonies.
What giant are you trusting Jesus to help you overcome?
if God is still writing your story.
if you refuse to give up on your faith.
Your testimony may encourage someone else who feels alone.
Sometimes one share becomes the answer to someone's prayer.
Because the giant was never the end of the story.
The same God who defeated Og.
The same God who raised Jesus from the dead.
The same God who can redeem your past, restore your future, and rewrite your story through His grace.
The giant looked invincible until God stepped onto the battlefield.
The cross looked like defeat until the stone rolled away.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Cain's Real Problem Wasn't Anger
paragraphs:
Cain's Real Problem Wasn't Anger
The First Murder in Human History Began Long Before Cain Raised His Hand
Most people think Cain's story is about anger.
A man gets jealous. His emotions spiral. He loses control. He commits the first murder in human history.
That is how many people remember the story.
But that is not what the text actually reveals.
The real problem was something far more dangerous because it still lives inside human hearts today.
And if left unchecked, it can quietly destroy a soul while convincing the person they are still close to God.
Two brothers stand before the Lord.

"וַיִּשַׁע יְהוָה אֶל־הֶבֶל וְאֶל־מִנְחָתוֹ"
(Vayyisha YHWH el-Hevel ve'el-minchato)
"The LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering."

"וְאֶל־קַיִן וְאֶל־מִנְחָתוֹ לֹא שָׁעָה"
(Ve'el-Qayin ve'el-minchato lo sha'ah)
"But on Cain and his offering He did not look with favor."
God's attention first falls upon the person.
The text does not merely say God rejected Cain's gift.
Because worship is never ultimately about what is in your hands.
It is about what is happening in your heart.
Abel brought the firstborn and the fat portions.
The text intentionally highlights a difference.
The other merely performed for Him.
"By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain."
Cain's problem was not that he became angry.
Cain became angry because something deeper had already taken root.
The moment God exposed his heart, Cain became furious.
Many people can handle being praised.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Have you ever been corrected and immediately become defensive?
Have you ever felt resentment when someone else's obedience was honored?
Have you ever secretly compared yourself to another believer?
Have you ever felt bitterness when God seemed to bless someone else while your prayers remained unanswered?
Then Cain's story is not ancient history.
Genesis 4:6-7 contains one of the most astonishing warnings in all of Scripture.
"If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is contrary to you, but you must rule over it."
Sin is pictured like a predator.
God warns Cain before he sins.
The Lord is not trying to condemn Cain.
He is trying to rescue him.
This is one of the most overlooked displays of God's mercy in the Old Testament.
God still offers a path back.
Because God's first instinct toward sinners is not destruction.
The murder itself happened in a field.
But the real murder happened earlier.
Long before Abel's blood touched the ground, pride, envy, self-righteousness, and rebellion had already poisoned Cain's soul.
Jesus later revealed this same principle.
Sin begins internally before it becomes visible externally.
The outward act simply reveals what was already living within.
After the murder, God asks another question.
The Hebrew word "shomer" means guardian, protector, watcher.
And suddenly the issue becomes even clearer.
The man who would not worship God rightly could no longer love his neighbor rightly.
When our relationship with God breaks down, our relationships with people soon follow.
Then comes one of the most haunting statements in Scripture.
"The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground."
Abel's blood cried out for justice.
But thousands of years later another blood would cry out as well.
Hebrews 12:24 tells us Jesus' blood speaks "a better word than the blood of Abel."
Jesus absorbed justice on behalf of sinners.
This is where Cain's story ultimately points.
Because if we are honest, every one of us carries traces of Cain inside us.
We have all struggled with pride.
We have all offered God half-hearted devotion at times.
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
The Gospel is not the story of good people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of guilty people receiving mercy they could never earn.
The Greek word used in Ephesians 2:8 for grace is "χάρις" (charis).
A gift that cannot be purchased.
A gift that cannot be earned.
A gift that can only be received.
That is why the theme of Scripture is not Cain's failure.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The woman at the well carried a history of broken relationships.
The thief on the cross had wasted his life.
Yet Jesus rewrote every one of those stories.
And He is still doing it today.
Maybe your anger isn't the real problem either.
Maybe beneath the frustration is a wound you never surrendered.
Maybe beneath the bitterness is pride.
Maybe beneath the jealousy is unbelief.
Maybe beneath the exhaustion is a heart trying to carry burdens God never asked you to carry.
The good news is that Jesus does not merely treat symptoms.
He doesn't simply improve broken people.
And that is why no scandal is beyond grace.
No sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
Maybe that realization hit harder than you expected.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
You may need this reminder again when comparison, pride, anger, or discouragement tries to take root.
Because one surrendered heart can reach a family, a family can reach a community, and a community can help carry the Gospel to the world.
The greatest tragedy is not being exposed by God.
The greatest tragedy is refusing the mercy that came looking for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BLESSING YOU IGNORE MAY BE SOMEONE ELSE'S PRAYER
paragraphs: THE BLESSING YOU IGNORE MAY BE SOMEONE ELSE'S PRAYER
There are prayers being whispered tonight that sound nothing like victory.
A mother is praying for food she cannot afford.
A father is praying for another chance after losing everything.
A widow is praying for one more conversation she knows will never come.
A teenager is praying for a friend because loneliness has become louder than hope.
A believer is praying simply to feel God's presence again.
And somewhere in the middle of all those desperate prayers, someone else is complaining about the very blessing being requested from heaven.
That is one of the most sobering realities of the human heart.
We often become blind to miracles through familiarity.
The thing we call ordinary may be the very thing another person would fall to their knees and thank God for.
The Bible sitting unopened on the shelf.
The blessing we ignore may be someone else's prayer.
The tragedy is not merely losing blessings.
The tragedy is forgetting they were blessings at all.
Scripture repeatedly reveals a pattern that stretches from Genesis to Revelation.
Then suddenly they realize what they had only after it is gone.
The ancient Hebrew language captures this beautifully through a word often translated as "remember."
It means far more than simply recalling information.
It carries the idea of actively bringing something before your mind and responding accordingly.
Biblical remembrance is not passive memory.
It is grateful awareness that changes how you live.
God repeatedly called Israel to remember because forgetfulness is one of humanity's oldest spiritual diseases.
In Deuteronomy, as Israel stood on the edge of the Promised Land, Moses warned them about a danger greater than enemies, armies, or famine.
The danger was not that they would suffer.
The danger was that they would prosper and forget.
"Take care lest you forget the LORD your God."
"Guard yourself lest you forget the LORD your God."
Forgetfulness is not portrayed as an accident.
It is presented as a threat that requires vigilance.
Because gratitude does not disappear overnight.
One unanswered prayer at a time.
One social media scroll at a time.
Many people are frustrated with God not because He has been absent, but because they have stopped seeing what He has already provided.
Imagine someone who has prayed for years to walk again.
How valuable would your legs seem to them?
Imagine someone sitting beside a hospital bed begging God for another month with their spouse.
How valuable would your marriage seem to them?
Imagine a believer in a persecuted nation secretly gathering to worship Christ.
How valuable would your church seem to them?
Imagine someone opening an empty refrigerator tonight.
How valuable would your next meal seem to them?
Jesus understood this better than anyone.
One of the most overlooked moments in the Gospels happens before one of His greatest miracles.
Before feeding thousands, Jesus took the small amount available and gave thanks.
The Greek text uses the word:
How different would our lives be if we thanked God for what already exists before asking Him for what does not?
Perhaps some miracles are missed because gratitude never opened our eyes to see them.
The Apostle Paul later echoed this truth.
Writing from prison—not a palace, not a comfortable home, but prison—he said:
Biblical gratitude is not pretending pain does not exist.
It is recognizing that God still exists in the middle of pain.
The Greek word translated "give thanks" is:
It reminds us that God is still writing a story we cannot fully see.
One of the greatest deceptions of modern culture is convincing people that joy lives one blessing away.
But Scripture repeatedly teaches that joy is often hidden inside blessings we already possess.
The enemy of contentment is not scarcity.
The enemy of worship is not suffering.
The enemy of gratitude is not need.
Perhaps that is why Jesus frequently drew attention to things people overlooked.
Because heaven often hides extraordinary grace inside ordinary gifts.
"Every good and perfect gift is from above."
All of them ultimately trace back to the goodness of God.
And perhaps the most overlooked blessing of all is Jesus Himself.
Many people seek God's hand while ignoring God's heart.
They seek provision while overlooking salvation.
They seek comfort while overlooking the cross.
They seek blessings while overlooking the Blesser.
Yet Scripture teaches that the greatest gift heaven ever gave was not wealth, health, success, influence, or comfort.
The Father did not merely send help.
John 3:16 remains astonishing precisely because of its simplicity.
The cross stands as eternal proof that God's love reaches farther than our failures.
At Calvary, the greatest blessing in history was hanging before a world that largely ignored Him.
"He was despised and rejected by men."
The tragedy of humanity has never been merely missing blessings.
It has been overlooking the greatest blessing standing right in front of us.
The One who carried our sin.
The One who offers forgiveness, restoration, reconciliation, and eternal life.
Perhaps today God is not asking what you still lack.
Perhaps He is asking what you have forgotten.
What blessing have you stopped noticing?
What prayer has already been answered that no longer amazes you?
What mercy have you mistaken for entitlement?
Because somewhere tonight, someone is praying for what you already have.
And somewhere in heaven, God is patiently waiting for His children to recognize that some of the greatest miracles in their lives arrived so quietly they forgot they were miracles at all.
Some of the prayers you are waiting on tomorrow are standing quietly in your life today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM ATHALIAH:
paragraphs:
THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM ATHALIAH:
THE WOMAN WHO KILLED HER OWN FAMILY
There are villains in Scripture who shock us.
But there is one woman whose story feels so dark, so disturbing, and so painfully human that many Christians read her name and quickly move on.
A woman who murdered her own family.
And if we rush past her story too quickly, we may miss one of the most terrifying warnings God ever preserved in His Word.
Because Athaliah's story is not ultimately about politics.
It is about what happens when power becomes more important than people.
When a heart becomes so consumed by control that even family becomes disposable.
And if we are honest, that temptation still exists today.
Not in the form of royal assassinations.
Ways that can quietly destroy marriages, friendships, churches, and even our own souls.
Athaliah appears prominently in 2 Kings 11 and 2 Chronicles 22–23.
To understand her story, we must first understand her roots.
She was connected to the wicked house of Ahab and Jezebel.
Scripture repeatedly portrays that dynasty as one of the most corrupt royal families Israel ever produced.
Their influence was not merely political.
The Hebrew Scriptures often use language that reveals the deeper issue beneath outward behavior.
The Hebrew word for wickedness is often רֶשַׁע (resha‘), referring not merely to mistakes but active rebellion against God's ways.
Athaliah inherited a culture where power mattered more than obedience.
And that is where her story takes a horrifying turn.
"When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family."
"She destroyed all the seed of the kingdom."
The phrase "seed of the kingdom" carries enormous weight.
Every potential heir represented a threat to her throne.
So she attempted to erase them.
Because power had become her god.
Hidden away by faithful people who feared God more than they feared a queen.
For six years Athaliah ruled Judah.
Six years where evil looked like it had won.
This is where many believers struggle.
Because sometimes wickedness appears to prosper.
The faithful hide in the shadows while darkness occupies the throne.
But Scripture repeatedly reminds us that God's silence is never God's surrender.
Psalm 37 repeatedly warns believers not to envy evil people who seem successful because their triumph is temporary.
But she sat on borrowed time.
Eventually the priest Jehoiada revealed young Joash.
And suddenly Athaliah realized everything she had built was collapsing.
The woman who stole a kingdom accused others of stealing it.
The woman who murdered heirs accused others of wrongdoing.
The woman who committed betrayal screamed betrayal.
Sin has a remarkable ability to blind us to ourselves.
The Greek language of the New Testament uses the word τύφλωσις (typhlōsis), meaning blindness or hardening.
That is exactly what sin does.
The greatest danger of sin is not that we see ourselves as evil.
The greatest danger is that we often see ourselves as justified.
Athaliah probably believed she had reasons.
That is why repentance is so difficult.
Repentance requires the death of self-deception.
The New Testament word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
Her story became a warning preserved forever in Scripture.
But Athaliah's story is not merely about a wicked queen from long ago.
It asks every reader an uncomfortable question.
What am I willing to sacrifice to protect my idols?
Maybe it is always being right.
Maybe it is winning every argument.
Maybe it is preserving an image.
The human heart has not changed nearly as much as we think.
We may not destroy royal heirs.
But people still destroy relationships for power.
Families still fracture because of pride.
Friendships still die because someone refuses to surrender control.
Churches still split because individuals crave influence more than unity.
Athaliah's spirit still appears wherever power becomes more valuable than love.
And that is why the Gospel is such good news.
Jesus is the exact opposite of Athaliah.
Philippians 2 tells us that Christ, though existing in the form of God, humbled Himself.
The Greek word used is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), often translated "emptied Himself."
The innocent died for the guilty.
Athaliah's story shows us what humanity looks like when power reigns.
Jesus shows us what God looks like when love reigns.
One built her kingdom through death.
The other established His Kingdom through His own death and resurrection.
That is the great divide running through all human history.
Perhaps that is why her story remains so unforgettable.
Because somewhere deep inside, we recognize pieces of ourselves.
The temptation to protect our image.
The instinct to preserve ourselves at any cost.
And the Gospel confronts those impulses with a cross.
The cross declares that life is not found through grasping but through surrender.
Not through taking but through giving.
Not through self-preservation but through self-denial.
Athaliah teaches us what happens when power becomes god.
Jesus teaches us what happens when God becomes King.
One is remembered for taking life.
The other is worshiped because He gave His.
And maybe the most sobering lesson of all is this:
The throne you fight hardest to keep may be the very thing keeping you from Christ.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
The most dangerous throne is often the one nobody else can see—the one hidden inside the human heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LAW ABOUT ROOFS MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER NOTICE
paragraphs: THE LAW ABOUT ROOFS MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER NOTICE
There are verses in Scripture that believers underline, memorize, frame on walls, print on coffee mugs, and quote during life's hardest moments.
Then there are verses we almost step over.
Verses that seem so ordinary that most people never stop long enough to ask why God included them.
This is one of those verses.
It appears in a section of Deuteronomy that many modern readers rush through.
Yet hidden inside this seemingly mundane command is one of the most breathtaking revelations about the heart of God.
"When you build a new house, then you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring bloodguilt upon your house if anyone should fall from it."
At first glance, it sounds like construction advice.
"כִּי תִבְנֶה בַּיִת חָדָשׁ וְעָשִׂיתָ מַעֲקֶה לְגַגֶּךָ"
Ki tivneh bayit chadash, v'asita ma'akeh l'gagekha.
"When you build a new house, you shall make a guardrail for your roof."
Something intentionally designed to stop tragedy before tragedy happens.
God did not wait until someone fell.
He commanded protection before danger appeared.
This is not merely a law about architecture.
It is a revelation about divine love.
Because the God of Scripture is not only concerned with rescuing people after disaster.
He is concerned with preventing disaster whenever possible.
Many ancient homes in Israel had flat roofs.
The roof was part of daily life.
Without protection, one careless step could change everything.
So God required His people to think beyond themselves.
Before anyone stepped onto that roof, the homeowner was already responsible for their safety.
Because throughout Scripture, God's people are repeatedly called to build spiritual parapets.
But because we understand human weakness.
The modern world often celebrates living without boundaries.
Yet Scripture tells a different story.
And a fall can happen faster than anyone imagined.
Long before a crisis emerges, wisdom builds a parapet.
Long before an affair begins, a parapet exists.
Long before addiction develops, a parapet exists.
Long before ministry collapses, a parapet exists.
Long before faith drifts into compromise, a parapet exists.
The world asks how close it can get to the edge.
Wisdom asks how strong the railing should be.
This principle appears throughout the Bible.
In Proverbs, wisdom repeatedly urges preparation before danger arrives.
In the teachings of Jesus, disciples are warned to watch and pray before temptation overtakes them.
In Paul's letters, believers are instructed to flee certain dangers rather than test their strength against them.
Yet there is another layer hidden beneath this law.
"that you may not bring bloodguilt upon your house."
The homeowner was not only responsible for himself.
That truth cuts deeply into modern culture.
Because Christianity has never been merely individual.
The faith of Scripture constantly asks:
Who could be affected by my choices?
Who could be strengthened by my obedience?
Who could be harmed by my negligence?
We often think holiness is private.
God repeatedly shows that holiness has public consequences.
Every believer is called to consider whether those around them are protected or exposed because of their influence.
The Gospel itself reveals the greatest parapet ever built.
Sin had already pushed mankind to the edge.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal a people unable to save themselves.
Every generation proved that fallen humanity could not build a sufficient barrier against sin and death.
Not merely as a moral example.
The Greek New Testament uses the word σωτήρ (sōtēr).
The One who intervenes before destruction has the final word.
At Calvary, Jesus did what no human being could do.
He became the protection we could never construct ourselves.
He built a bridge where humanity faced an uncrossable chasm.
The cross stands as history's greatest declaration that God does not delight in watching people fall.
This is why the Gospel is so powerful.
It is not merely about forgiveness after failure.
It is about a God who loves people enough to provide a way of escape.
Perhaps that is where this ancient law suddenly becomes very personal.
Some readers are standing dangerously close to an edge.
Bitterness that has been growing for years.
The edge often appears harmless before the fall.
That is why God teaches us through a rooftop command hidden in Deuteronomy.
Do not wait for the catastrophe.
And if you have already fallen?
If your story contains scandal, failure, regret, shame, betrayal, addiction, rebellion, divorce, hypocrisy, or years wasted running from God?
Then this ancient law points beyond itself.
Because the God who commanded parapets is also the God who restores the fallen.
But neither does it exaggerate failure beyond the reach of grace.
The cross stands as eternal evidence.
Your worst chapter is not stronger than Christ's redemption.
Your deepest wound is not deeper than His mercy.
Your greatest scandal is not greater than His grace.
The Bible is filled with people who fell.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
And perhaps the reason this forgotten rooftop law still matters today.
Because behind the command stands a God who cares enough to warn us before we fall and loves us enough to restore us when we do.
Maybe more than you realized when you first read a verse about roofs.
How many edges has God been warning you about lately?
What guardrails need to be rebuilt?
What compromises need to be surrendered?
What repentance can no longer be postponed?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because one act of support may help place Gospel truth in front of someone whose eternity hangs in the balance.
The railing on the roof was never really about the roof.
It was always about the heart of the God who refuses to stop reaching for people before—and after—they fall.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Benjamin: Born Through Sorrow, Chosen for Strength
paragraphs:
Benjamin: Born Through Sorrow, Chosen for Strength
The Child Who Entered the World Through Tears—and Became Proof That God Can Rewrite Any Story
There are moments in Scripture that happen so quietly we almost miss them.
Only the painful cries of a dying mother.
A newborn taking his very first breath.
And in the silence between life and death, a name is spoken that would echo through biblical history for thousands of years.
Most people know him simply as the youngest son of Jacob.
Few realize he was born inside one of the greatest emotional tragedies recorded in Genesis.
Even fewer understand why his story still speaks to people carrying invisible wounds today.
Because Benjamin's life began exactly where many people think their own future has ended—in unimaginable sorrow.
Maybe your life began in brokenness.
Maybe your childhood carries memories you wish never happened.
Maybe you've wondered if the pain you've inherited has already determined the rest of your life.
Benjamin's story whispers a different answer.
But because Jesus Christ has always been writing redemption into stories long before the cross ever stood on Calvary.
That is the heartbeat of Scripture.
The account begins in Genesis 35 as Jacob and his family journey toward Ephrath, later known as Bethlehem. Rachel—the beloved wife for whom Jacob had labored fourteen years—goes into difficult labor.
The Hebrew text describes the intensity of the moment with striking realism:
"And it happened as she suffered severe difficulty in giving birth."

The verb קָשָׁה (qāšāh) means to become hard, severe, difficult, or grievous. Scripture does not romanticize suffering. It tells the truth. Childbirth became devastating. Rachel's strength faded with every contraction.
Then the midwife spoke words that every frightened mother longs to hear:
Those words were not empty encouragement.

Throughout Scripture, "Do not fear" repeatedly accompanies God's unfolding purposes. While Rachel would never live to raise Benjamin, the child she delivered would become part of God's covenant story in ways neither she nor Jacob could yet imagine.
But then comes one of the most heartbreaking verses in Genesis.
"As her soul was departing—for she was dying..."
With what little strength remained, Rachel named her son:
Nearly every English Bible translates this as "Son of My Sorrow."
That translation is faithful, but the Hebrew carries even deeper emotional weight.

The word אוֹן ('on) can refer to sorrow, grief, affliction, trouble, or the crushing burden of suffering. Rachel was not simply naming her pain. She was naming the entire emotional atmosphere surrounding the child's birth.
Every time someone would call his name, they would remember the day his mother died.
Imagine growing up carrying a name that constantly reminded everyone of tragedy.
Some people understand that feeling all too well.
Not because of their literal name.
But because labels have followed them their entire lives.
Many people spend decades believing that the worst thing that happened to them is the truest thing about them.
Benjamin never had to keep that name.
Before the identity of sorrow could define his future, his father intervened.
The name is traditionally understood as "Son of the Right Hand."
The phrase joins two Hebrew words:
In biblical thought, the right hand was not merely a direction. It symbolized honor, authority, favor, strength, protection, inheritance, and victory.
The right hand represented the place of dignity.
Jacob refused to let grief become his son's permanent identity.
The child born through death would instead be remembered through promise.
Centuries later, the symbolism becomes even more breathtaking.
The Messiah Himself would be exalted to the right hand of God.

"YHWH says to my Lord:
'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies Your footstool.'"

The New Testament repeatedly identifies Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of this promise. After His death, burial, resurrection, and ascension, He was exalted to the Father's right hand (Acts 2:33; Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 10:12), the supreme place of authority, glory, and honor.
Benjamin's name does not predict Christ directly, but it beautifully foreshadows a biblical pattern: God delights in transforming what begins in suffering into a testimony of His redeeming grace.

That pattern reaches its climax in Jesus Himself. The cross—Rome's instrument of shame—became the means of salvation. The tomb—humanity's symbol of finality—became the place from which eternal life was proclaimed. What appeared to be history's greatest scandal became the greatest display of divine grace.

Benjamin's life continued to reflect this surprising reversal. He became the beloved youngest son of Jacob, deeply cherished by his father. His presence tested the hearts of Joseph's brothers during the famine, revealing repentance where jealousy had once ruled. From Benjamin's tribe came courageous warriors described as exceptionally skilled with bow and sling (1 Chronicles 8:40; 12:2). Israel's first king, Saul, came from this tribe, reminding us that earthly power without wholehearted obedience cannot secure God's favor. Yet God's redemptive purpose for Benjamin's descendants did not end there.

The apostle Paul—formerly Saul of Tarsus—identified himself as "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Philippians 3:5). Once a persecutor of the church, he encountered the risen Christ and became one of the greatest proclaimers of the Gospel. Once again, God rewrote a story marked by violence into one overflowing with grace.

This is the rhythm of redemption woven throughout Scripture. God does not minimize grief, nor does He deny the reality of suffering. Instead, He enters into it, transforms it, and ultimately points us to the One who bore our deepest sorrow. Isaiah foretold the Messiah as "a man of sorrows" (Isaiah 53:3), and Jesus fulfilled that prophecy by taking our sin, shame, and judgment upon Himself. Through His death and resurrection, those who trust in Him receive a new identity—not defined by their wounds, but by His redeeming love.

Perhaps you have spent years believing that your past has the final word. Perhaps you carry labels spoken over you by others, or names you have silently repeated to yourself. Benjamin's story reminds us that the God of Scripture is not bound by the names that pain gives us. In Christ, there is forgiveness for the guilty, hope for the despairing, healing for the broken, and adoption for all who repent and believe the Gospel. He does not erase your history, but He redeems it for His glory.
If this story has stirred something in your heart, don't keep it to yourself.

I'd also love to hear from you. If this message encouraged you to trust Him more deeply, comment, "Jesus is rewriting my story." Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
One surrendered life can become the beginning of countless redeemed stories.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN HEAVEN WAITED TO OPEN THE SCROLL
paragraphs:
WHEN HEAVEN WAITED TO OPEN THE SCROLL
The Moment That Changed Eternity: God's Perfect Timing, Humanity's Greatest Need, and Why Jesus Alone Was Worthy
There are moments in life that feel unbearable because nothing seems to happen.
You ask God for direction and hear only silence.
You beg for healing and see no immediate change.
You plead for justice and evil appears to keep winning.
In those moments, many people quietly wonder:
What if the greatest acts of God have always depended on perfect timing rather than immediate action?
What if Heaven's delays are never signs of neglect but evidence of divine precision?
There is a scene in Scripture that reveals this truth with breathtaking clarity.
A scene so emotional that even Heaven itself seemed suspended in anticipation.
A scene where the future of creation appeared to hang in the balance.
A scene where one man began to weep because no one could move God's plan forward.
The Apostle John was given a vision unlike anything humanity had ever seen.
In Revelation 5, he stood before the throne of God and saw a scroll in the right hand of the One seated upon the throne.
A scroll, a legal document, a decree.
It represented God's sovereign plan for judgment, redemption, restoration, and the final reclaiming of all creation.
"Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?" (Revelation 5:2)
Meaning deserving, qualified, possessing the rightful authority.
Every human who had ever lived.
"No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look into it." (Revelation 5:3)
The Greek phrase carries the force of deep, uncontrollable sobbing.
John was not shedding polite tears.
Because if no one could open the scroll, history would remain unresolved.
Have you ever felt that way?
As if your own story might never be resolved?
As if the broken pieces will never fit together?
As if the chapter you're trapped in will become your permanent reality?
John's tears speak for every wounded heart that has ever wondered whether redemption will ever arrive.
The delay was never the end of the story.
"Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered."
A title rooted in Genesis 49:10 where Jacob prophesied over Judah.
John turns expecting to see a conquering Lion.
"A Lamb standing, as though it had been slain." (Revelation 5:6)
But death no longer had authority.
This is the Gospel in a single image.
Jesus conquered not by taking life.
He conquered by giving His life.
He won not through domination but through sacrifice.
He defeated sin by bearing sin.
He defeated death by entering death.
He defeated Satan by crushing the power of accusation through His blood.
This is why only Jesus was worthy.
Because only Jesus was fully God.
Only Jesus fulfilled the Law perfectly.
Only Jesus could become the substitute humanity desperately needed.
Only Jesus could satisfy both justice and mercy simultaneously.
The scroll could not be opened before the cross.
The timing had to be perfect.
"But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth His Son." (Galatians 4:4)
The phrase "fullness of time" comes from the Greek:
The complete, appointed, divinely determined moment.
The cross happened at the exact moment ordained by God.
The resurrection happened at the exact moment ordained by God.
The ascension happened at the exact moment ordained by God.
The opening of the scroll happened at the exact moment ordained by God.
God's timing has never been accidental.
And neither is His timing in your life.
Many people assume delay means denial.
Even Heaven waited for the moment when the Lamb would step forward and take the scroll.
Perhaps the greatest danger is not that God is late.
Perhaps the greatest danger is assuming we know better than God when events should happen.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal God's sovereignty over time.
"He has made everything beautiful in its time."
The Hebrew word for time here is:
Not merely a point on a calendar.
A purpose-filled appointment established by God Himself.
When Jesus took the scroll, Heaven erupted.
Because redemption was moving forward exactly as God intended.
Maybe someone reading this feels trapped inside a chapter that makes no sense.
Praying for answers that seem painfully delayed.
Remember Heaven's silence before the Lamb stepped forward.
Remember that what looked hopeless for a moment became one of the greatest revelations of God's glory.
God's clock has never been broken.
The same Jesus who opened the scroll is still directing history today.
The same Lamb who was slain is still reigning.
The same Savior who redeemed creation is still redeeming lives.
Maybe this is why your story is not finished.
Because the Author is still writing.
Because Jesus has never abandoned the pages that seem unfinished.
If this message stirred your heart, don't let it stop with you.
What promise are you still trusting God to fulfill?
Your testimony may become someone else's encouragement.
One day you may discover that the delay you feared was actually the mercy that prepared you for God's greater purpose.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why God Waited Four Days for Lazarus
paragraphs:
Why God Waited Four Days for Lazarus
The Delay That Felt Like Abandonment Became the Miracle That Changed Everything
Have you ever prayed with all your heart... and heaven stayed silent?
But long enough for hope to start dying.
Long enough for tears to become exhaustion.
Long enough for you to wonder if God even heard you at all.
That is exactly where the story of Lazarus begins.
It begins with a family that loved Jesus deeply and could not understand why He was not coming.
The Gospel of John tells us:
"Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus." (John 11:5)
"So, when He heard that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was two more days." (John 11:6)
John uses the word ἀγαπάω (agapaō) for Jesus' love—a deep, covenantal, self-giving love.
In other words, Jesus delayed not because He lacked love.
He delayed because He loved them.
Because we often assume God's love means immediate rescue.
But Scripture repeatedly shows something different.
Sometimes God's deepest love appears in the form of a painful delay.
Mary and Martha knew Jesus could heal.
They believed His power was sufficient.
Can you imagine the conversations inside that house?
Can you imagine looking down the road every few minutes hoping to see Him arrive?
Some readers know exactly what that feels like.
But John carefully tells us something important.
When Jesus finally arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days.
Why wait until all hope appeared completely gone?
To understand the answer, we need to understand something from the Jewish culture of that time.
While this was not biblical doctrine, many Jews held a traditional belief that a person's spirit lingered near the body for three days after death before finally departing.
By the fourth day, death was considered unquestionably irreversible.
The body had already begun decomposing.
"Lord, by this time there is a bad odor, for he has been there four days." (John 11:39)
Scripture does not sanitize the moment.
This was not a recently deceased man.
This was not a near-death experience.
This was not someone merely unconscious.
The situation was beyond human repair.
Exactly where God often does His greatest work.
Because Jesus was never trying merely to heal Lazarus.
He was revealing who He truly is.
Standing before a grieving Martha, Jesus makes one of the most powerful declarations in all Scripture:

ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
(Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē)
"I am the resurrection and the life." (John 11:25)
Resurrection is not merely something Jesus does.
The Son of God stands before the grave.
The shortest verse in the Bible contains one of the deepest revelations of God's heart.
Jesus already knew Lazarus would walk out of that tomb.
He knew the miracle was moments away.
Yet He still entered their pain.
Because God does not stand distant from human suffering.
The cross would prove that forever.
Then came the moment that changed history.
Jesus stood before the tomb and cried out:
A man who had been dead four days walked out alive.
And that is where this story becomes intensely personal.
Many people reading this are standing in front of their own "four-day tomb."
Mary and Martha likely thought the same thing.
But God's delays are not God's denials.
The God who waited four days was not absent.
He was preparing a greater revelation.
Because if Jesus had arrived immediately, He would have been known as a healer.
By arriving after four days, He revealed Himself as Lord over death itself.
The delay became part of the miracle.
The waiting became part of the testimony.
The heartbreak became part of the glory.
Jesus had already explained this earlier:
"This sickness will not end in death. It is for the glory of God." (John 11:4)
The Greek word for glory is:
Meaning splendor, honor, divine majesty revealed.
What looked like disaster was actually becoming a stage upon which God's glory would be displayed.
And perhaps that is exactly what is happening in your story right now.
The chapter that feels abandoned may actually be preparation.
Because Jesus specializes in situations that look impossible.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel itself.
Through His death and resurrection, He called dead sinners into eternal life.
The story of Lazarus is ultimately a preview of something even greater.
It points to Christ's own death.
And the salvation He offers every person willing to trust Him.
This is why our theme is more than a slogan.
If this message stirred something inside you, don't keep it to yourself.
Someone you know is standing in front of a four-day tomb right now.
Someone believes their story is finished.
Not because we are building a platform.
But because together we are advancing Gospel-centered discipleship, biblical truth, and the message of Jesus Christ to people who desperately need hope.
Have you been waiting on God longer than you expected?
The grave thought it had the final chapter, but Jesus was only turning the page.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID LUCIFER FALL DESPITE BEING CLOSE TO GLORY?
paragraphs: WHY DID LUCIFER FALL DESPITE BEING CLOSE TO GLORY?
The Tragedy That Still Echoes Through Every Human Heart
There is a question that has haunted theologians, pastors, scholars, and ordinary believers for centuries.
How can someone stand so close to the glory of God and still fall?
The one Scripture describes with language so breathtaking that generations have struggled to comprehend it.
If a being created in beauty, wisdom, splendor, and heavenly privilege could fall, what does that reveal about pride, worship, and the human heart?
What does it reveal about us?
Because the story of Lucifer is not merely about an ancient rebellion.
A prophecy written into every soul that has ever wrestled with self-exaltation.
The fall of Lucifer is not merely history.
The primary biblical passages associated with Lucifer's fall are Isaiah 14:12-15 and Ezekiel 28:11-19.

While these passages directly address earthly kings, many scholars throughout church history have recognized language that appears to extend beyond human rulers and points toward a deeper spiritual reality.
"How you have fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!" (Isaiah 14:12, KJV)
The name does not originally mean "devil."
A being associated with extraordinary glory.
Ezekiel's description becomes even more astonishing:
"You were the seal of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty." (Ezekiel 28:12)
חוֹתֵם תָּכְנִית מָלֵא חָכְמָה וּכְלִיל יֹפִי
Chotem tachnit male chokhmah u'kelil yofi
"The completed pattern, full of wisdom and complete in beauty."
Created perfection within God's intended design.
Lucifer was not ugly before he became evil.
His fall did not begin with weakness.
That is what makes the story so terrifying.
Many people assume their greatest danger is their weakness.
Often our greatest danger is our strength.
Ezekiel reveals the fatal turning point.
"Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty." (Ezekiel 28:17)
"Your heart became proud because of your beauty."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say beauty was sinful.
The problem was not the gift.
The problem was forgetting the Giver.
Pride begins the moment we start admiring ourselves more than the God who created us.
"I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation."
"I will ascend above the heights of the clouds."
"I will be like the Most High."
In Hebrew, the repeated phrase is:
Sin at its deepest level is not merely breaking rules.
Sin is attempting to occupy a place that belongs to God alone.
Lucifer's rebellion was ultimately worship directed at self.
And that same temptation has followed humanity ever since Eden.
The First Sin Was Not Murder
Many people think humanity's greatest problem is violence.
The first cosmic sin was pride.
The belief that we can become our own god.
The serpent's temptation in Genesis echoes Lucifer's ambition.
The lie had already destroyed heaven before it entered Eden.
The same poison simply changed locations.
Many believers have heard Lucifer described as heaven's worship leader.
The Bible does not explicitly use those exact words.
However, Ezekiel 28:13 contains difficult Hebrew language connected to craftsmanship, settings, and musical terminology.
Some translations suggest musical instruments or artistic adornments.
Because of the complexity of the Hebrew text, faithful scholars differ regarding the precise meaning.
What can be stated confidently is that Lucifer was associated with extraordinary beauty, magnificence, and privilege before his fall.
The danger for every worshipper is clear.
You can stand near worship without actually worshipping.
You can sing about God while secretly exalting yourself.
You can serve in ministry while slowly building your own kingdom.
You can be surrounded by holy things and still develop an unholy heart.
Proximity to glory is not the same thing as surrender to glory.
That truth should humble every pastor, worship leader, teacher, influencer, author, and ministry builder alive today.
Lucifer did not fall because God failed him.
He fell because he became impressed with himself.
The tragedy is not merely that he lost heaven.
The tragedy is that he exchanged infinite glory for self-glory.
Every act of pride repeats that exchange.
Every moment of self-exaltation echoes that ancient rebellion.
Every refusal to surrender whispers the same words:
Yet the Gospel introduces a completely different voice.
"Not My will, but Yours, be done." (Luke 22:42)
While Lucifer grasped for a throne.
The kingdom of darkness climbs upward through pride.
The kingdom of God kneels downward through humility.
Lucifer attempted to rise and was cast down.
Jesus willingly descended and was highly exalted.
The story of Lucifer is not ultimately about an angel.
Every human being eventually chooses a throne.
Either God remains at the center.
The question is not whether we worship.
The question is what we worship.
And perhaps the most dangerous idols are the ones staring back at us from the mirror.
Maybe that is why this ancient story still feels so personal.
Because every believer knows the battle.
The temptation to make life about ourselves instead of Christ.
Lucifer's fall reminds us that closeness to glory does not guarantee safety.
And maybe someone reading this needed that reminder today.
You can know Scripture and still drift.
You can serve in ministry and still drift.
You can be gifted and still drift.
The safest place in the universe is not close to power.
It is low at the feet of Christ.
Maybe that's why heaven is filled with worship and not mirrors.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
The devil lost heaven because he wanted God's throne. The redeemed inherit heaven because they wanted God's heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Are You Afraid?
paragraphs:
Why Are You Afraid?
The Question That Exposed the Storm Inside the Disciples—and the Storm Inside Us
Yet the most shocking part of the story was not the storm.
It was the question Jesus asked afterward.
For many people, that question almost feels unfair.

After all, the disciples were not imagining things. They were not overreacting. They were not creating drama. They were trapped in a violent storm on the Sea of Galilee. Experienced fishermen believed they were about to die.
But Jesus asked the question anyway.
And perhaps that is because His question was never really about the storm around them.
It was about the storm within them.
The account appears in multiple Gospel narratives, but Matthew records it with striking clarity:
"Then He arose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. But He said to them, 'Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?'" (Matthew 8:26).
The Greek text preserves the force of Jesus' words:
"Τί δειλοί ἐστε, ὀλιγόπιστοι;" (Ti deiloi este, oligopistoi?)
"Why are you cowardly, you of little faith?"
The word "δειλοί" (deiloi) is stronger than simple nervousness. It describes a fear that overwhelms trust. A fear that forgets who is present.
Jesus was not condemning human emotion.
Scripture never teaches that fear itself is sin.
Again and again, God's people experienced fear.
Even in Gethsemane, Jesus experienced deep anguish.
The issue was not that the disciples felt afraid.
The issue was that they allowed fear to become larger than the One who was in the boat with them.
That is why this story still pierces the human heart thousands of years later.
Because most of us are not drowning in Galilee.
Some are drowning in regret over sins they cannot seem to forget.
Some are drowning in shame from scandals they hope nobody ever discovers.
Some are drowning in questions they cannot answer.
Some are drowning in prayers that seem unanswered.
And when the waves keep crashing, we often ask the same question the disciples asked:
But the Gospel reveals something astonishing.
Before the disciples ever questioned Jesus, Jesus already knew the storm was coming.
He intentionally allowed them to experience what appeared to be impossible circumstances.
Jesus saw an opportunity to reveal His glory.
That truth becomes even more powerful when viewed through the Hebrew understanding of faith.
The Hebrew word often associated with faith is "אֱמוּנָה" (emunah).
Emunah is not merely believing that God exists.
A settled confidence in God's character even when circumstances appear contradictory.
The disciples believed Jesus could perform miracles.
But at that moment they struggled to trust Him while the storm was still raging.
And if we are honest, so do we.
We trust God when the diagnosis is negative.
Can we trust Him when the diagnosis is positive?
We trust God when money is abundant.
Can we trust Him when the account is nearly empty?
We trust God when relationships are flourishing.
Can we trust Him when hearts are breaking?
This is where the story stops being about fishermen and becomes about us.
Because every believer eventually discovers that faith is easy in calm waters.
And yet the most beautiful detail in the entire account is often overlooked.
He slept because He possessed perfect confidence in His Father's sovereignty.
The storm that terrified the disciples never threatened the peace of Christ.
The same storm that convinced the disciples they were dying failed to disturb the rest of Jesus.
What if the peace we desperately seek is not found in the absence of storms?
What if true peace is found in the presence of Christ?
The Gospel repeatedly points us toward that reality.
The world's definition of peace is the removal of problems.
The biblical definition of peace is the presence of God.
The Hebrew word "שָׁלוֹם" (shalom) means far more than the absence of conflict.
The disciples wanted the storm removed.
And that is often how God works in our lives.
The storm you wish would disappear may be the very place where God intends to reveal Himself most clearly.
Not because He enjoys your suffering.
Not because He delights in pain.
But because He loves you too much to leave your faith shallow.
The darkest day in human history became the greatest demonstration of divine love.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like tragedy became redemption.
What looked like scandal became grace.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
From Eden to Calvary to the empty tomb, God has been rewriting impossible stories.
Peter the failure became Peter the preacher.
Paul the persecutor became Paul the apostle.
The woman caught in adultery received mercy.
The thief on the cross received paradise.
Perhaps that is why His question remains so powerful.
But because the One asking the question is the same One who conquered death.
The One who commands the wind.
The One who commands the sea.
The One who carries scars that purchased our redemption.
"Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." (Matthew 28:20)
If Christ is in the boat, the storm does not get the final word.
Maybe today your greatest fear is not financial.
Maybe your deepest fear is that your failures have disqualified you from God's love.
If so, hear the Gospel clearly.
Your sin is not greater than His grace.
Your shame is not greater than His mercy.
Your past is not greater than His redemption.
Your scandal is not greater than His power to rewrite your story.
That is why He rose again.
And that is why His question still echoes through every generation:
Because when Jesus is present, fear no longer gets to sit on the throne.
If this message stirred your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What storm has God been teaching you through lately?
Your testimony may become someone else's lifeline.
Together, we can reach more hearts with biblical truth, grace, hope, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
One day you will realize the storm was never sent to destroy you—it was the place where you finally saw who was in the boat.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Detail in Noah’s Ark Most People Miss
paragraphs: The Detail in Noah’s Ark Most People Miss
The rain had not fallen yet.
That detail alone should stop us.
Most people imagine Noah hammering away beneath dark clouds while neighbors mocked him as thunder rumbled in the distance. But Scripture paints a far more uncomfortable picture.
And one man who believed Him.
Thousands of years later, we still talk about the size of the Ark, the animals, the floodwaters, and the rainbow. Yet one of the most astonishing details in the entire account is often overlooked.
It is a detail so small many readers pass over it.
Yet hidden inside it is one of the most powerful pictures of salvation in all of Scripture.
And once you see it, you may never read the story of Noah the same way again.
The account begins in Genesis 6, where humanity had descended into shocking corruption.
Genesis is not describing isolated sins.
It is describing a civilization rotting from the inside out.
Humanity was not merely making mistakes.
Yet in the middle of a collapsing world, one sentence changes everything.

"But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD."
(Genesis 6:8)
It means favor, kindness, undeserved acceptance.
Noah was not saved because he built an Ark.
He built the Ark because he had already found grace.
And grace still comes before every act of genuine faith today.
This is where the story becomes intensely personal.
Most of us know what it feels like to live in a world that seems increasingly confused.
Many know what it feels like to carry regrets, failures, hidden wounds, secret sins, broken relationships, or seasons of rebellion.
The flood narrative is not merely about ancient judgment.
It is about the human condition.
The world before the flood is not nearly as distant as we would like to think.
Yet buried in God's instructions for the Ark is the detail most readers miss.
"And the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof."
God could have instructed Noah to construct countless access points.
The significance becomes even more stunning when we discover who closed it.
Noah did not close the door.
Salvation was God's work from beginning to end.
That single detail echoes throughout the entire Bible.
Centuries later, Jesus would make a statement that shocked His listeners.

"ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα"
(Egō eimi hē thyra)
If God had not provided a door, nobody would survive.
The scandal of Scripture is not that there was one way.
The scandal is that there was any way at all.
Because every person aboard that Ark was a sinner.
Every one of them needed grace.
Every one of them depended entirely upon God's mercy.
The Ark itself points directly to Christ.
Notice what God told Noah to do.
"Pitch it within and without with pitch."
The Hebrew word for pitch is:
This is where things become extraordinary.
